Recommendation/Observation  
13. Land acquisition is a major problem due to land scarcity and huge capital 
requirement. The Committee feels that there are many regional airports which can be 
developed by States on their own or in collaboration with the Airports Authority of India 
(AAI) and that the State Governments should explore the setting up of “no-frill airports”. 
(Para 20.3) 
Reply of the Ministry 
13.1 Government of India (GoI) has formulated a Greenfield Airports (G FA) Policy, 2008 
which provides guidelines, procedure and conditions for establishment of new Greenfield 
Airports in the country. As per Policy, an airport developer, including the State Government, 
willing to establish an airport is required to send a pro posal to the Ministry of Civil Aviation 
(MoCA). There is a 2-stage process for approval of the proposal i.e., 'Site Clearance' and 'In -
Principle' approval stage. In accordance with this policy, MoCA receives proposals from the 
State Governments or Airport Developers from time to time for establishment of airports. 
After due examination, the approval for development of a new Greenfield Airport is granted. 
The responsibility of implementation of airport project including funding of the project rests 
with the concerned airport developer. Generally, land for airport projects is provided by 
concerned State Government/ Union Territory (UT) Administration to AAI free of cost and 
free from all encumbrances. As per the AAI Act, in case a State Government wishes to 
facilitate setting up of the airport, it could provide the following incentives to an Airport 
Company: 
(a) land, concessional or otherwise; 

24 
 
(b) real estate development rights in and around the airports; 
(c) airport connectivity; rail, road; 
(d) fiscal incentives by way of exemptions from State taxes; and 
(e) any other assistance that the State Government deem fit. State Governments may 
evolve their respective policies for providing any or all of the aforesaid incentives to an 
Airport Company. If the sel ection of a private entity or JVC partner is to be made by the 
State Government or its entity it shall be done through open competitive bidding. While 
granting land and other benefits, the State Government may, if it deems fit, stipulate the 
rights and obl igations of the Airport Company as conditions of such grant. State 
Governments can also provide land to AAI for development of greenfield airports through 
concessions to be granted to private entities in accordance with the provisions of the AAI 
Act. State s may also provide any of the above concessions to AAI for facilitating the 
development of airports in their respective States. 
Recommendation/Observation  
14. The Committee understands that major airports find it difficult to allocate slots to 
regional airlines, which mostly fly turboprop aircraft that take longer to land and take off. 
This forces some of the regional airlines to depend on larger aircraft, which do not have 
adequate demand. The Committee is of the view that if the States tie up with the to urism 
boards and other tourism stakeholders and formulate packages in order to market potential 
tourist destinations under the RCS scheme, it would attract more passengers, thereby, 
enhancing the demand for air travel. 
(Para 20.4) 
Reply of the Ministry 
14.1 RCS-UDAN is market driven scheme. Interested airlines depending upon their 
assessment of demand on a particular route submit proposal at the time of bidding under 
UDAN. MoCA has been working in association with the Ministry of Tourism  (MoT) and 
offered t ourist destinations suggested by MoT under UDAN for bidding. To facilitate the 
allied sector of tourism, RCS -UDAN introduced the concept of Tourism RCS routes in 
collaboration with Ministry of Tourism. These were routes connecting airports in line with 
the aspirations of MoT to boost tourism and connect iconic tourist destinations. So far, 48

been operationalized. Prominent tourist destinations viz. Dimapur, Agra, Bhopal, Bengaluru, 
Mysuru, Amritsar, Jaipur, Kolkata, Patna, Bhubaneswar, Varanasi, Rajamundri,

interacting with the MoT, tour operators and other stakeholders to promote tourism

requested to communicate to all the airlines/airports for extending necessary facilitation in the 
event of cancellation/delay of flights, as per CAR. Accordingly, DGCA also sensitized to 
airlines & airports. A copy of MoCA’s communication to DGCA is attached at Annexure C. 
Further Recommendation/ Observation 
16.2  The Committee notes with appreciation that based on the directions of the 
Committee, the Ministry has issued guidelines to all airlines/ airports to extend facilities 
to passengers in case of cancellation or delay of flights. The Committee would like to be 
apprised of the ground level implementation of the Ministry’s orders and the number of 
airports and airlines which have implemented it and the details of facilities extended 
and the number of  passengers who have availed the facilities, airport-wise and airlines-
wise.  
 
 
Making Airports Accessible to all under the ‘Accessible India Campaign’ 
Recommendation/Observation  
17. The Committee appreciates the sensitivity and empathy s hown by the Ministry, 
towards the genuine needs and concerns of the differently abled people. The Committee 
hopes that the Ministry will be able to fulfill the objective of the campaign to ensure a barrier 
free and conducive travel environment for differently abled people. 
 (Para 41.2) 
Reply of the Ministry 
17.1 Noted. As per RPwD Act 2016, accessibility standards/guidelines are required to be 
notified by Ministry of Civil Aviation. In this regard, ‘Accessibility Standards and Guidelines 
for Civil Aviation’ containing all the details on Accessible Airport Infrastr ucture has been 

57 
 
prepared and placed in public domain for comments/suggestion by stakeholders after due 
consultation with Chief Commissioner of Persons with Disability (CCPD). Recently, 
comments/suggestions from stakeholders have been deliberated and final guidelines are 
expected by year end. Accessibility data for 67 airports has already been uploaded on the 
MIS portal of AIC and data of other airports is being uploaded. Further, AAI has initiated the 
procurement process of Ambulifts at 20 Airports having C ode C or above Aircraft Operation 
wherein aerobridge facility is not available to ensure seamless transfer of Divyang 
passengers. The work order has been awarded for procurement of 20 Ambulift on 
19.02.2021. Ambulifts for two locations (Dehradun & Gorakhpu r Airports) have been 
installed and at remaining 18 are likely to be completed by March, 2022. 
Further Recommendation/ Observation 
17.2  The Committee notes that ‘Accessibility Standards and Guidelines for Civil 
Aviation’ containing all the details on Accessible Airport Infrastructure has been 
prepared and placed in public domain for comments/suggestion by stakeholders after 
due consultation with Chief Commissioner of  Persons with Disability (CCPD) and that 
comments/suggestions from stakeholders have been deliberated and final guidelines are 
expected by year end. The Committee desires to know the present status of issues of 
guidelines for a ssisting the differently abled people and the timeline set for its 
implementation at all airports.  
 
Inefficiency of hangars 
Recommendation/Observation  
18. The Committee is of the considered view that since the Ministry is taking 
commendable steps to ensure air connectivity to remote areas also, it is an essential corollary 
that well equipped hangars are also built in such places, in order to ensure proper and time 
efficient maintenance of aircrafts and helicopters. 
 (Para 48.1)  
Reply of the Ministry 
18.1 Noted. 
Further Recommendation/ Observation 
18.2  The Committee desires to know the plans of the Ministry to build well equipped 
hangars at remote places.   
 
 
 
 

58 
 
 
 
CHAPTER-IV 
 
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS IN RESPECT OF WHICH THE FINAL 
REPLIES OF THE MINISTRY ARE STILL AWAITED 
 
 
 
-N i l - 
 
**** 
 
 
  

59 
 
RECOMMENDATIONS/ OBSERVATIONS AT A GLANCE 
CHAPTER-III 
 
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS IN RESPECT OF WHICH REPLIES OF 
THE MINISTRY HAVE NOT BEEN ACCEPTED BY THE COMMITTEE 
 
Airport Infrastructure  
 
The Committee notes that in its reply, the Ministry has only enumerated the provisions of 
the Greenfield Airport Policy, NCAP 2016 and the sources of revenue. However, the 
Ministry has not spelt out the actual airport amenities, infrastructure or plans or land 
allocation for setting up hotels. The Committee desires complete and full details of all 
such actual infrastructure created by the Ministry at all new airports. It also desires to 
know whether plans are made in advance to include such amenities & infr astructure 
during the construction stage of airports.  
(Para 1.2) 
Regional Connectivity Scheme  
 
The Committee notes with dismay that out of 948 valid routes for RCS -UDAN Scheme, 
only 403 routes have been operationalized after elapse of 5 years, since the launch of 
scheme in October, 2016. The Committee also notes that an extension of benefits has been 
granted for a period of one year only to routes completing three years tenure. The 
Committee feels that helping hand should be given to the fledging RCS -UDAN routes 
considering the low number of operationalized routes and adverse impact of Covid -19 
pandemic, which has resulted in lower passenger traffic and therefore, strongly reiterates 
its recommendation that benefits should be extended by another two years,  instead of one 
year as granted by Ministry now. 
(Para 2.3) 
Development, Upgradation and Modernization of Airports 
 
The Committee expresses satisfaction that out of 48 Tourism RCS routes, 31 have been 
operationalized. The Committee desires to know the effo rts made to expeditiously 
operationalise the remaining 17 routes, through renewed efforts and effective 
coordination between the Ministries of Civil Aviation and Tourism to boost the tourism 
potential of iconic destinations.  
(Para 3.2) 
The Committee desires specific details of the State -wise efforts made by the Ministry of 
Civil Aviation to improve connectivity of airports and the result of its interaction with 
various stakeholders including States/ UTs.  
(Para 4.2) 
Helicopter operations 
 
The Committee notes that in its reply, the Ministry has only noted the salient features of 
the ‘Policy for promotion of helicopter operations’. The Committee desires to know the 
actual steps taken by the Ministry to ensure the ground level implementation of the policy 

60 
 
in various States, especially the States which do not have the benefit of airport 
connectivity so far. 
(Para 5.2) 
Aviation Turbine Fuel (ATF) prices and aviation taxes 
 
The Committee notes with satisfaction that through the Ministry’s effort s, eight States 
have reduced the VAT on ATF substantially. The Committee stresses upon the 
importance of reduced VAT rates on the financial viability of airlines keeping in view the 
negative impact of Covid -19 and urges the Ministry to take up the issue of  VAT rate 
reduction with other State Governments as well.  
(Para 6.2) 
The Committee feels that the Civil Aviation Sector is reeling under the burden of high 
aviation sector taxes on one hand and huge losses due to Covid -19 on the other hand. The 
Committee, therefore, reiterates its recommendation that Civil Aviation Sector should be 
considered for priority sector lending as to enable it to get access to funds at cheaper 
rates. The Committee may be apprised of the steps taken by the Ministry in this regard 
and whether the proposal has been taken up with the Ministry of Finance. The 
Committee also desires to know the break -up of the ECLGS 3.0 benefits which have been 
extended to the Civil Aviation Sector.  
(Para 7.2) 
Maintenance, Repair and Overhaul (MRO)  
 
The Committee desires to know the impact of the measures undertaken to support the 
Indian MRO sector and the resultant increase, if any, in MRO services. The Committee 
reiterating its recommendation, stresses upon the urgent need for growth in MRO 
services k eeping in view the existing technical manpower, low labour cost and the 
expected growth in the aviation sector.  
(Para 8.3) 
Krishi Udan 
 
The Committee appreciates the steps taken by the Ministry on coordination with seven 
other Ministries/ Departments name ly Department of Agriculture & Farmer’s Welfare; 
Department of Animal Husbandry & Dairying; Department of Fisheries; Ministry of 
Food Processing Industries; Department of Commerce; Ministry of Tribal Affairs; and 
Ministry of Development of North -eastern Re gion (DoNER),  to successfully implement 
the Krishi Udan Scheme for transportation of agri -produce. The Committee desires to 
know the progress of plan to create 33% of more of domestic terminals by FY 2023 -24 
and the increase in volume of cold storages at a irports. The Committee would also desire 
to know the status of implementation of e -Kushal (Krishi Udan for Sustainable Holistic 
Agri Logistics) and the result of planned collaboration with the stakeholders.   
(Para 9.3) 
Connectivity to North East and other remote areas 
 
The Committee has time and again stressed upon the need for increasing connectivity at 
inaccessible locations in the NER, especially the Hollongi Airport in Arunachal Pradesh. 

61 
 
The Committee notes that work of a new Greenfield airport at Hollongi is in progress and 
desires to know the status of work completion and the tentative date to operationalise the 
airport. The Committee also stresses upon the need for renewed efforts in development of 
water aerodromes and heliports as it requires less s pace and less capital as compared to 
airports. 
(Para 10.4) 
Shortage of Pilots 
 
The Committee notes the reply. It also desires specific information regarding the progress 
of establishment of nine FTOs at five airports and the timeline set for it. The Commit tee 
also recommends that a space should be allocated at each airport for the FTOs to enable 
them to keep their training equipments. 
(Para 11.2) 
Aero Club of India 
 
The Committee understands that the Draft aero -sports policy for development of aero -
sports activities in India has been published for public feedback on 1 st January, 2022. The 
Committee is surprised that while the Ministry is replying to the subject, it has not notified 
that the policy has been framed and put for public circulation. Therefore the Committee 
observed that the proposal may be brought over for discussion and recommendation of the 
committee prior to the notification at the policy level. The Committee also took note that 
such policies, which are being formulated by the Government, are approved and 
thereafter subject to examination of the committee w hich is not a reasonable practice. The 
Committee would like to state that the aero -sports policy must be first put up for 
examination of the Standing Committee prior to seeking its recommendation before it is 
notified as a policy. 
(Para 12.5) 
 
13.2 The Committee has taken note of the explanation and it is felt that the real issue has 
not been addressed which relates to issue of allotment of Land by the Ministry of Urban 
Development. The Committee would like to understand that once the nature of allotment 
to the Aero Club of India was in the form of license agreement dated 27.12.1984 which was 
irrecoverable in the nature as specified in section 60 (b) of the Indian Easement Act, 1882. 
The Committee observes that the basic issue of cancellation of allotment of  a license plot 
on which the Aero Club of India has constructed its building as per the norms and the 
Committee does not find justifiable reason for its Cancellation.  
(Para 13.2) 
Carbon Offsetting and Reduction Scheme for International Aviation (CORSIA) 
The Committee stresses upon the need for protecting India’s interests on the adverse 
implication of CORSIA. It approves the proposal of the Ministry to take up the matter at 
diplomatic level through Ministry of External Affairs and hopes that all efforts w ould be 
made to bring on board like -minded developing countries, so that a unified effort can be 
made to review the CORSIA scheme in favour of our country.  
(Para 14.2) 
Cancellation charges 

62 
 
The Committee notes with concern the reply of the Ministry that cancellation charges are 
not regulated by Government, which has resulted in no uniformity in cancellation 
charges levied by different airlines. The Committee feels that it defies logic that fl ights of 
different airlines on a particular sector having the same starting and destination points, 
and where the duration of the flight is also the same, should have different cancellation 
charges. The Committee, therefore, strongly recommends that there should be uniform 
cancellation charges across all airlines.  
(Para 15.2) 
Cancellation or delaying of flights 
 
The Committee notes with appreciation that based on the directions of the Committee, 
the Ministry has issued guidelines to all airlines/ airports to extend facilities to passengers 
in case of cancellation or delay of flights. The Committee would like to be apprised of the 
ground level implementation of the Ministry’s orders and the number of airports and 
airlines which have implemented it and the de tails of facilities extended and the number 
of passengers who have availed the facilities, airport-wise and airlines-wise.  
(Para 16.2) 
Making Airports Accessible to all under the ‘Accessible India Campaign’ 
 
The Committee notes that ‘Accessibility Standards and Guidelines for Civil Aviation’ 
containing all the details on Accessible Airport Infrastructure has been prepared and 
placed in public domain for comments/suggestion by stakeholders after due consultatio n 
with Chief Commissioner of Persons with Disability (CCPD) and that 
comments/suggestions from stakeholders have been deliberated and final guidelines are 
expected by year end. The Committee desires to know the present status of issues of 
guidelines for as sisting the differently abled people and the timeline set for its 
implementation at all airports.  
(Para 17.2) 
Inefficiency of hangars 
 
The Committee desires to know the plans of the Ministry to build well equipped hangars 
at remote places.   
(Para 18.2)

DEVELOPMENT AND CONSERVATION OF MUSEUMS: CHALLENGES AND

Recommendation/Observation 
 1. The Committee takes note of the steps taken by the Ministry for the upgradation of the 
security infrastructure, Reception Halls, Auditorium etc., with the latest technology. and 
desires that the betterment of the Galleries may be completed at all the Museu ms within a 
fixed timeframe. The Committee strongly recommends that the Museums in India should be 
adequately equipped with conservation labs, storage facilities, written and graphic records, 
documentation facilities, modern photography techniques etc. 
(Para 4.6)  
Reply of Ministry  
 
1.1 National Museum:  National Museum has recently upgraded reception area, CCTV 
infrastructure and auditorium with latest technology. NM has also upgraded 6 halls with latest 
technology. Remaining galleries and storage spaces are being upgraded in phased manner. 
NM has also recently upgraded its Conservation Laboratory. NM has also created digital 
infrastructure for safekeeping on digital record.   
1.2 Indian Museum: - Indian Museum, Kolkata has made the following progress 
pertaining to the upgradation of security infrastructure –

Funding 
Recommendation/Observation 
6. The Committee further recommends that efforts may be made to encourage voluntary 
donations for the purpose of development and conservation of the Museum and its artefacts. 
This can be done by making the tickets pay -as-you-wish, setting a minimum price that  needs 
to be paid for an entry ticket and suggesting a higher amount to help the Museums generate 
funds for its operations. An option may also be provided to interested people to contribute 
towards the maintenance of any given artefact for a certain time p eriod. The possibility of 
providing special tours of Museums before and after public hours, by charging higher ticket 
prices may also be explored. The Committee suggests that Museums across India should look 
into the issue of charging higher fees to foreig n nationals and analyzing the possible impact 
of lowering the same on the footfall received and revenue generated by the Museums, 
targeting the maximization of both the footfall and the revenue.

Safety and security of Museum artefacts 
Recommendation/Observation 
9. The Committee takes note of several media reports pointing out theft of antiquities 
and artefacts, involving the participation of organized international mafia, This, according to 
the Committee is a major cause of concern in safeguarding the artefacts in o ur country. The 
Committee underlined the need of security of artefacts deployed at the different National 
Museums across the country to ensure the safety of our valuable antiquities and artefacts. 
The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Ministry may come up with a set of rules to 
ensure certain level of safety and security across all the National Museums. Needless to 
mention, installation of CCTV systems, armed personnel, burglar alarm systems, etc. in the 
museums are must and therefore the budgetary requirements, alongwith provisions thereof 
within strict timeline be made for compliance of security requirements. The Committee 
recommends the Ministry to explore the usage of blockchain technology for digital 
cataloguing of Museum artefacts, so as to mai ntain permanent, unalterable records of the 
artefacts. The Committee hopes that this would also deter the possible connivance of the 
Museum staff with organized art smuggling groups.  
(Para 4.11.37)  
 Reply of Ministry. 
9.1 National Museum:  NM has fully operational CCTV system and CISF security 
system for safe guarding its objects. NM has also been doing digital cataloguing of its 
objects; about 40% is already completed. 
9.2 NGMA: The Security measures mentioned by the Committee are already available in 
the NGMA, New Delhi. The NGMA, New Delhi is equipped with CCTV Surveillance 
system with 274 Cameras, Armed Personnel i.e., guarded by Ex-servicemen. There is no theft 
reported in the NGMA, New Delhi for the last 30 years. Museum had digitized 80% artefacts 
and uploaded to the national website www.museumsofindia.gov.in. 
9.3 Salar Jung Museum : The security measures mentioned by the Committee are 
already available in the Salar Jung Museum. The Museum is equipped with CCTV 
Surveillance system with 330 Cameras, Armed Personnel i.e., guarded by CISF, Burglar 
Alarm System etc. There is no theft reported in the Museum for the last 30 years. Museum 
had digitized 95% artefacts and uploaded to the national web site 
www.museumsofindia.gov.in. 
9.4 Allahabad Museum: The process of digital cataloguing is going on in AM and there 
is CCTV round the clock surveillance system. 

8 
 
9.5 Indian Museum: Indian Museum takes note of the observations made by the Hon’ble 
Committee. As a precautionary measure, Standard Operating Procedure on security measures 
pertaining to various activities of the Museum have been framed in consultation with CISF 
deployed at Indian Museum and being implemented. It may also be appropriate to place on 
record that Indian Museum is presently using JATAN software developed by C -DAC for 
digitisation of artefacts and the digitised data is being regularly shared with C -DAC for 
uploading on the server. Recommendations for use of Blockchain technology for digital 
cataloguing of artefacts may be taken up by the Ministry with C -DAC which will be at the

9.6 NCSM: NCSM has installed CCTV cameras in all the units under NCSM for such

9.7 ASI: - The security aspect is given primary preference while approving the annual

identified by the Ministry of Culture. Museum attendants/ Gallery attendants are deputed 
inside the galleries to look after the antiquities and visitors. CISF is deployed at sites with

deputed both inside and outside the site museums. Electronic and Mechanical Surveillance/

Opportunities:- 
Addressing the dearth of Human Resources in Museology 
Recommendation/Observation 
11. The Committee feels that the issue of shortage of human resources in the field of 
museology in the country can only be resolved by long -term planning and introducing 
students to this field at a young age. Accordingly, the Committee recommends that the 
Ministry may request the Ministry of Human Resource Development to include an 
introductory course on museology in the curriculum at the senior secondary school level. The 
Committee further recommends that schools should be persuaded by the Ministry to arrange 
at least one Museum visit per year for students at every level. Such visits should include a 
brief behind-the-curtains overview of the process of conservation of Museum artefacts and 
Museum curation. Doing so would instill a sense of respect for our rich c ultural heritage and 
the efforts that go behind preserving the same stimulate the curiosity of students, and 
encourage them to pick up careers in the field of museology and conservation of historical 
artefacts. The Committee observes that the establishment of the Indian Institute of Heritage is 
a step in the right direction and will help tackle the issue of dearth of human resources in the 
field of museology in a significant way. The Ministry should hire curators who have exposure 
in international best standards of Museum curation. 
(Para 4.12.4) 
Reply of Ministry 
11.1 NGMA: The NGMA, New Delhi allows free entry to the students with School ID.  
The NGMA, New Delhi also conducts tours to the Students who visit the Museum with prior

artefacts.

Museum also allows the students to do research on Museum artefacts and also visits to the 
conservation lab.

ARCHAEOLOGICAL SITES 
Challenges:- 
Encroachment and Vandalism 
Recommendation/Observation 
14. The Committee urges upon the Ministry to strive towards prevention of vandalism and 
encroachment at archaeological sites and monuments fraught with safety and security 
problems, particularly those in the UT of Jammu and Kashmir, Chhatisgarh, North -Eastern 
States etc., in close coordination with local law and order authorities. The Committee desires 
the Ministry to take necessary actions to ensure that strict penal provisions are in place to 
deter incidents of vandalism and defacing of monuments. 
(Para 5.6.15) 
Reply of Ministry 
14.1 State Level Coordination Committee (SLCC) has already been constituted in the State 
of Chhattisgarh, Assam, Meghalaya, and Jammu & Kashmir. The States which have not set 
up a State Level Coordination Committee yet, have been requested to form a SLCC. In this 
regard, Archaeological Survey of India is making correspondence continuously with these 
states to constitute State Level coordination Committee. However, few states had held the 
meeting to address the flagged issues of ASI.   

12 
 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
15. The Committee takes serious note of the growing incidents of demolition of several 
temples of immense cultural importance by anti -social elements in certain States. The 
Committee is of the firm view that such incidents s hould be prevented at any cost and exhorts 
the Ministry to ensure a foolproof mechanism to arrest such incidents and protect our 
cherished cultural heritage. The Committee underlines the need for an infallible procedure 
prescribing close coordination among st the Ministry of Culture, Ministry of Home Affairs 
and the State Governments. 
(Para 5.6.16)  
 Reply of Ministry  
15.1 ASI protected Monuments are generally safe from vandalism due to security 
apparatus in place. However, to further strengthen this apparatus, a policy and detailed SoPs 
are being developed. 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
16. The Committee recommends that ASI may undertake a physical security audit for all 
the monuments under its ambit and estimate the financial requirements for installing CCTV 
security systems at all the monuments and sites under its control. Thereafter, a plan may be 
devised to install such systems at the earliest so as to deter and punish vandals. 
(Para 5.6.20) 
Reply of Ministry  
16.1 Yes, this will be done and used as input for the security policy.

documented scientific research. The Committee further recommends that modern technology 
such as photogrammetry, 3D laser scanning, blockchain technology etc. may be explored and

utilized, wherever possible, to improve the documentation of the monuments since quality

(Para 5.7.15) 
Reply of Ministry 
17.1 The recommendation is noted for compliance.

(Para 9.2) 
ARCHAEOLOGICAL SITES 
Challenges:-  

75 
 
Conservation Problems 
 The Committee may be apprised as to whether the works being undertaken 
under the Annual repair plan cover those monuments and sites which are not present in 
the list of Centrally Protected Monuments and State Protected Monuments. I n case  
such monuments are presently not covered at all, the Committee recommends that the 
Ministry may include repair works of urgent nature for such monuments under i ts 
Annual repair plan.  
(Para 10.2) 
 The Committee notes that only a few sites/monuments are having a 
Conservation/ Management plan at present and reiterates its original recommendation 
that ASI may prepare such a plan for all Centrally Protected Monuments. Further, the 
reply furnished by the Ministry does not clarify whether the site inspection of all 
monuments is carr ied out periodically. The Committee therefore reiterates its 
recommendation that a Site Inspection Register may be maintained and periodically 
updated for all Centrally Protected Monuments.  
(Para 11.2) 
Urbanization around Centrally Protected Monuments 
 The Committee desires to be apprised of the action taken by the Ministry for 
conducting research to explore way s and means to protect our archaeological sites and 
monuments from the ill-effects of air pollution in urban centres.  
(Para 12.2) 
Encroachment and Vandalism  
  The Committee reiterates that the Ministry may examine the efficacy of the 
powers it presently has to deal with encroachments in and around monuments and 
propose suitable amendments to the Ancient Monuments and Archaeological Sites and 
Remains Act 1958 and Rules 1959, and Public Premises (Eviction of Unauthorised 
Occupants) Act, 1971 with a view to adequately empower the Estate Officer for tackling 
the issue of encroachment of Centrally protected monuments.  
(Para 13.2) 
 The Committee is not satisfied with the reason given by ASI for not being able to 
provide boundary walls for monuments where only name of the monument is 
mentioned in the notification and ASI faces difficulties in marking the protected limit of 
the monument. The Committee recommends that urgent action may be taken to finalize 
the protected limits of all such monuments so that at least boundary walls can be 
constructed for their protection urgently.  
(Para 14.2) 

76 
 
Lack of funds  
 The Committee notes that the special tours before and after regular hours are 
not feasible because as per AMASR Act, 1958, monuments/sites can remain open only 
from sunrise to sunset. The Committee recommends that a suitable amendment may be 
brought into t he Act in order to permit flexibility in timings till it can be kept open in 
order to open more avenues for prospects of revenue generation and boost tourism of 
every monument.  
(Para 15.2) 
Human Resources at ASI  
 The Co mmittee is concerned to note that a  large number of vacancies are 
existing in ASI at present. The Committee notes that the Ministry has not furnished any 
convincing reply for existence of  such large number of vacancies. The Ministry may 
take immediate concrete action to fill the existing vacancies in ASI at the earliest so as to 
permit it to fulfil its mandate effectively.  
(Para 16.2) 
Opportunities:-  
Promotion of Tourism and Business  
 The Committee may be apprised of the action taken by ASI for developing 
garden spaces presently associated with the monuments. The Committee feels that 
doing so would not only help beautify the monument as a whol e, but also put a check on 
the encroachment of such nearby area that is being developed as a green space.  
(Para 17.2) 
Model Conservation Process 
 The Committee recommends that the Ministry/ASI may periodically update the 
Conservation Manual and Works Code so as to document new knowledge and 
experiences gained by ASI in the field of conservation and preservation of monuments 
and artefacts. The concerned State Government Departments may also be notified of all 
such updates made, so that they can benefit from the experiences of ASI.  
(Para 18.2) 
Involvement of Communities 
 The Committee desires to know about the specif ic actions taken by ASI in order 
to integrate local governance and communities for protection and preservation of 
historical sites and monuments.  

77 
 
(Para 19.3) 
Preparation of database of archaeological sites/monuments 
 The Committee recommends that the Ministry may recruit a higher number of 
Young Archaeologists at the NMMA as opposed to the 20 Young Archaeologists that 
are presently being recruited. The Committee recommends that the Ministry may give 
top priority to the exercise for identification of unprotected monuments and sites across 
the country and personnel and budgetary requirements for such exercise may also be 
met.  
(Para 20.2) 
MISCELLANEOUS 
 The Committee reiterates its recommendation that ASI may replicate such joint 
efforts with other State Governments  in the country in order  to ensure that the historic 
forts as well as other archaeological sites are developed for tourism purposes.  
(Para 21.2) 
 The Committee notes that the Ministry has not furnished  any information 
pertaining to the recommendation made by the Committee to consider granting special 
discount for entry tickets  to young international tourists. The Committee may be 
apprised of the response of the Ministry in this regard.  
(Para 22.3) 
 The Committee notes that as and when any proposal/ request is received from 
the State Government or from the public for inclusion of a monument as Centrally 
Protected Monument, ASI examines and approves the proposal, if it is found suitable. 
The Committee fee ls that the approach of State Governments towards protection and 
preservation of historical monuments is often lethargic  and therefore, ASI must also 
proactively consider taking up important historical monuments presently in neglected 
state of conservation, for inclusion in the list of Centrally Protected Monuments.  
(Para 23.2) 
 The Committee recommends that ASI may analyze the  positive impact of 
illumination of monuments on the footfall received by such monuments and on the basis 
of the same, ASI may take a proactive approach towards illumination of more Centrally 
Protected Monuments across the country.  
(Para 24.2) 
ISSUES COMMON TO MUS EUMS AND ARCHAEOLOGICAL SITES AND 
MONUMENTS 

78 
 
Partnering with the private sector for development and conservation of Museums and 
archaeological sites 
 The Committee desires to be apprised of the reasons behind abolishing the post 
of CEO, DMCS and the fate of  the proposals that were being worked upon by DMCS 
for development of Museums and Cultural Spaces.  
(Para 25.2) 
Re-examination and updation of Acts and Laws pertaining to Museums and 
Archaeological Sites 
 The Committee recommends that the Ministry may undertake review of the 
Indian Museum Act, 1910 in order to ensure that the legislation in place suffices the 
present day requirements for development of museums across the country. The 
Committee further reite rates its recommendation that the blanket ban on construction 
works within the prohibited area of 100 meters around all Centrally Protected 
Monuments, should be reviewed in consultation with experts and stakeholders.  
(Para 26.2) 
 Coordination with different Ministries and State Governments 
 The Committee is of the view that there is a lot of scope for improvement of 
connectivity to museums and monuments/ sites across the country. Having robust 
connectivity to our museums and archaeological monuments / sites is crucial for 
attracting more tourists to such places. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the 
Ministry/ ASI may carry out an exercise to identify projects that can enhance the 
connectivity to the various museums and historical monuments/ si tes across the country 
and the projects thus identified should then be communicated to the relevant Ministry/ 
Department for implementation.  
(Para 27.4) 
Allocation of funds generated from Museums and ASI, to the Ministry of Culture 
 The Committee recommen ds that the Ministry may consider amending/ 
modifying the existing Legislation/ Rules so that the receipts collected by ASI are not 
deposited in the Consolidated Fund of India but into a special fund dedicated to the 
protection and preservation of historical monuments and sites.  The Committee feels 
that doing so would bridge the gap between the budgetary requirements of ASI and 
actual allocation made to it, to some extent.  
(Para 28.4) 
Lowering the fees charged for filming at Centrally Protected Monuments 
 The Committee does not agree with ASI’s view regarding Rs. 1.00 lakh and Rs. 
50 thousand filming charges being meagre amount s. The Committee is of the view that 

79 
 
films being shot on low budget can find these charges to be prohibitive and thus 
disallow them from featuring our historical monuments and heritage. The Committee, 
therefore, recommends that ASI should review the filming charges presently being 
charged, in light of the prohibitive effect of the same on low -budget movies and the 
opportunity for promotion of historical sites and monuments thus lost by ASI. 
(Para 29.7)

PROGRESS REPORT 
 
Recommendation/ Observation 
 
1 The Committee also notes that availability of land free from all encumbrances is the 
responsibility of the respective State Governments/ Union Territories. The Committee would 
like to be apprised of the progress made in this regard.  
(Para 11) 
 
Reply of the Ministry 
 
1.1 Providing the land free from all encumbrances is the responsibility of the State 
Governments/ Union Territory Administrations. As per the draft guidelines of the Swadesh 
Darshan 2.0, land is a non -admissible component and will not be funded under the Swade sh 
Darshan scheme of the Ministry. The Ministry of Tourism (MoT) further vide OM no. SD-
8/10/2020 dated 11.6.2021 has issued the format for „Physical Completion Certificate‟ 
which is to be submitted by Head of the Implementing Agency and Administrative Sec retary. 
Vide this certificate state has to undertake that the facility and the land on which the project 
has been executed will not be transferred/ sold / alienated in any matter whatsoever without 
the written consent and prior approval of the MoT, Government of India and facilities created 
shall be used only for tourism purposes.  
 
1.2 Under the Scheme Assistance to Central Agencies for Tourism Infrastructure 
Development, Central Agencies which are the recipient of the financial assistance are 
responsible for making the land available for development & other allied facilities related to 
execution of the project.  
 

3 
 
1.3 Providing the land, free from any kind of encumbrances, is the responsibility of the 
State Governments/ Union Territory Administrations. In t erms of the guidelines of 
PRASHAD Scheme land is an inadmissible item under the scheme and hence, no funds are 
released for the purpose of acquisition of the land for the project.  
1.4 To address the issue of unavailability of land parcels for the approved  works under 
PRASHAD Scheme, as per the check -list for preparation of DPRs for the project under 
PRASHAD Scheme it has been made obligatory on part of the State Government to provide a 
land availability certificate duly signed by an officer of the level of  at least Secretary of 
Tourism Department of the State / UT concerned. In addition, the interventions for which 
land availability is not confirmed by the respective State Government / UT Administration 
are not being approved under the projects in the Scheme.  
 
1.5 Moreover, under PRASHAD Scheme first installment is released only for those 
interventions for which works have been awarded after completion of tendering process by 
the State/UT.  
In addition, further releases are done only for those interventions on which physical execution 
is in progress. To calculate the amount of second or further releases, the costs of works for 
which tender have not been completed or without any physical progress, are not accounted 
for.  
 
 
STALLED PROJECTS 
 
Recommendation/ Observation 
 
2. The Committee notes that for all the projects that have been sanctioned since the year 
2017, only 50 percent of the sanctioned amount was released so far. The Committee, 
therefore, recommends the Ministry to adopt strategies for speedy completion of the stalled 
projects. The Committee is of the view that this will also help in effective utilization of funds 
and skilled manpower to the maximum possible extent. 
(Para 28) 
 
Reply of the Ministry 
 

4 
 
2.1 Under the scheme Assistance to Central Agencies for Tourism Infrastructure 
Development, funds are released to the Central Agency/ implementing agency in three 
instalments as per following details: 
As regards project taken up by IDD of the Ministry under the scheme Assistance to Central

with an affidavit for Management of Assets created and an undertaking for

2.2 The second instalment is released only after receipt of Utilisation Certificate of the 
first instalment. Continued efforts are being made for timely submission of UCs 
2.3 The second instalment is released only after receipt of Utilisation Certificate of the 
first instalment. Continued efforts are being made for timely submission of UCs. 
2.4 Now Ministry is also se tting up IT based monitoring portals for even closer progress 
of the projects. 
2.5 As far as PRASHAD Scheme is concerned, in addition to rigours follow -ups at the 
Division level, timely review done at the Joint Secretary levels with respect to the pending 
Utilizations Certificates.   It may kindly be appreciated that under PRASHAD Scheme the 
only pending UC amount to Rs. 10 Cr. for the fund released for the project “Infrastructure

Recommendation/ Observation 

5 
 
 
3 The Committee recommends that an audit of the expenditure incurred under the 
Scheme of 'Assistance to Central Agencies for Tourism Infrastructure Development' should 
also be conducted, the details of which should be uploaded on a web based platform for 
effective monitoring of the progress of the implementation. 
 (Para 29) 
 
Reply of the Ministry 
 
3.1 The expenditure of the Ministry is audited by the designated audited officer (Internal 
as well as Statuary audits) . Further, the Ministry has got engaged third party (Quality 
Council of India) for evaluation of  the projects undertaken by it. 
3.2  Internal audit is conducted from time to time. 
3.3 All the projects undertaken with Ministry of Railways under the joint development of 
creation of amenities and facilities at the identified railway stations are being evaluated by 
QCI. 
 
 
 
INTEGRATED TOURISM DEVELOPMENT 
 
Recommendation/ Observation 
 
4. The Committee observes that the tourism sector not only provides employment to wide 
spectrum of job seekers from the unskilled to the specialized but also makes significant 
contribution to the national e conomy by stimulating other economic factors through its 
backward and forward linkages. Since tourism is multi -sectoral activity and the related 
sector includes airlines, surface transport, hotels, basic infrastructure, etc, the growth of the 
sector cannot  be attained unless issues related to all these sectors are addressed 
simultaneously. The Committee notes from the information furnished by the Ministry that 
with a view to make India a 5 trillion dollar economy by 2024 -25, the SGoS Tourism Sector 
Plan aims at implementation of 21 tourism development projects over the next five years. The 
Committee is of the considered view that if the goal of becoming a 5 trillion dollar economy 
is to be achieved, the Government needs to fastrack the development of these 2 1 tourism 

6 
 
infrastructure projects in collaboration with all the Ministries/ entities concerned. The 
Committee, therefore, recommends that convergence and synergy be created across 
programmes of Ministries/ Departments so that the implementation of these 21  tourism 
development projects could be expedited and an integrated development of enabling 
infrastructure through partnerships with all the stakeholders could be accomplished. The 
Committee desires to be kept apprised of the strategies adopted in this regard. 
(Para 31) 
 
Reply of the Ministry 
 
4.1 Ministry of Tourism works in close collaboration with Central Ministries/State 
Governments/various Stakeholders for the development of tourism in the country. Different 
mechanisms and strategies to seek synergy and  convergence with stakeholders for integrated 
development of enabling tourism infrastructure are: 
 
i. National & Regional Conference of State Tourism Ministers are held to discuss 
various issues related to the development of tourism sector in the country. 
ii. National Tourism Advisory Council serves as a ‘Think Tank’ of experts in the field 
of tourism and advises the Ministry on various tourism related issues. It includes 
representatives of various Union Ministries, Trade and Industry Associations and 
Individual Experts in the field of travel and tourism management.  
iii. The Inter -Ministerial Coordination Committee on Tourism Sector (IMCCTS) 
facilitates resolution of Inter -Ministerial issues involved in the development of 
tourism in the country.  
iv. A Task Force has been constituted under the Chairmanship of Secretary (Tourism), 
Govt. of India to address various issues related to tourism as per the 
recommendations of the Sectoral Groups of Secretaries (SGoS) for Tourism 
Sectoral Plan. The Task Force comprises representativ es from the Ministries of 
Civil Aviation, External Affairs, Home Affairs, Railways, Road T ransport & 
Highways, Culture, DoNER, Environment & Forests and IRCTC, ASI. 
 
4.2 Meetings/Consultations are held from time to time with various stakeholders to 
take suggestions/inputs for the development and promotion of tourism sector in the country. 
 

7 
 
i. The last National Conference of Tourism Ministers was held at Ashok Hotel, New 
Delhi in August 2019. The conference was attended by around 20 State Tourism 
Ministers and Senior Officers from State and Central Ministries. In the above meeting 
various issues such as Development of Adventure Tourism, Status of projects 
sanctioned under Swadesh Darshan & PRASHAD Schemes, Bed & 
Breakfast/Homestay Scheme Guidelines as well as be st practices in tourism sector 
and social media campaigns undertaken by the selected State Governments were 
discussed.  
ii. Ministry of Tourism (MoT) organized Regional Tourism & Culture Ministers 
Conference of the North Eastern States on 9th & 10th September 2021at Guwahati, 
Assam to discuss development of tourism and connectivity related issues in the North 
Eastern Region. The North East State Tourism Ministers Conference featured 
presentations by M/o Tourism, M/o DoNER, M/o Civil Aviation, M/o Road Transport 
& Highways and M/o Railways to apprise the participants about the various projects 
and initiatives being taken by the Central Government for the development of North 
Eastern Region. Technical sessions were held to review the progress of the various

23. The Committee observes that the tourism, travel and hospitality sector which has 
direct as well as multiplier effect on a host of sectors and contributes significantly to the  
national economy, has suffered unemployment and bankruptcies due to the COVID -19 
pandemic. Though the Government of India has undertaken various fiscal and relief 
measures under the Atmanirbhar Bharat to restore the growth momentum of the economy, 
these m easures have not been supplemented with sector specific credit measures for the 
tourism sector. The Committee notes that as per  the "Report of the Working Group on 

21 
 
Tourism" of the 12th Five Year Plan in India, the travel and tourism sector is estimated to 
create 78 jobs per million rupees of investment compared to 45 jobs in the manufacturing 
sector for similar investment. This critical sector is one of India's large st contributors to 
GDP. The sector which has huge potential to stimulate overall economic growth and can act 
as a catalyst for the recovery of the currently battered economy needs direct Government 
support by way of relief measures like a stimulus package,  rationalization of GST, liquidity 
support, etc.  
 
23.1 The Committee has been informed that governments across the world are undertaking 
measures to mitigate the impact of COVID -19 pandemic on this critical sector. For example, 
the United Kingdom has prov ided a 12 -month business tax rates holiday for all retail, 
hospitality and leisure businesses in England; France has set up a €2 billion Solidarity Fund 
for which many Tourism Businesses will be eligible; in Singapore, tourism businesses 
affected by COVID -19 received wage subsidies of up to 75%. Taking all the above factors 
into account, the Committee is of the considered view that since the COVID-19 pandemic and 
the consequent lockdowns have a crippling blow to the Indian tourism, travel and hospitality 
industry and the whole value chain has been hit hard, the Government needs to provide 
targeted support to the sector. The Committee accordingly recommends that the Government 
should inject tourism sector -specific financial/monetary stimulus in the system and  offer 
immediate liquidity support and rationalization of the GST structure for the sector. The 
Committee observes, even at the cost of sounding repetitive, that such a critical sector 
contributing so much to the GDP and generating employment opportunities  should not be 
ignored, especially when it is in dire straits. The Committee would like the Ministry to pursue 
this matter with the Ministry of Finance with a sense of urgency and promptitude and apprise 
the Committee of their response.

26. The Committee observes that one of the bottlenecks in tapping the full potential of the 
hospitality sector is the high incidence and multiplicity of taxes. While some States like 
Maharashtra, Gujarat, Uttarakhand, etc., have accorded industry status to hos pitality sector,

Ministry should imme diately initiate policy measures for according Industry status to hotels

3. The Committee takes note of the of the Ministry that the Public Private Partnership

Darshan Scheme and PRASHASD Schemes also have a provision to explore for PPP partner 
for operation, maintenance and sustenance of the facilities created. The Co mmittee observes 
that creation of quality infrastructure for developing tourist products and for providing better 
services to both domestic and international tourists is a pre -requisite not only to generate 
employment and achieve broad based and inclusive growth of the economy on a sustained 
basis, but also to have a favorable impact on the preservation of art, culture and heritage. 
However, projects like the SDS and PRASHAD have high social but an unacceptable 
commercial rate of return and are generally ch aracterised by long gestation periods, 
substantial investments, fixed returns due to which they require financial support from the 
Government through appropriate financial investments and incentives. Since the development

public financing alone, the engagement of the private sector in provisioning of tourism 
infrastructure under the SDS and PRASHAD is warranted. The Committee is of the firm view

sector and commercial enterprise but will also go a long way in supplementing the scarce 
public sector resources vis -a-vis the requirements of bridging the infrastructure deficit. T he 
Committee, therefore, recommends that in order to meet the funding gap, make SDS and 
PRASHAD commercially viable and facilitate private sector efficiencies in the development 
of tourism infrastructure under the SDS and PRASHAD, the Ministry should formu late a 
transparent policy framework for participation of private operators in developing products 
such as hotels, resorts, convention centers, tourist trains, etc., with the Government acting as 
a facilitator and catalyst and also set up a Viability Gap Fu nding window for tourism 
infrastructure development under the SDS and PRASHAD.

Recommendation/ Observation 
 
21The Committee in Paras 44 to Para 77 of its 288th Report on Demands for Grants (2021 -

Reply of the Ministry 
 
21.1 MoT has engaged National Council of Applied Economic Research (NCAER) in 
January, 2021 to conduct study on India and the Coronavirus Pandemic: Economic Losses for 
Households Engaged in Tourism and Policies for Recovery. The key findings of study are:  

51 
 
a. Due to overall economic slowdown during 2020 -21, tourism economy or tourism 
direct gross value added (TDGVA) saw a fall of 42.8 percent in Q1; 15.5 percent in 
Q2 and fall of 1.1 percent in Q3.  
b. Due to significant drop in tourist arrivals and hence tourism expenditure, during the

was implemented.14.5 million direct jobs during Q1, 5.2 million during Q2 and 1.8 
million direct jobs during Q3 are expected to have lost as compared to estimated 34. 8 
million direct jobs in tourism sector in the pre-pandemic period of 2019-20.  
 
288th COMMITTEE RECOMMENDATIONS 
 
288th Committee Recommendation (Para 72) 
 
22 The Committee observes that the Government under the leadership of Prime Minister 
Narendra Modi has set a target of taking the economy to 5 Trillion dollar Gross Domestic 
Product (GDP) by 2024. It has been widely accepted that the tourism sector in the cou ntry 
has the potential to emerge as key economic driver for this economic growth and can create 
large scale employment. The Committee feels that the country can make giant leap towards 
reaching the 5 –trillion dollar GDP target by focusing on this critical  sector. However, this 
cannot be achieved without the active cooperation from the state and Union Territories - 
because a comprehensive set of strategies for a diversity of actions from macro to micro 
level, including product and infrastructure development,  marketing, branding promotion 
planning , policy and investment would need to be developed and the multiple challenges 
thrown up by capacity constraints and inadequate policies would need to be addressed. The 
Committee, however, notes that the Travel and T ourism Sector does not figure in the Central, 
State or Concurrent List. Ours is federal Policy making and implementation are fragmented 
across levels of Government and coordination between them is often lacking due to absence 
of clearly defined mandate. Since tourism is a Multi- Sectoral activity, inclusion of tourism in 
the Concurrent List an important role in facilitating the issue involved with multiple 

52 
 
Ministries/ Organizations at Central level as well as with the States/Union Territories to 
create convergence and synergy of actions across multiple agencies and programmes. The 
Committee, therefore, recommends that Tourism be included in the Concurrent List.

288th Committee Recommendation (Para 73) 
 
23 The Committee observes that the hospitality industry is in huge distress under the 
impact of the COVID -19pandemic and is looking at mass unemployment and pan India 
bankruptcies. The Committee notes from the written submissions of the MoT that all star -
rated hotels with a project cost of over Rs. 200 crores were granted infrastructure status by 
their inclusion in the Harmonized Master List of Infrastructure sub -sectors vide gazette 
Notification dated 07.10.2013 which lapsed three years after notification via  sunset clause. 
The Ministry's proposal for grant of infrastructure status to investment in hotel industry of 
over Rs. 50 crore and in towns with less than 5 lakh population has been turned down by the 
Ministry of  Finance. Subsequently, the Ministry of Fin ance was requested to grant 
infrastructure status to hotel projects with lower investment, i.e. hotel capex above Rs. 25 
crore (excluding land) capex, but the Department of Economic Affairs is yet to respond to the 
proposal. The Committee has been given to  understand that the Reserve Bank of India has 
equated the hotel sector with real estate which leads to lending at high interest rate from 
banks. The Committee observes that shortage of quality accommodation to tourists is a big 
deterrent to development of  tourism. One of the key impediments for investment in the 
hospitality and hotel sectors has been the non -availability of credit at low interest terms. 
Considering the fact that construction of hotels is highly capital intensive and  has a long 
gestation pe riod with a long break even period, availability of quality hotel has a direct 
correlation to the Ministry's vision of taking the share of India's Foreign Tourist Arrivals 
(FTAs) from 0.75% in 2019 to 2% by 2025. The Committee is of the considered view tha t 
there is an imperative need to accord infrastructure status to hotel projects with capex above 

53 
 
Rs. 25 crore ( excluding land) and include the same in the infrastructure lending list of the 
RBI. The Committee exhorts the Ministry of Tourism to immediately  bring the above 
recommendation to the notice of the Ministry of Finance who should enumerate their policy

limit to Rs. 25 crore. This move will attract more investme nt in hotel projects which in turn 
shall drive employment generation. The Committee desires to be kept apprised of the decision 
taken by the Ministry of Finance in this regard so that the matter could be 
deliberated/pursued with them in the right earnest. The Committee is convinced that 
according infrastructure status to hotels will not only attract more investments in hotel 
projects but also go a long way in reviving the growth momentum of this sector which has 
witnessed a major slump since the outbreak of the COVID-19 pandemic.

TOURISM CIRCUITS 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
 
1. The Committee is constrained to note that despite the SDS being launched way back 
in January, 2015, only one of the 15 thematic circuits under the Scheme has been completed 
and the physical progress in res pect of the remaining 14 circuits ranges from 16 percent to 
90 percent which is far from being satisfactory. The Committee recommends the Ministry that 
all the destination points covered under the thematic Ramayana circuit; Buddhist circuit and 
Himalayan c ircuit have high tourist value and mythological significance, which will go a 
long way in promoting cultural and heritage value of the country besides earning valuable 
foreign exchange income. Even the important thematic circuits that have potential of  
attracting  both international and domestic tourists, the physical progress and development 
of amenities in these circuits from 2015 is less than 70%. Therefore, we cannot give impetus 
to tourism without providing an integrated approach where apart from good  stay 
arrangements, multi modal connectivity and wayside amenities should also be developed. 
Hence the potential of many tourist sites under these identified circuits is still untapped. 
Since the creation of good tourism infrastructure is a per -requisite towards attracting more 
tourist, both domestic and international, to the tourist destinations and also has had its 
multiplier effect in terms of employment generation and increased National and State 
revenues apart from improving the country's tourism produ ctive capacity, the Committee 
recommends that the Government must take stringent measures for expediting the completion 
of remaining 14 thematic circuits in a time bound manner. 
(Para 7)

Recommendation/Observation 
 
3 The Committee observes that rural tourism is one of the few emerging dimensions of 
the Tourism industry, but is very less emphasized upon. Till date, only two projects have been 
approved under the rural circuit of SDS and funds were released only for the o ne. India 
being rich in tradition of arts, crafts and culture, rural tourism, if exploited intelligently in a 
sustainable manner has the potential to provide sustainable livelihood to rural communities.

interventionist approach to ensure that the pro-poor tourism approach leads to redistribution

CHAPTER-I 
 
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS WHICH HAVE BEEN ACCEPTED BY 
THE MINISTRY 
 
Recommendation/Observation  
1. The Committee notes that Highway Safety has been given 35% weightage in NHAI’s 
parameters for assessment and ranking of National Highways. Number of accidents and 
deaths happening on the particular National Highway must be taken into account while 
calculating such scores. 
(Para 21) 
Reply of the Ministry 
1.1. As per the highway rating criteria for evaluation of Highway Safety scores, 4 marks 
have been allocated to Accidents per km per annum and 4 marks have been allocated to 
Accident Severity Index (fatalities per 100 accidents). 
 
Recommendation/Observation  
2. The Committee recommends that the Ministry may take steps to assign scores to all 
the National Highways projects, including the ones executed by State Government PWDs, 
after assessing their quality of construction. A central database may store the scores obtained 
by the different road projects of each concessionaire/contractor, which may be analyzed to 
ascertain the quality of work executed by all the concessionaires. Th e Committee 
recommends that the quality of previous works carried out by the concessionaires should also 
be a factor, besides the bid amount, during the awarding process of a road project tender. 
This would ensure that concessionaires that produce quality roads are not left out of having 
the opportunity to work on a project because of minor differences in bidding amounts. 
(Para 22) 
Reply of the Ministry 
2.1. Ministry has issued a letter no. RW/NH-33044/15/2021-S&R (P&P) dated 16.04.2021 
regarding Highways Rating Criteria and SOP for undivided carriageway upto 2 -Lane with 
paved shoulders on National Highways. Similarly, NHAI has prepared Highways Rating 
Criteria and SOP for undivided carriageways (four lanes and above) vide its letter 
NHAI/HO/Highways rating/2020 dated 07.07.2020. The rating shall be used to prioritize the 

3 
 
allocation of funds for improving/widening/strengthening different sections of NH on 
different elements of efficiency, safety and user services. The r ating shall also help in 
performance appraisal of deployed contractor/concessionaire/maintaining agency. 
 
 
Recommendation/Observation  
3. The Committee recommends that the Ministry may consider breaking down big road 
projects into smaller chunks so as to attract the interest of the small contractors themselves. 
The Committee feels that provisions should be in place to ensure that there is a well -defined 
lower limit, below which bids for a road project would not be accepted. The Committee 
agrees with the ap prehension raised by the Member of the Committee regarding a likely hit 
on the quality of work that can be carried out by a contractor who bids substantially lower 
than the approved project cost. The Committee believes that such bids are made with the sole  
intent of winning the bid and more often than not, it would not be possible for such bidders to 
do quality work with such low bids. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Ministry 
may lay even greater focus on arriving at accurate estimates for the  project cost for a given 
road project and specify an upper and lower limits within which bids can be placed. 
(Para 25) 
Reply of the Ministry 
3.1. The Ministry has been able to reduce the overall cost of development of highways 
through increasing competition by right -sizing of construction packages to ensure optimum 
competition during the bidding stage and refinement of eligibility criteria to promot e 
competition. For example, flagship corridors like Delhi Mumbai Expressway and Delhi 
Amritsar Katra Expressway have been segmented into packages of INR ~ 1,000 Cr which has 
made it accessible for upcoming firms. Combined with improvements to the model 
concession agreements the competitiveness of the overall sector has been improved 
significantly.  
3.2. The reduction in average project package sizes (~55 km before FY 17 to ~ 30 km 
currently) led to higher competition - average no. of bids from 5 – 7 in FY 2 0 to 15+ in Q4 
FY 21. This has led to higher discounts competition and increased average discount on EPC 
projects from 7% in FY 20 to 10% in FY 21. 
3.3. The Ministry adheres to the procurement guidelines set by the Ministry of Finance for 
procurement, bidd ing and awarding contracts. The authority is cognizant about such 
aggressive bidding practices by some contractors and has installed checks and balances to 
ensure that project completion is not hindered due to lack of financial resources required for 
the project. One such step is the mandating of the contractors and concessionaires to provide 
additional performance security in cases where significant discounted prices are quoted. 
Recommendation/Observation  

4 
 
4. The Committee recommends that thorough quality checks may be performed before 
the issuance of completion certificate for any NH project, with special focus on rigorous 
testing of quality of the construction material used. The frequency of quality checks 
performed during the construction stage of a proj ect may be increased suitably and 
independent third party audits may be conducted more often in order to deter the connivance 
of the Authority’s Engineer with the road contractors. The Committee further desires that 
extensive quality checks may be performe d when the defect liability period of a project is 
nearing its end, so as to ensure that the issues arising near the end of the defect liability 
period are addressed by the contractor before their liability for the same is over. 
(Para 28) 
Reply of the Ministry 
4.1. The quality checks before issue of completion certificate for any NH projects are 
being carried out as specified under Schedule -K of EPC contract and Schedule -I of BOT 
contract. 
 Random quality inspection by engaging retired Senior Govt. officials  are being 
carried out in order to deter the connivance of the Authority’s Engineer with the road 
contractors. 
 During Defect Liability Period, the equipment based monitoring at specified interval 
is being carried out. 
Recommendation/Observation  
5. The Committee further recommends that the Ministry should look into the authenticity 
of the quality checks cleared by road projects, which later performed poorly and/or 
deteriorated at a quick pace, since the same alludes to either the insufficiency of the qualit y 
checks in place, or the connivance of the officials/engineers in charge of conducting the 
quality checks. A suitable mechanism may be put in place to ensure that the IRC guidelines 
are followed in the execution of road works without fail. 
(Para 29) 
Reply of the Ministry 
5.1. To ensure that the requisite quality standards are followed during the execution of the 
project and work is carried out as per specifications and standards, the frequency of test 
checks has been prescribed. 
5.2. NHAI also conducts ran dom Quality Inspection of the projects by involving retired 
senior government officials, as Independent Team Leaders.   Accordingly, quality checks are 
being carried out on various projects under implementation from time to time. 

5 
 
5.3. Standard Operating Pro cedure for action against the Consultant/Contractor has been 
notified by MoRTH vide letter No. RW/NH -33044/76/2021-S&R(P&B) dated 06.10.2021 
and 07.10.2021. 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
 
6.  The Committee feels that Infrastructure Finance Companies such as IIFCL play an 
important role in meeting the huge financial requirements of the road infrastructure sector in 
India. The Committee therefore desires to know the reasons for not permitting IFCs to lend to 
InvITs and desires that NHAI may grant such permission to IFCs with suitable limits, if need 
be, so as to ensure InvITs attract the amount of targeted funds. 
              (Para 43) 
  
 Reply of Ministry 
 
6.1    It is understood that IIFCL has been recently permitted by RBI to invest and lend 
funds to Infrastructure Investment Trusts (InvITs). We are in discussion with IIFCL for 
investment in units of NHIT in current round and for providing debt in future rounds. 
  
 
Recommendation/Observation  
7. The Committee reiterates its recommendation made at para 43 of this Report and 
desires that suitable steps may be taken to permit IIFCL to play a bigger role in long -term 
lending to the road infrastructure sector, by way of subscribing to corporate bonds , investing 
in InvITs, and by allowing IIFCL to lend directly to NHAI and State Departments concerned 
to finance long-term road projects. 
(Para 60) 
Reply of the Ministry 
7.1. NHAI sets up its bonds issues (private placement) through EBP platform of the stock 
exchanges and always invite all the investors (Corporate, QIBs, Bank and NBFC) without 
any restriction on any category/investor. This is in line with the guidelines issued by SEBI 
and negotiation for investment on bilateral basis is not permitted. 
 
Recommendation/Observation  
8. The Committee recommends that the Ministry may review the current mechanism in 
place to deter the connivance of the Authority’s Engineers with contractors/concessionaires. 

6 
 
Cases where roads deteriorate shortly after their completion should be looked into a nd the 
basis on which completion certificate for the project had been issued, should be scrutinized. 
Accountability may be fixed in cases wherein guidelines have been blatantly ignored during 
execution of road projects. 
(Para 63) 
Reply of the Ministry 
8.1. Random quality inspection by engaging retired Senior Govt. officials are being 
carried out in order to deter the connivance of the Authority’s Engineer with the road 
contractors. 
 Equipment based monitoring at specified intervals has been made mandatory in all the 
projects of NHAI. 
 Directions for suitable action against contractors/consultants in cases of default has 
been specified. 
Recommendation/Observation  
9. The Committee recommends that it should be made compulsory to submit video 
recordings of the specifications of the completed works, wherever possible, confirming that 
all works have been carried out by the concessionaire/contractors, before the grant of 
completion certificate of the road project to any concessionaire/contractor. This would 
ensure that ancillary specifications such as road signs, markings, shoulders etc. are duly 
completed as per the provisions of the contract. 
(Para 65) 
Reply of the Ministry 
9.1 As regard to compulsory submission of video recording to ensure specification of 
completed work before grant of completion certificate of the road project, Ministry vide 
circular No. RW/NH/33044/32/2019. -S&R (P&B) dated 13.11.2019 made it mandatory to 
carry out detailed condition survey of road by the AE/I/DPR consultant using network survey 
Vehicle (NSV). The NSV survey must record: 
Inventory of road such as GPS coordinates, pavement type, pavement width, terrain, 
land uses, shoulder type and width drain type and width, Median type and width, 
wayside amenities, crash barriers, road sig nage etc. Besides condition of road such 
as roughness, rutting, distress (cracking potholes, bleeding, surface failure etc.)  
The time intervals for carrying out NSV survey are as under: 
i. Before start of work. 
ii. Before issue of provisional/final completion certificate 

7 
 
iii. Every six months after completion. 
These data of condition survey shall be uploaded on PMIS Portal. 
Accordingly, videography of completed work is invariably prepared and furnished as 
an authentic documentary evidence of completion of works, without which completion 
certificate is not issued.   
Recommendation/Observation  
10. The Committee observes that land acquisition issues are at the core of delays faced in 
road projects. The Committee takes note of the guidelines issued by the Ministry to 
streamline acquisition of land for NH projects in the country and recommends that the 
Ministry may ensure that these guidelines may be re viewed from time to time, incorporating 
suitable modifications to simplify the process of land acquisition and ironing out the various 
constraints faced in land acquisition. 
(Para 71) 
Reply of the Ministry 
10.1 The observation of the Committee has been not ed and it has been decided to review 
the LA guidelines/manual. In the first instance, this Ministry has requested all concerned 
agencies to suggest necessary modification that needs to be incorporated in the proposed 
revised guidelines.   
Recommendation/Observation  
11. The Committee recommends that the Ministry may take immediate steps to ensure that 
adequate manpower is present with the land acquisition units at the field level across the 
country. The alignment given for any given project  should be finalized only after taking in 
inputs from all stakeholders and the local population, with due consideration to the future 
traffic projections, environmental concerns etc. Changing the alignment at a later stage of 
the project can be a costly af fair and should be avoided at all costs, through application of 
foresight. 
(Para 72) 
Reply of the Ministry 
11.1 The Ministry has authorised regional officer (s) to engage the services of retired 
revenue officials as Consultant (LA) for avoiding delay in Land Acquisition. Further, RO’s 
have been authorised to provide certain facilities such as furniture, office equipment’s, 
manpower etc., to CALAs for the purpose of acquiring land for NH Projects, from project 
contingencies. 
11.2 Also, of late, the Ministr y has requested all State Govt. for setting up of special Land 
Acquisition Unit (SLAU) for the work of Land Acquisition for National Highways across the

16. The Committee takes note of the discrepancies pointed out by the Punjab PWD in the 
value of land determined at present based on registered sale deed/ collector rates and the 
actual market rate of the land. The Comm ittee feels that such discrepancy, if present, would 
invariably cause dissatisfaction among the land owners and the ensuing delays on account of 
arbitration and legal procedures cost the public exchequer a lot of money due to project cost 
overruns. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Ministry may review the accuracy 
of the provisions existing at present in determining the amount of compensation to be paid to 
land-owners, as compared to the actual market value of the land. If substantial difference s 
are noticed in the compensation value and the market value in many instances, the Ministry 
may come up with a suitable mechanism for determination of a more fair value for the land to 
be acquired. 
(Para 94) 
Reply of the Ministry 
16.1 The compensation for the Land acquired for NH is determined in accordance with the 
First scheduled of the RFCTLARR ACT, 2013 with effect from 01.01.2015. As per Section 
26 of the RFCTLARR ACT, 2013, the market value of the land is determined as (a) the 
market value, if any specified in the Indian Stamp Act, 1899 for the registration of sale deed 
or agreement to sale, as the case may be, in the area where the land is situated; or (b) the 
average sale price for similar type of land situated in the nearest vil lage or nearest vicinity 
area. The average sale price refer to in clause (b) is determined by taken into account the sale 
deeds of the agreement to sale registered for similar type of area in the near village or near 
vicinity during the year immediately pr eceding the issue of notification under Section 3A of 
the NH Act, 1956. The higher rate arrived from (a) and (b) above is adopted for 
determination for compensation of land acquisition in NH Projects  
16.2 Hence, the value of land which is more beneficial to the land owner is paid to him/her. 
It is a matter of fact that the Circle rate of land is notified by concerned State Governments 
and this Ministry has no role in this regard.

1. The Committee notes that the concessionaire is responsible for the Operation and 
Maintenance (O&M) of the road projects for the entire Concession Period (BOT (Toll) and 
BOT (Annuity) projects) or 15 years (HAM projects) in PPP projects, but in case of Public 
funded projects, the contractor is responsible for rectification of defects/ maintenance only 
during the defects/maintenance-cum-defects liability period which varies between one to four 
years. Since a large number of road projects are Public funded projects, especially the ones 
that are deemed not to be financially viable for private sector participation, the o nus of their 
maintenance falls on the Ministry/NHAI/State PWDs. In this regard, the Committee feels that 
the amount of funds allocated for the maintenance of National Highways every year is 
minuscule given the vast lengths of the National Highways across t he country. The 
Committee strongly recommends that the maintenance of the existing network of National 
Highways should be given topmost priority and the same should be reflected in the budgetary 
allocation made for the same. 
(Para 12)   
 Reply of Ministry 
1.1  Maintenance and Repair (M&R) of National Highways (NHs) is carried out for the 
stretches not covered under any programme or completed stretches where there are no 
liabilities of contractors to maintain such stretches. For the NH stretches developed on  EPC 
mode (Engineering, Procurement, Construction), the contractor is responsible for rectification 
of the defects and concurrent maintenance of project highway during the defect liability 
period after completion of the work. For the NH stretches developed  on BOT mode/ HAM, 
the Concessionaire is responsible for the maintenance of the project highway during the 
concession period. For some of the developed NH stretches through public funding, 
maintenance contracts have been taken up for a definite time period  (4 to 9 years) on 
Operation, Maintenance and Transfer (OMT) basis. Maintenance of the project highway 
under OMT contracts is the responsibility of the Concessionaire. 
1.2 For the remaining NH length, not covered under any programme, the Ministry 
allocates funds under for their M&R. Since inception of Bharatmala Pariyojana, Ministry is 
taking up more and more stretches under development and after development of these 
stretches, maintenance & operation is being done through contract, e.g. OMT, TOT etc. InvIT 
is also being initiated. Further, to overcome the shortfall in allocation under M&R head, the 
scheme of Periodical Repair/IRQP from Revenue Section (M&R) has been shifted to Capital 
Section (NH -O) w.e.f. 2021 -22. Hence, more fund is available for keeping the National 
Highways traffic worthy and no shortage of funds is anticipated at this stage.
