2.      The Committee reiterates the recommendation made in para 184 of its 287 th Report on 
Demands for Grants (2 021-22) of the Ministry of Road Transport and Highways, which is 
reproduced below verbatim. 
The Committee is of the view that roads across the country require frequent trenching 
for the purpose of laying of fiber lines, gas pipelines, and other similar amenities. The 
patchwork done thereafter is often delayed and rarely meets the desired construction 
quality, thus thwarting the speed of vehicles on the road and acting as a safety 
hazard. The Committee recommends that the Ministry may consider the inclusion of a 
provision for dedicated underground utility corridors in its upcoming National 
Highways projects to prevent frequent trenching. The provision for construction of 
dedicated underground utility corridor should be included at the DPR stage itself. The 
extra cost incurred for building the underground utility corridors may be replenished 
by monetizing the constructed utility corridors by charging the Departments and 
Companies which will benefit from avoid ance of frequent trenching of roads. The 
Committee recommends that the Ministry may create a Special Purpose Vehicle (SPV) 
for the purpose of monetization of the utility corridors. 
 (Para 16) 
Reply of Ministry 
 
2.1    The Ministry agrees that the developme nt of essential utility corridors to lay down 
water pipelines, OFC cable, power line, drainage/sewerage network, gas pipelines etc. along 
with highway development shall be definitely time and cost saver as well as it will enhance 
economic viability and environment sustainability.  
2.2    This is to inform that the existing National Highway Right of Way (ROW) varies 
from 12 -60 m and depending upon the availability of space in ROW, permissions to lay 
utilities in a width of 2 m on extreme edges of ROW are bei ng given. As the different 
agencies approach this Ministry for such permissions at different timelines, the utility space is 
utilized mostly in an unorganized manner. While developing the National Highways of 
standards to serve projected future traffic, th e additional ROW is being acquired to make a 
consistent ROW of 30 -60 m. For a 4 -lane divided carriageway development, 45 -60 m ROW 

59 
 
is maintained through acquisition while for a 2 -lane paved shoulder development ROW upto 
30 m is maintained. Further the Natio nal Highways passes through rural and urban areas and 
in some cases, ROWs are compromised in urban areas.  
2.3    The need of utility corridors may also be divided into two parts i.e.   long distance 
utilities viz. OFC, gas/oil pipelines etc. passing through rural areas and short distance utilities 
viz. power lines, drainage/ sewerage, water pipelines etc. needing urban space. There are also 
security/safety & operational issues related to par allel and close running of power & OFC 
lines, power & gas/oil pipelines etc. 
Another area of concerns is: - 
i. The economical viability - whether such ducts are compulsorily to be built 
along highways without actual assessment of need in the area, or to be bu ilt 
on the basis of need after getting requirements from various agencies and 
ii. Cost of such ducts - cost sharing of construction of ducts and required land to 
be acquired specifically for such utility corridor, investments & tariff, 
operation & maintenance cost etc. 
2.4    In order to get all the above issues examined and to have a draft Policy Note/SOP, it has 
been decided by Ministry to take consultancy services of Andhra Pradesh Urban 
Infrastructure Asset Management Limited (APUIAML). Necessary instructio ns have been 
given to NHAI on 25th September 2020 to engage APUIAML. The draft policy so prepared 
shall be shared with all stake holders before its finalization. Based on the finalized policy, the 
decision on creation of a Special Purpose Vehicle (SPV) for  the purpose of monetization of 
the utility corridors may be taken. 
2.5  In this connection, APUIAML has recently submitted an interim feasibility report for 
laying of integrated utility corridors along greenfield NHs.   
 Further Recommendation/Observation: 
2.6  The Committee desires to be kept apprised of the progress made by the Ministry 
with regard to preparation of draft Policy Note/ SOP on the viability of having 
provisions for utility corridors and the decision regarding creation of a Special Purpose 
Vehicle for the purpose of monetization of the utility corridors, based on the finalized 
policy.

drastically and the most effective way to do so is by  way of training people to drive better. 
Therefore, IDTRs and RDTCs should be present in every district of the country. The

Reply of Ministry  
30.1  The Ministry of Road Transport & Highways has been implementing a nation -wide 
scheme of setting of Driving Training Institutes (DTIs) since FY 2002 -03. The scheme was 
renamed as Institute of Driving Training & Research (IDTR) in 12 th FY Plan period (2012 -
17) with central financial assistance of Rs.17.00 crore and land requirement of 10 acre. A 
new component as Regional Driving Training Centre (RDTCs) with less capacity with 
financial assistance of Rs.5.00 crore and land require ment (3 acre) as Tier II in the 12th  Five 

79 
 
Year plan period was added.   The financial implication of IDTR was revised from 17.00 
crore to 18.50 crore during the 14th  Financial cycle. During 14th Finance Commission Cycle 
another new component i.e. setting up  of Driving Training Centres at District level was 
added. However, due to stay on the scheme of setting up of Driving Training Centre, no 
proposal was sanctioned during the 14 th Finance Commission Cycle period.

driving test track to provide quality training to vehicle drivers, improve road and environment 
safety and strengthen overall mobility on roads.

different States/UTs. Continuation of the scheme during the 15 th Finance Commission Cycle 
i.e. FY 2021-22 to FY 2025 -26 has been approved by the Competent Authority. The scheme 
is a national-wide scheme covering all States/U Ts and more centres under the scheme would 
be sanctioned under the scheme based on the proposals from the State Governments/UT 
administration as per provisions under the scheme guidelines. 
  
30.4 In addition,  the Ministry has also notified rules for  accredited Drivers Training 
Centers to make the driving training scientific and systematic, vest the accredited Driving 
Training Center with certain functions like testing of aspirants for issue of driving license and 
to make accredited driving Training Center a  commercially viable business 
proposition, notification G.S.R 394(E) dated 7 th June, 2021 effect from 01 st July, 2021. The 
requirements to be fulfilled by accredited driver training centres have been mandated in these 
rules. The relevant provisions contain ed in Rules 12 to Rules 31A of the Center Motor 
Vehicles Rules, 1989 . This will help in imparting proper training and knowledge to 
candidates who enrol at such centres. The salient features of Accredited Driver Training 
Centers are as under: 
 
● The centre sh all be equipped with simulators and dedicated driving test track to 
provide high quality training to candidates.  
● Remedial and refresher courses, as per the requirement of Motor Vehicles Act, 1988, 
can be availed at these centres.  
● The candidates who successfully pass the test at these centers will be exempted from 
the driving test requirement at the time of applying for driving license, which is 
currently being taken at the RTO. This will  help in getting the driving license after 
completing  training from such accredited driving training centres. 
● These centres are allowed to provide industry- specific specialized training as well." 
● The States/UTs are responsible for establish a system to grant accreditation, promote, 
monitor, audit etc. of such centre. 
● These Institutes would not only impart scientific and systematic Training to driving 
aspirants but also inculcate good behaviour among road users and road safety. 
● Any legal entity such as Companies, Associations, Firms, NGOs, Private 
establishment etc. are also eligible to apply for accreditation of DTC. 
 
30.5 These rules would promote  private sector to set up well equipped driving training 
centres fulfilling the  prescribed criteria in terms of land, premises, manpower etc., in the 
country.

crores as on 30th June, 2020, which is about 7% of the bank’s overall outstanding credit to 
the road sector. This is the best figure in terms of NPAs in road sector, as compared to the 
data regarding NPAs furnished to the Committ ee by the other banks/ financial institutions. 
The Committee recommends that other banks/ financial institutions should look into the 
methodologies followed by State Bank of India while extending loans to concessionaires in 
road infrastructure sector, and apply the same in their own institution in order to bring their 
respective NPA levels down. 
(Para 193) 
Reply of Ministry 
21.1  This recommendation pertains to Ministry of Finance (Department of Financial 
Services). They have been requested for comments/ATNs which are awaited. 
  
 
Recommendation/Observation 
22.  The Committee is alarmed by the high level of NPA in Central Bank of India’s road 
sector exposure, which has been at such highs even before the start of the COVID -19 
pandemic. The Committee feels that this might point to grant of loans without high quality in -
depth analysis of the inherent risk in extending the loans, and should be looked into on 
priority basis by the bank so as to prevent this from snowballing into a bigger problem in the 
future. 
(Para 196) 
Reply of Ministry 
22.1   This recommendation pertains to Ministry of Finance (Department of Financial 
Services). They have been requested for comments/ATNs which are awaited. 
  
 
Recommendation/Observation 
23.  The Committee is concerned to note that  61% of the outstanding exposure of IFCI is 
NPA. The Committee is not convinced by IFCI’s justification that the figure looks inflated 
due to exposure to IL&FS road projects. The Committee recommends that RBI may look into 
the matter and consider issuing g uidelines limiting the extent to which a financial 
institution/bank can lend the funds to a particular infrastructure company. 
     (Para 203) 
 
Reply of Ministry 

94 
 
 
23.1  This recommendation pertains to Ministry of Finance (Department of Financial 
Services). They have been requested for comments/ATNs which are awaited. 
  
 
Recommendation/Observation 
24.  The Committee sought to know from the various financial institutions and Public 
Sector Banks regarding how the NPA figures in the road sector for their instit ution compare 
with that of their peers and in case their institution fared poorly in this regard, the Committee 
desired to know the reasons for the same. In the written replies received regarding this query, 
the Committee was informed that the Banks did no t have the sector -wise NPA details of the 
other Banks are not available in the public domain. The Committee feels that sector -wise 
exposure information, at least in respect of public sector banks, should be made available in 
the public domain to permit mor e transparency and public scrutiny. The Committee 
recommends that RBI must analyze the reasons behind substantial variations in the 
percentage of sub -standard assets of NPAs in different Public Sector financial 
institutions/banks and come up with stricter rules and regulations that must be followed while 
sanctioning long-term loans to the infrastructure sector. 
(Para 217) 
Reply of Ministry 
 
24.1  This recommendation pertains to Ministry of Finance (Department of Financial 
Services). They have been requested for comments/ATNs which are awaited. 
  
 
Recommendation/Observation 
25.  The Committee further recommends that the financial institutions/banks with more 
than acceptable level of NPAs in the road sector should also undertake a study into the 
possible inefficacy of their existing mechanism to analyse the financial soundness as well as 
project execution capabilities of the concessionaire. The Committee strongly recommends 
that the financial institutions/banks should revisit their policies in this regard, whil e also 
having strong checks in place to ensure that there is no connivance between the bank's 
officials responsible for assessing the loan proposals received from the concessionaire, and 
the concessionaire themselves. 
(Para 218) 
Reply of Ministry 
25.1  This recommendation pertains to Ministry of Finance (Department of Financial 
Services). They have been requested for comments/ATNs which are awaited. 
 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
26.  The Committee notes the submission made by PNB that non -servicing of instalments 
within 90 days renders the account NPA, which attracts additional provisioning on such sub -

95 
 
standard assets. The Committee recommends that RBI may look into the possibility of setting 
a higher limit for long -term infrastructure projects, since u nfortunately as for now, delays of 
several months is not too uncommon in infrastructure projects in India, often for no fault of 
the concessionaire.  
(Para 220) 
  
Reply of Ministry 
 
26.1 This recommendation pertains to Ministry of Finance (Department of Financial 
Services). They have been requested for comments/ATNs which are awaited.. 
 
  
Recommendation/Observation 
27.  The Committee recommends that the Ministry may reach out to the private sector with 
proposals to invest their CSR funds into road safety initiatives such as training of drivers, 
road safety awareness drives, developing infrastructure for quickly reaching out to road 
accident victims etc., which will undoubtedly save many lives each year, across the country. 
(Para 285) 
Reply of Ministry 
27.1   Under examination 
  
Recommendation/Observation 
28.  The Committee notes the steps being taken by the Government of Karnataka to reduce 
the number of road accidents in the State and hopes that the black spots identified by 
Karnataka PWD are rectified as soon as possible.  
 (Para 301) 
Reply of Ministry 
28.1   Under examination 
  
 
Recommendation/Observation 
 
 29.  The Committee takes note of the status of the ongoing road projects in Andhra 
Pradesh and desires that the Ministry may analyze the need of upgradation of suitable State 
Highways in Andhra Pradesh into National Highways. 
 (Para 342) 
Reply of Ministry 
 
29.1   Under examination 
  
 
Recommendation/Observation 
30.   The Committee notes from the Annual report (2020 -2021) of the Ministry that the 
total number of registers vehicles in India is 29.57 crores, according to the provisional data 

96 
 
for the year 2019, with a CAGR of 9.91 percent for the years 2009 to 2019. The percentage of 
electric vehicles in the country this comes out to somewhere around 0.17 percent of the total 
vehicles plying in the country. The Committee is disappointed to note the very slow adoption 
of electric vehicles in India, with several countries acr oss the world already having share of 
electric cars in double digits. The Committee desires that concrete measures are taken by the 
Ministry to enact policies to aid much faster growth of adoption of electric vehicles in the 
country. The Committee recommen ds that the Ministry, in coordination with Ministry of 
Power and automobile manufacturers may come up with a time-bound plan to create a robust 
vehicle charging infrastructure is critical to give a boost to the adoption of electric vehicles 
in the country, which would lead to considerable environmental benefits and help resolve the 
issue of pollution to some extent. 
(Para 359) 
Reply of Ministry 
30.1  Recommendation is under examination in consultation with  Ministry of Power and 
Heavy Industries. 
   
 
Recommendation/Observation 
 
31.  Further, the Committee Strongly  recommends that the Ministry may exempt electric 
vehicles from registration charges and toll tax. Financial incentives are necessary to create a 
spurt in the adoption of electric vehicles in the country, which, in turn, will increase the pace 
at which inf rastructure is being created for the shift to such vehicles. The Committee 
recommends that the Ministry may undertake an in depth analysis of the policies adopted by 
countries across the world which have succeeded in   enabling mass adoption of the electric  
vehicles in the country, and come with an effective time -bound plan with well-defined targets 
for electric vehicle adoption in India. 
(Para 360) 
 
 Reply of Ministry 
 
31.1  Under examination in consultation with Ministry of Power and Heavy Industries.

97 
 
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS – AT A GLANCE 
 
CHAPTER-III 
 
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS IN RESPECT OF WHICH REPLIES OF 
THE MINISTRY HAVE NOT BEEN ACCEPTED BY THE COMMITTEE 
 
 The Committee feels that a large number of National Highways across the 
country are marred by dangerous potholes and need s to be maintained in a better state. 
The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Ministry may allocate some part of the 
maintenance budget to thor oughly monitor the vast network of National Highways 
across the country to be able to carry out the repair works of potholes within no times, 
which will enable to prevent any possible accidents due to poor state of NHs.  
(Para 1.3) 
 
 The Committee desires to be kept apprised of the progress made by the Ministry 
with regard to preparation of draft Policy Note/ SOP on the viability of having 
provisions for utility corridors and the decision regarding creation of a Special Purpose 
Vehicle for the purpose of mo netization of the utility corridors, based on the finalized 
policy.  
(Para 2.6) 
 
 The Committee recommends that the Ministry may allocate Research Funds not 
only regarding road construction techniques and materials utilized etc., but also to 
study and develop better mechanisms to monitor the quality of roads across the vast NH 
network in the country. Specific budget may be allocated for carrying out research 
activities to evolve a master plan to drastically improve the worrisome state of road 
safety in the country.  
(Para 3.4) 
 
 The Committee takes note of the various hindrances being faced in the filling up 
of vacancies in NHAI and appreciates the remedial actions being taken to overcome the 
same. The Committee, however, is anguished to note that the total manpower working 
in NHAI, including both regular officials and those on deputation, as on 30.08.2021 is 
just 1189 out of the total sanctioned strength of 1882. The Committee reiterates its 
observations made in para 10.4 of Chapter III of its 301 st Report on Action Taken by 
the Government on the Recommendations/ Observations of the Committee contained in 
its 287 th Report on the Demands for Grants (2021 - 22) of the Ministry that given the 
huge financial allocation made to NHAI each year, it is pertinent to en sure that 
sufficient manpower is in place so as to make optimal utilization of the available funds. 

98 
 
The Committee, therefore, recommends that the ongoing comprehensive review of 
existing Recruitment Rules of NHAI may be finalized at the earliest and sincer e efforts 
may be made to ensure that the vacancies presently lying unfilled in NHAI are filled up 
at the earliest.  
(Para 5.5) 
 
 The Committee notes that a significant percentage of vacancies still exist at the 
GM, DGM, Manager and Deputy Manager level, th e vacancies at Manager and Deputy 
Manager level hovering around 90 percent of the sanctioned strength. The Committee 
fails to understand how NHAI can be expected to carry out its mandate effectively when 
such a large number of senior posts are lying vacant  that too for a long time . The 
Committee recommends that the Ministry may take a serious look on this matter and 
resolve the underlying issues that are causing such a grave situation in NHAI , at the 
earliest.  
(Para 6.3) 
 
 The Committee recommends that NHAI may consider coming up with some sort 
of incentive scheme for its personnel having good experience to encourage them to gain 
professional qualifications. NHAI should aim to strike a balance between experience 
and professional qualifications while recruiting officers at high -level positions and the 
balance should be reflected in the Recruitment Rules for such posts. The Committee 
further recommends that NHAI should assess the anticipated vacancies well in advance 
since doin g so would allow NHAI more time to find the right candidates with good 
experience as well as professional qualifications.  
(Para 7.2) 
 
 The Committee feels that it might not be reasonable to assign heavy 
responsibilities to the existing officers with lesse r qualifications only to permit good 
promotional avenues to them. Only officers with enough experience and sufficient 
expertise should be granted the responsibility of high -level posts after carrying out the 
required assessment. Grant of timely financial upgradation may be considered for other 
officers. The Committee reiterates the recommendation made in para 7.2 of  Chapter III 
of this Report.  
(Para 9.3) 
 
 The Committee notes the various reasons behind the delays in completion of 
various road projects across the country. The Committee recommends that excepting 
the negative impact of the Coronavirus pandemic restrictions on the execution of 
projects, the Mini stry should take serious view of road projects being delayed on 
account of below -par performance by road contractors/ concessionaires. A mechanism 
may be put in place to award the road contract to a different concessionaire once a 
delay in execution has oc curred because of the existing concessionaire. The previous 

99 
 
performance of concessionaires may be taken into  consideration for award of future 
road project contracts.  
(Para 10.3) 
 
 The Committee desires to be apprised of the progress made by the Ministry in 
this regard.  
(Para 11.2) 
 
 The Committee desires to be apprised of the action taken by the Ministry to 
request formation of a panel of retired judges having expertise in infrastructural 
litigations in order to enable quicker judgements in case of disputes with 
concessionaires.  
(Para 12.2) 
 
 The Committee recommends that NHAI may give due importance to improving 
the Sukhad Yatra mobile application since the data submitted by the app users can help 
NHAI a lot in monitoring the state of National High ways across the country. User 
feedback received on the various application distribution platforms such as Google Play 
Store and Apple App Store, may be duly factored in future updates of the application 
and the data received from the users.  
(Para 13.3) 
 
 The Committee feels that the number of complaints received by NHAI through 
the app are minuscule, given the vast network of NHs across the country. The 
Committee recommends that the Ministry and NHAI may promote the Sukhad Yatra 
app through social media an d other means, so as to gain crucial information about 
requirement of maintenance of National Highways, which will also help in preventing 
the occurrence of road accidents due to poor state of Highways.  
(Para 14.3) 
  
 The Committee feels that without the existence of a central database, it would 
not be possible for the Ministry/NHAI to keep track of the road projects across the 
country that have been awarded to a concessionaire. The Committee, therefore, may be 
updated about the action taken by NHAI to cre ate and maintain a central database of 
road projects awarded to various concessionaires so as to permit NHAI to factor in the 
contract award history and performance history of a given concessionaire before 
awarding them a new road project.  
(Para 15.3) 
 
 The Committee recommends that the knowledge gained from such regular 
meetings with the lenders may be utilized to periodically update and revise the Model 

100 
 
Concession Agreement so as to encourage lenders to finance a higher number of 
National Highway projects.  
(Para 16.2) 
 
 The Committee reiterates its recommendation made in para 16.2 of  Chapter III 
of this Report.  
(Para 17.2) 
 
 The Committee had been informed by various financial institutions  that the 
construction of parallel roads is a major issue faced by them causing loss of revenue on 
tolled projects. The Committee, therefore, reiterates its original recommend ation that 
the Ministry may introduce appropriate rules/laws to ensure that const ruction of 
parallel roads by State or other agencies may be avoided at all costs and some sort of 
provision for payment of compensation to the concessionaire may be considered  by the 
Ministry.  
(Para 19.2) 
 
 The Committee recommends that the task of creating new PIUs may be 
completed at the earliest so as to share the workload of the overburdened PIUs. The 
Committee further recommends that action may be taken at the earliest indications of a 
project running of f-schedule and the performance of the concessionaires in terms of 
progress of work completed may be monitored closely for all road projects across the 
country.  
(Para 20.5 
 
 The Committee notes that the reply of the Ministry does not furnish any 
information regarding why the SARDP -NE Phase -B cannot be taken up along with 
SARDP-NE Phase A, since implementing both Phases in parallel might help complete 
the SARDP-NE programme at a quicker pace. The Committee, therefore, desires to be 
apprised of the reasons for not considering parallel execution of both Phases of SARDP-
NE.  
(Para 21.2) 
 
 The Committee notes the efforts made by the Ministry for timely execution of 
projects under SARDP -NE but given the huge delays that are currently faced in the 
programme, the Committee recommends that the Ministry may undertake a holistic 
review of the reasons for which the remedial efforts of the Ministry are not effective in 
resolving the delays being faced in SARDP-NE.  
(Para 22.2) 
  
 

101 
 
 The C ommittee feels that awarding road projects, especially in the North -East 
region, to the lowest bidder might be leading to below -par quality of roads being 
constructed, besides incapable concessionaires causing delays in road projects because 
of their financial and technical incapacities. T he Committee, therefore, reiterates its 
recommendation made in Para 26 of its 296 th Report, which is reproduced below 
verbatim: 
“The Committee further recommends the Ministry to carefully analyze the 
shortcomings of the existing mechanism for awarding road  projects to the lowest 
bidder, since doing so includes little thought for ensuring quality of the work. The 
Committee believes that there should be consideration for other importance factors 
besides the bidding amount, while awarding a project to a conces sionaire. A 
qualitative approach must be formulated for awarding road projects. The 
Committee recommends that the Ministry may take up with the Central Vigilance 
Commission (CVC), the shortcomings of the existing system of awarding a project 
to the lowest bidder, presenting its arguments for modification of the CVC 
guidelines for awarding of tender in a suitable way to permit an element of 
qualitative approach in the tender awarding process for road projects. The 
Committee feels that a criterion may be deve loped where certain weightage is given 
to objective parameters such as the awards presently being executed by the 
contractor, their financial record, and most importantly, the past performance of a 
contractor, in terms of quality of work and timely executi on. The database 
recommended by the Committee in para 22 of this Report may be useful for such 
purposes.” 
(Para 23.2) 
 
 The Committee recommends that the Ministry may lay special focus on timely 
completion of road projects in LWE affected areas in close co ordination with local law 
enforcement and other concerned departments.  
(Para 24.2) 
 
 The Committee may be apprised of the details of the various research activities 
that are being carried out by the SRD& Q Division of NHAI. The Committee further 
recommends that the Ministry may consider increasing the budget for research 
purposes in the upcoming years so as to allow research for improving construction 
quality in hilly and flood -prone regions, improving roa d safety across the country and 
developing a mechanism to effectively monitor the pliability of National Highways 
across the country so as to proactively prevent accidents from happening because of 
shoddy quality of roads.  
(Para 25.2) 
 
 The Committee notes the various steps being taken by the Ministry and the 
policy guidelines brought out by NHAI to improve road safety across the country but 
feels that given the ever-increasing number of deaths occurring due to road accidents in 
the country, a lot more  needs to be done urgently in order to minimize the same. The 

102 
 
Committee recommends that the Ministry/NHAI may review the safety audit process 
itself and ensure that the same is carried out in a transparent and honest manner. The 
Committee further recommend s that the identified black spots may be rectified at the 
earliest and the definition for identification of black spots may be tightened so as to 
identify and rectify more accident-prone spots across the NH network in the country.  
(Para 26.3) 
 
 The Committee recommends that the Ministry may speed up the process of 
rectification of black spots that have already been identified since these spots are very 
likely to cause more accidents if left unrectified. The status of all black spots may be 
kept regularly updated on the NHAI website and any delay in the rectification of black 
spots may be looked into urgently.  
(Para 27.3) 
 
 The Committee recommends that the tender for Computer Aided Dispatch 
System may be finalized at the earliest since providing timely emergency care during 
the golden hour can help save countless lives involved in road accidents across the 
country. The Committee desires to be kept apprised in this regard.   
(Para 28.2) 
 
 The Committee recommends that dedicated efforts may be made to promote the 
tollfree helpline number 1033 amongst highway users. The Committee may be apprised 
of the action taken by the Ministry to promote the usage of the number 1033 through 
social media and other means.  
(Para 29.2) 
 
 The Committee appreciates the  efforts of the Ministry to rope in the private 
sector by vesting Driving Training Centres with functions such as testing of aspirants 
for issuance of driving licence, which will hopefully make such centres a successful 
business proposition. Having well -trained drivers on the Indian roads would go a long 
way in improving road safety and aiming to have Driving Training Centres in all 
districts of the country would be the first step towards that. The Committee, therefore, 
recommends that the Ministry may cons ider providing some aid to the interested 
parties in terms of lending for setting up such Driving Training Centres, in 
collaboration with financial institutions.  
(Para 30.6) 
 
 The Committee recommends that latest safety standards adopted for vehicles 
globally, may be suitably incorporated in the Indian vehicle safety standards from time 
to time, so as to minimize the number of deaths occurring on Indian roads due to road 
accidents.  

103 
 
(Para 31.4) 
 
 The Committee hopes that the Ministry would be able to complete the remaining 
projects under the Char dham Pariyojana within the targeted date of completion of 
December, 2024. The Committee recommends that all possible measures may be taken 
from the planning stage itself to ensure that the road projects of the M inistry cause 
minimal impact on the environment, especially in eco -sensitive hilly regions. This would 
help lower the delays faced on account of Court litigations and petitions in the NGT.  
(Para 32.2) 
 
 The Committee reiterates its recommendation made in para 32.2 of  Chapter III 
of this Report.  
(Para 33.3) 
 
 The Committee notes the reply. The Committee further recommends that in 
future, such Rapid Environmental Impact Assessment may be proactively carried out 
by the Ministry for all of its major National Highways projects in ecologically sensitive 
regions.  
(Para 34.2) 
 
 The Committee may be apprised about the action taken by the Ministry in this 
regard.  
(Para 35.2) 
 
 The Committee notes the advisories put in place at present by the Ministry with 
regard to PUC centres. The Committee recommends that the Ministry may  consider 
incorporation of stricter guidelines in its advisory  in order to curb malpractices that 
allow polluting vehicles to pass the pollution test, by way of video recording when 
pollution tests are conducted.  
(Para 36.8) 
 
 The Committee recommends that NHAI may include the option to report 
requirement of maintenance of roadside plantations on National Highways, so that 
highway users can bring such requirement to the notice of NHAI for timely  action. 
Besides, NHAI may ensure that such maintenance activities are carried out periodically 
without fail, since overgrown trees and bushes can lead to visibility issues, which in turn 
can lead to lethal accidents.  
(Para 37.5) 
 

104 
 
 The Committee recommend s that guidelines similar to those that have been 
issued regarding construction of bridge structures passing over declared National 
Waterways, may be issued for construction of such bridge structures over other inland 
waterways as well. The guidelines in t his regard may be framed in close coordination 
with the Ministry of Ports, Shipping and Waterways and other concerned departments. 
The Committee feels that doing it is necessary to ensure the development of road 
infrastructure may not cause hindrance in us age of inland waterways as a means of 
transportation.  
(Para 38.2)

CHAPTER-I 
 
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS WHICH HAVE BEEN ACCEPTED BY 
THE MINISTRY 
Air Traffic Services 
Recommendation/Observation  
1. The Committee recommends that a High Powered Committee should be constituted 
both for flexi air space management and issues related to Civil Enclaves to address these 
issues comprehensively. 
(Para 9.8) 
Reply of the Ministry 
1.1 NHLAPB (National High Level Airspace Policy Body) has been constituted in 2013 
for the flexible use of Airspace  (FUA) in accordance with the FUA Manual approved by 
Government of India in 2011  
1.2 Based on the directives of Government of India under the AtmaNirbhar Bharat 
Abhiyan (ANB), AAI had taken up issue of e fficient use of airspace usi ng Flexible Use of 
Airspace concept with IAF, Indian Navy and HAL for optimum use of airspace in May 2020. 
The airspace released on daily basis is being utilized by all stakeholders. 
1.3 Actions Taken:- 
(i) 116 Conditional Routes (CDRs) implemented. 
 
(ii) National Airspace Management Cells (NAMC) at Delhi Air Traffic Flow 
Management (ATFM) centre and Regional Airspace Management Cells (RAMC) 
at Delhi (IGIA) & Chennai Airport have been established. 
(iii) Upper Airspace of 46 Restricted Areas of IAF has been converted as Temporary 
Reserved Airspace (TRA). 
(iv) 24 Danger Areas of Army de-notified. Upper limit of Two Danger Areas lowered 
to 10000 ft Above Mean Sea Level (AMSL). 
(v) Five new CDR proposals sent to IAF for concurrence in September 2021. 
 
Development, Upgradation and Modernization of Airports 
Recommendation/Observation  
2. The Committee underlines the need for a well chalked out Master Plan with regard to 
aviation infrastructure, in order to ensure that the requirements of the growth in the civil 

3 
 
aviation sector are properly catered to. The Committee urges the Ministry to ensure that 
adequate parking space and landing slots are available at the airports. 
(Para 10.8) 
Reply of the Ministry 
2.1 All Airports are being comprehensively planned and develo ped considering 30 years 
forecast. Accordingly, land is earmarked/ additional land is requested from State 
Governments based on long-term futuristic development of single runway or parallel runway 
configurations and the type of aircraft expected to operate  in future considering the potential 
of traffic it will be handling. Due to the dynamic nature of development, the Master Plans are 
reviewed regularly based on the revised growth forecast. 
2.2 Based on the futuristic traffic projections adequate Aircraft parking bays and slot 
management are created and planned at the airports, such that it would be able to meet all the 
future traffic demand. 
2.3 Around Rs.  90,000 crores of investments are expected to be pumped into Civil 
Aviation Sector in the next 5 years  out of which AAI alone will invest Rs.25000 crores for 
infrastructure creation. The remaining approx. Rs. 65,000 is being spent by the private sector. 
2.4 To meet the demand, AAI has embarked upon a capital expenditure (CAPEX) plan of 
Rs. 25000 crores in next five years for development / modernization / up gradation of airport 
infrastructure projects of AAI airports in the country.   418 additional parking bays are 
planned at various AAI airports in next five years for night parking of new aircrafts being 
purchased by airline operators. In addition, big ticket projects like expansion of existing 
Delhi, Hyderabad and Be ngaluru airports are being executed by private airport operators. 
Further, new mega Greenfield airports such as Navi Mumbai, Mopa, Jewar, Dhol era, Rajkot, 
Hollongi etc. are also under implementation.  
Recommendation/Observation  
3. The Committee notes that potential growth in the passenger and cargo traffic would 
require enormous investments in terms of construction of new airports and expansion  & 
modernization of existing airports. The Committee understands that lenders are cautious 
about issuing long -term debt to airport operators. The Committee, therefore, would like the 
Ministry to formulate necessary policies, schemes and guidelines, to attr act the requisite 
investment for airport projects. 
(Para 10.9) 
Reply of the Ministry 
3.1 Government of India has put the Greenfield Airports Policy, 2008 in place. The policy 
outlines the guidelines for setting up of Greenfield Airports across the country by Government 
or private entities. A Greenfield airport can be developed and operated eit her by AAI / State 
Government or by an Airport Company that has been given a license by DGCA as per its 

4 
 
licensing conditions. As per the policy provisions, the airport developer is solely responsible 
for execution of the airport including funding arrangement.  
3.2 Government has granted “In -Principle” approval for construction of 21 green -field 
airports, out of which 8 airports Durgapur, Kurnool, Shirdi, Kannur, Pakyong  & Kalaburagi 
,Kushinagar and Sindhdurghave been commissioned and the other airports like  Dholera, 
Hirasar, Navi Mumbai, Jewar, Mopa (Goa), Hollongi are under development. 
 
Vande Bharat Mission (VBM)  
 Recommendation/Observation  
4. The Committee desires that the Ministry should ensure that amenities which match up 
to international standards a re available at all the airports and that periodic maintenance is 
carried out efficiently. The Committee recommends that the Ministry should ensure sufficient 
space for commercial shops, while granting approval for new airports. The Committee 
recommends that the Ministry should consider mandatorily earmarking minimum 100 acres 
of land, while making plans for future airports. Further, 5 Star/3 Star hotels and multiplexes 
should be constructed near the new airports. The Committee also desires that extra land,  if 
any, that has been allocated for the airports should not be sold and should be kept for future 
aviation developmental activities. 
(Para 10.10) 
Reply of the Ministry 
4.1 The prevailing best practices followed in the world have already been adopted by the 
Airports Authority of India (AAI) while developing Airport infrastructure. Terminal 
Buildings are being designed to accommodate state of Art technologies with world class 
facilities. Terminals are being incorporated with technologies to have touch less movement of 
passengers which includes scanners and monitors at various check points such as entry gates, 
immigration etc. Further Body scanners are being procured for touchless Security checks at 
the Indian Airports. 
4.2 To have a smooth Passenger experience, AAI is in process of implementing Biometric 
Access Control System at 43 airports. AAI also has plans to initiate DIGIYATRA, Bio -
Metric e-boarding system with a facial recognition facilitating seamless passenger movement 
across multiple touch points at  Airport Terminal Buildings, being implemented at 4 AAI 
airports. Kolkata, Pune, Varanasi and Vizag. 
4.3 AAI is also emphasizing the barrier free environment at the Airport by providing 
ramps, toilets for differently abled persons, Braille symbols in lift and auditory signals in lift 
as well as escalators and aerobridges. Efforts are being made to provide ambulifts wherever 
the aerobridges could not be provided. The disabled friendly passenger coaches on airside are 
also being procured.  

5 
 
4.4 Further, Airports Authority of India earns revenues from Aeronautical and Non -
Aeronautical resources. Non -Aeronautical resources include earmarking 10 -15% area of a 
Terminal building for Offices, Retail and F&B. Also city side land is leased for non -
Aeronautical activities as identified in the AAI Act which include hotels, restaurants, 
warehouses etc. 
Recommendation/Observation  
5. The Committee has been given to understand that large num ber of institutional 
clearances are required for airport projects, w hich leads to delays and cost escalation. 
Therefore, the Committee recommends in this regard that the Ministry should set up a single -
window clearance mechanism in order to facilitate timely grant of institutional clearances for 
airport projects and ensure completion of such projects within the stipulated time period. 
(Para 10.12) 
Reply of the Ministry 
5.1. For any airport to be developed, activities relating to Air Traffic Services (ATS), 
security, customs and immigration would be reserved for central government agencies. 
Provision of these services would be governed by the policy to be laid down by the Cent ral 
Government from time to time. These activities include Defence clearance, Air Traffic 
Services (ATS) Functions by AAI (CNS-ATM), Security clearances as per Guidelines for this 
purpose, issued by the Ministry of Civil Aviation from time to time, Customs  clearance from 
the Department of Revenue for provision of Custom services, MHA Clearance for 
Immigration in case of an international airport, BCAS Clearance for security and IMD 
clearances for Airport Meteorological Services.  
5.2 Ministry of Civil Aviation (MoCA) has been signing Memorandum of 
Understandings ( MoUs) with all the airport operators given under lease to private parties 
whereas there is a provision to provide single window clearances for necessary clearance. 
Further, under Greenfield Airports Policy of MoCA, clearances for new airport projects are 
granted by MoCA as a single window. Therefore, single-window clearance mechanism for 
airport projects is already in place. 
 
 
Privatization of Airports 
Recommendation/Observation  
6. The Committee realizes the huge demand for more airports in the country. The 
Committee recognizes the fact that it is not feasible for AAI to meet the investment 
requirements to develop and maintain all the airports in the co untry. The Committee 
appreciates the inevitable need for Public Private Partnership in the development and 
maintenance of airports. The Committee endorses the provisions proposed in the Airports 

6 
 
Economic Regulatory Authority of India (Amendment) Bill, 2021  which would facilitate the 
development of both high traffic volume and low traffic volume airports together, in a holistic 
manner. 
(Para 11.10) 
Reply of the Ministry 
6.1 On the similar endorsement by the Hon'ble Committee, AAI has awarded six airports 
namely, Ahmedabad, Lucknow, Mangaluru, Jaipur, Thiruvananthapuram and Guwahati 
under PPP mode during 2019-2020. 
6.2 AAI is in the process of undertaking next round of PPP transaction of 06 select 
Airports by clubbin g them with 7 smaller Airports for PPP bi dding. Each group will be 
treated as a single airport by the AERA for the purpose of tariff determination. 
6.3 For the purpose, the AERA Act has been amended which will enable AAI to club 
small airports with select airport forming a group while undertaking  PPP transaction of 
Airport. 
Recommendation/Observation  
7. The Committee emphasizes the need to ensure absolute transparency in all PPP 
airport projects. The Committee desires that the Ministry should ensure that a proper policy 
and regulatory framework g overning the PPP airport projects, is put in place. The 
Committee underlines the need to ensure a proper auditing mechanism with regard to PPP 
projects. The Committee strongly recommends that the Ministry should ensure that the 
airport charges on the passe ngers are equitable and commensurate with the operational 
costs. 
(Para 11.11) 
Reply of the Ministry 
7.1. The Concession Agreement has provision of auditing of book of accounts of the 
concessionaires by independent auditors. 
7.2 AAI has the right, either through itself or through any of its authorized representative, 
to inspect the records of the Concessionaire during office hours and require copies of relevant 
extracts of books of accounts, duly certified by the Statutory Auditors, to be provided to the 
Authority for verification of basis of payments, and in the event of any discrepancy or error 
being found, the same shall be rectified and such rectified account shall form the basis of 
payments by either Party under this Agreement. 
7.3 Additionally, the Airport charges of the Airports being taken up for PPP transactions 
are determined by an independent regulator i.e. Airports Economic Regulatory 
Authority AERA. AERA determines the aeronautical tariffs of major airport in accordance to 

7 
 
AERA Act and AERA guid elines issued from time to time. The tariffs are determined to 
maintain and operate the airport along with a reasonable return on investment.

Development of Cargo Sector 
Recommendation/Observation  
10. The Committee takes serious note of the fact that due to the Open Sky Policy for cargo 
in India, foreign carriers carry 90% - 95% of the international cargo, to and from India, 
while Indian air cargo operators face many barriers when they go into other countries. The 
Committee, therefore, recommends that in order to provide a level playing field for Indian air 
cargo operators, the Ministry of Civil Aviation should make appropriate changes in the Open 
Sky Policy for cargo. The Committee also recommends that Ministry/DGCA should take note 
of Indian cargo operators facing discriminatory and restrictive practices or regulatory 
impediments in operating international cargo flights in any of the foreign countries and take 
urgent steps to address/resolve them. The Committee may be apprised of the action ta ken and 
the outcome achieved in this regard. 
(Para 13.9) 
Reply of the Ministry 
10.1 Ministry of Civil Aviation has already reviewed the Open Sky Policy for Foreign 
Cargo carriers as promulgated vide AIC/1992 dated 11.05.1992 and appropriate changes have 
been made with a view to ensure fair and equal opportunity in the air cargo capacity offered 
by Indian registered airlines and airlines registered elsewhere. The revised open sky policy 
has been promulgated vide AIC 41/2020 dated 31-12-2020. 
10.2 Under the  revised policy, the operations of foreign ad hoc pure and pure non -
scheduled freighter charter service flights have been restricted to 6 airports, namely 
Bengaluru, Chennai, Delhi, Kolkata, Hyderabad, and Mumbai, and Operations of Scheduled 

9 
 
cargo operatio n by foreign carriers is permitted as per the provisions of the Bilateral Air 
Service Agreement (ASA) with the respective country. 
Impact of the COVID-19 pandemic 
Recommendation/Observation  
11.  The Committee is well aware of the fact that the aviation sector has been badly hit by 
the COVID-19 pandemic. The Committee understands that the adverse effect of the COVID -
19 pandemic on the airlines operating in the country, which were already reeling under 
heavy losses, was unprecedented. The Committee recommends that the Ministry should adopt 
relief measures to help the airlines tide over the adverse impact of the pandemic and that the 
Ministry should envisage immediate and long term measures, to enable the resurgence of the

(Para 18.5) 
Reply of the Ministry 
11.1 On account of COVID -19 pandemic, Ministry of Civil Aviation has issued 
comprehensive guidelines in May, 2020 for ensuring safe travel. Directorate General of Civil

compliance of COVID-19 protocols at airport premises. 
11.2 In view of extraordinary situation arising due to spread of pandemic, Government of 
India invoking special provisions under Aircraft Act regulated the operations of sc heduled 
airlines through capacity capping and introduction of fare band which was reviewed from 
time to time depending on the pandemic situation and demand. As on date, there is no 
capping and fare bands are operational on 15 days cycle. 
Recommendation/Observation

Air Traffic Services 
Recommendation/Observation  
1. The Committee is of the considered opinion that keeping in view the exponential air 
traffic growth witnessed in the country in the past few years, it is essential that best 
international practices as regards the Air Navigatio n Services are adopted and implemented 
in the country. The Committee strongly feels that a futuristic Master Plan for Air Navigation 
Services is inevitable so that substantial benefits are accrued to all the stakeholders. The 
Committee emphasizes the need to ensure strict adherence to the international standards of 
safety and security. The Committee recommends that the Ministry should ensure that steps 
should be taken to upgrade the ANS facilities and procedures and to give due emphasis on 
research, development and training.  
(Para 9.3) 
Reply of the Ministry 
1.1 Airports Authority of India (AAI) is continuously upgrading its Air Navigation 
Services (ANS) Infrastructure to meet the air traffic growth. AAI has undertaken Upper 
Airspace Harmonization (UAH) Programme for better capacity and efficiency facilitating 
safe and seamless movement of air traffic within Indian airspace. Harmonization of Chennai 
and Kolkata airspace has been completed. 
1.2 The entire terrestrial airspace of India is under surveillance  coverage through a 
network of Primary & Secondary Radar and Automatic Dependent Surveiilance -Broadcast 
(ADS-B) surveillance system. From January 2020, the entire oceanic airspace controlled by 
AAI has been brought under surveillance coverage by hiring Satellite based ADS-B services. 
1.3 The communication facilities have been upgraded to Internet Protocol (IP) based 
technology for seamless coverage. AAI has established Futuristic Telecomm Infrastructure 
(FTI). It is a Service Level Agreement (SLA) based sys tem ensuring 99.99% to 99.999% 
availability, using latest technology and communication infrastructure at each AAI location. 
This will help improve airspace safety, capacity, and efficiency. ATM Automation equipment 
completing its lifecycle are continuously  upgraded. AAI planned to upgrade/ replace ATC 
automation System at 38 airports to modernize the ATC System. 
1.4 For optimum use of airport resources and airspace and thus reducing airspace/airport 
congestion AAI has implemented Central Air Traffic Flow Ma nagement (C -ATFM) from 
2017. This will also reduce environmental impact due to less emission and helping fuel 
saving by airlines. 

13 
 
1.5 To continue this modernization effort to meet the future demand, Airports Authority 
of India (AAI) entered into an agreeme nt with United States Trade and Development Agency 
(USTDA) to develop a Communications, Navigation and Surveillance/Air Traffic 
Management (CNS/ATM) roadmap to improve airspace utilization and implement 
CNS/ATM air and ground infrastructure in the short, m edium and long term (upto 10 years)  
for modernization on 16th November, 2018. 
1.6 The study has been carried out by M/s Boeing, USA in consultation with all 
stakeholders such as Airlines, Airport Operators, DGCA and AAI to assist AAI in preparing a 
futuristic comprehensive Masterplan for CNS and ATM facilities and services along with 
guidance on implementation process and regulatory requirements.    
1.7 The report has been submitted by M/s Boeing in October 2021.Based on this 
document, AAI will prepare its roadmap by December 2022 for next 10 years .The Roadmap 
will be dovetailed with th e National Air Navigation Plan to be developed by MoCA , which 
is an ICAO requirement. 
1.8 AAI is upgrading its ANS training facilities with state -of-the-art Training simulators 
(such as Aerodrome Tower Visual Simulator, Flight Simulator Training Device, A TC 
Procedural Simulator, ATC Radar Simulator) as part of training improvement plan.    
1.9 To promote Research & Development in Civil Aviation, AAI is developing a Civil

conditions, opening up new opportun ities in redelivery checks and aircraft 
component recycling.

(ix) Foreign manufacturers are being encouraged to set up their MRO facilities on 
their own or through joint ventures with Indian players.

Air Traffic Services 
Recommendation/Observation  
1. The Committee is disturbed to note that considerable delay in flight operations and 
cancellation of flights occur at various airports, due to non -availability of CAT-II or CAT-III 
facility. The Committee takes serious note of the inconvenience and delays faced by the flyers 
and international & domestic tourists, due to the dearth of requisite navigation technology at 
the airports. The Committee fails to understand the reason behind non -installation of CAT-II/ 
CAT-III facilities in all airports in the country, in the present age of modern technolo gy. The 
Committee recommends that the Ministry should ensure that the upgradation of air 
navigation infrastructure in the country should be given utmost priority and that the 
navigation facilities should be kept in line with international standards. 
(Para 9.5) 
Reply of the Ministry

feasibility at the airport.

1.5 Also, Low Visibility Procedures (LVP), which allows aircraft operations in low 
visibility condition, arising due to fog, have been implemented at most of the airports.

UDAN Scheme 
Recommendation/Observation  
5. The Committee takes note of the growing demand for regional air services, which 
would make it possible for our country to emerge as a major player in the aviation industry. 
The Committee feels that UDAN Scheme will help in relieving the congestion at major 
airports and enable us to develop the much needed hub -and-spoke mechanism. The 
Committee notes that although the airlines industry got a huge fillip with the launch of RCS, 
air connectivity in the country is largely confined to routes connecting State capitals and 
large towns; and many parts of the country still remain unconnected by air services. 
Therefore, the Committee recommends that the Ministry of Civil Aviation should take urgent 
effective steps to ensure adequate air connectivity in different parts of the country under RCS. 
The Committee also desires that the benefits under the Regional Connectivity Scheme, 
currently restricted to three years, should be extended by another two years, to give airlines 
an opportunity to transform a fledgling route into a strong and revenue-generating one.

5.1 UDAN Scheme was launched by MoCA on 21.10.2016. Since then 154 RCS airports

5.2 Against these routes, 403 routes connecting 65 unserved and underserved airports 
(including 8 heliports & 02 water aerodromes) have been operationalized as on 14.12.2021.  
5.3 The Special round of bidding 4.1, which is in progress, also includes past round 
(cancelled) routes, as well as the routes that are sponsored by State Government/UTs. 
5.4 With regard to recommendation of the committee for extension of benefits under the 
Regional Connectivity Scheme  by another two years which is currently restricted to three 
years  it is to mention that out of 94 RCS -Udan  routes that have completed 3 year tenure till 
30.11.2021, only 22 routes are in operation. Among 403 routes that have commenced 
operations so far, nearly 300 routes have been affected due to poor demand on account of 
covid-19 pandemic situation. For sustainability of awarded routes and scheme in general 
extension of 1 year benefits has been granted under the scheme in respect of the r outes which 
have completed or going to complete its tenure by 31.12.2021. 
Further Recommendation/ Observation 
5.5  The Committee notes with concern that among 403 routes that have commenced 
operations so far, nearly 300 routes have been affected due to poor demand on account 
of Covid-19 pandemic situation. The Committee recommends that the ministry should 

36 
 
formulate plans and expeditio usly revive all the 300 UDAN routes, as and when Covid-
19 pandemic situation improves across the country.

vi) Customs Brokers presence for Import Cargo Clearance & Export Cargo process.

viii) Customs app ointed Custodians presence with appropriate warehouse facility 
including for Trans-shipment facilities. 
ix) BCAS/DGCA Clearance/Presence. 
x) Appropriate Security Deployment.

Recommendations/ Observations:- 
1 The Committee would like the Ministry to elaborate upon how the establishment of 
various Coastal Employment Units (CEUs) creation of Port -linked industrial clusters have 
resulted in reduced logistics cost for EXIM and domestic trade. The Committee would also 
like the Ministry to formulate policies for generation of employment opportuni ties with 
involvement of personnel in various activities of construction, operations and maintenance of 
projects in regard to creation of Coastal Economic Zones (CEZs), Coastal Economic Units 
(CEUs), Port-Linked Industrial & Maritime Clusters and Smart Industrial Port Cities. 
   
(Para: 16) 
Reply of the Ministry 
1.1 The Government of India, under Sagarmala Programme, intends to develop Coastal 
Employment Unit in proximity to Major Ports. These industrial developments are envisaged 
to be large scale integrated multi -product industrial zone catering to both domestic and 
export-oriented manufacturing.  
1.2 The Coastal Economic Zone (CEZ) has been envisaged to facilitate p ort led 
industrialization and/or Export Import (EXIM)/coastal trade of goods & commodities. CEZ is 
a spatial economic region comprising a large area in a single district or in a group of coastal  
districts or in district(s) with strong linkage to ports in that region/vicinity with an intent to 
reduce the logistics costs from demand/supply center to port and vice versa. 
1.3 It has a dual focus – direct contribution of port traffic coupled with empl oyment 
generation and reduction of logistics costs. Such a zone is envisaged to comprise industrial 
areas / estates, housing & urban infrastructure, and logistics/ transport infrastructure within 
itself to be a self-contained region with a direct or a strong port linkage. 
1.4 The aim is to achieve the following objectives:  
a. Creating large scale employment opportunities in the coastal regions across identified 
sectors to promote development in coastal regions.  
b. Increasing competitiveness of India's EXIM trade  by reducing logistics costs through 
proximity and connectivity to ports.

MODEL CONCESSION AGREEMENT  
Recommendations/ Observations:- 
13 The Committee observes that the resources required to build the necessary Port 
infrastructure are huge and therefore, supplementation of public investment by private sector 
investment through PPP mode is inevitable. It is in this context that successful working of 
PPP model assumes added significance in realizing the targeted Port capacity augmentation. 
The Committee, therefore, welcomes th e changes ushered in by the MCA, 2018. While 
endorsing the revised MCA, 2018, the Committee desires to know as to what extent the Model 
Concession Agreement, 2018 (amended) has succeeded in obviating the problems faced in 
execution of PPP projects and make  the investment in Port sector attractive. Further, the 
Ministry should apprise the Committee of the provisions in MCA, 2018 which are proving to 
be impediments in the implementation and maintenance of PPP projects. 
 (Para: 90) 

11 
 
Reply of the Ministry 
13.1 The Model Concession Agreement (MCA) governing the PPP Projects in the Ports 
Sector was first introduced in the year 2008 and was subsequently revised in 2018 based  on 
the stakeholders‟ feedback.  Recently, Government of India has enacted Major Port 
Authorities Act, 2021 that aims to reorient the governance model in Major ports to landlord 
port model in line with the successful global practice. Further, the Act empowers the Major 
Ports to perform with greater efficiency on account of increased autonomy in de cision 
making and it also aims to make the sector more responsive to dynamic market needs.  The 
existing MCA needs to be aligned with these developments to encourage participation of the 
private players and address the requirements of stakeholders (Private  terminal operators, Port 
Authorities, and lenders) to ensure that risks of each of the stakeholder are well balanced. 
Accordingly, The Ministry of Ports, Shipping & Waterways (MoPSW), has revised the MCA, 
2018 for PPP Projects at Major Ports  and issued new MCA, 2021 on 12 November 2021.  
The new MCA will be applicable to all  the future PPP projects at Major Ports as well as 
projects which are already approved by the Government and are still under bidding stage. 
13.2 Some of the key changes ma de in the  new MCA, 2021 are as follows : - First, 
provision of Change in Cargo due to Change in Law or Unforeseen Events has been 
introduced. There have been cases in the past wherein due to external and unforeseen factors, 
traffic for a particular commodit y has dropped during the concession period thereby 
impacting the overall viability of the terminal. The concessionaire did not have flexibility to 
handle a different cargo and the asset constructed was not being utilized optimally. This 
provision gives the flexibility to undertake change in cargo in such situation and reduces risk 
for the concessionaire. Second, flexibility provided to the concessionaires to fix tariff based 
on market conditions which will allow level playing field for the private terminals  at Major 
Ports to compete with private ports for cargo. Further, to reduce risk to the lenders and make 
the project more bankable, provision of compensation for Concessionaire‟s event of default 
before Commercial Operations Date (COD) has been added. Anot her provision which lays 
out process for extension of concession period on the basis of performance and mutual 
agreement has been introduced. Overall, more clarity has been provided in terms of 
responsibilities of both public as well as private party while balancing the risks. 
13.3 With many other changes drawn from best practices from across the sectors and 
extensive stakeholder consultation, the MCA, 2021, will bring more confidence of 
developers, investors and lenders and other stakeholders in the Ports sector and catalyze the 
investment in the sector.

PROMOTION OF COASTAL SHIPPING  
Recommendations/ Observations 
7 The Committee is of the considered view that coastal shipping is a fuel efficient and 
an environment friendly mode that can ease traffic congestion. Despite having an extensive 
network of inland waterways in the form of rivers, canals, backwaters and creeks, freight 
transportation by waterways is highly under-utilized. Waterways currently contribute around 
6% to India's transportation modal mix, which is significantly less than that in deve loped 
economies and some of the developing economies as well. The Committee, therefore, 
recommends that availability of dedicated infrastructure will go a long way in promoting 
coastal shipping as a mode of freight transportation. Hence infrastructure at P orts and 
supporting infrastructure using rail/road and waterways to facilitate coastal movement 
should be created which includes development of dedicated coastal berths, bunkering and 
storage at Ports and creation of supporting hinterland transport infrast ructure with last mile 
connectivity.            
(Para: 65) 
Reply of the Ministry 
7.1 MoPSW acknowledges that availability of dedicated infrastructure will go a long way 
in promoting coastal shipping as a mode of freight transportation. Hence infrastructure  at 
ports and supporting infrastructure using rail/road and waterways to facilitate coastal 
movement are being created. These include development of dedicated coastal berths, 
bunkering and storage at ports and creation of supporting hinterland transport in frastructure 
with last mile connectivity. 
 7.2 To boost trade with up -gradation of port facilities to global standards and for making 
coastal shipping viable at many instances, there are 17 projects worth Rs. 1815 Crore which 
focus on providing infrastruct ure for coastal handling of cargo. 5 projects worth Rs. 321 

35 
 
Crore have been completed, 4 projects are currently under implementation and 8 more 
projects are under various stages of development. 5 projects are being implemented at major 
ports whereas 12 projects are for improving coastal infrastructure at non-major ports.  
Further Recommendations/ Observations

creation of supporting hinterland transport infrastructure with last mile connectivity. 
The Committee desires that the Ministry provide the details of funding and 
development time required by the  projects under implementation as well as projects 
under various stages of development.

8.2  Further, 
1. Maritime education and training in India is administrated by the Director General 
of Shipping, Gov. of India (DG Shipping), in accordance with the STCW 
Convention and Merchant Shipping (STCW) Rules, 2014 
2. India has 154 Maritime Training Institutes (MTIs) set up all over the country, 
offering Pre-sea and Post –sea maritime training in various streams / disciplines.  
3. In order to implement the applicable provisions of the international convention 
and to ensure the quality and uniformity of training among the growing number of 
such institutes, the DG Shipping has developed the Comprehensive Inspection 
Program (CIP) for the MTIs with grading mechanism. To achieve this objectives, 

36 
 
necessary guidelines and assessme nt checklists, identifying such structured and 
objective parameters against which every such institutes will be graded, on an 
annual basis, have been formalized. Authorized Classification Societies, as 
Recognized organizations (ROs) carries out such inspec tion, gradation and 
certification of MTIs.  
4. Any Classification Society authorized by the Government of India as Recognized 
Organisation (RO) vide Govt. of India, Ministry of Shipping Notification, S.O. 
2044 (E) dated 06.09.2011 having entered into agreemen t with DGS may offer 
their services for the inspection, gradation and certification of the institutes. 
5. Unscheduled inspections: The unscheduled inspection of any MTI may be carried 
out anytime. Unscheduled inspections may also be undertaken based on specif ic 
bona-fide complaints. The unscheduled inspections shall be carried out by the 
Directorate and/or MMDs. The inspection team shall be nominated by the 
Directorate or the Principal Officer (PO) and may comprise of officers from the 
Directorate and/or from any Mercantile Marine Department (MMD). The 
Directorate or the MMD may utilize the services of external assessors nominated 
by the Directorate. 
6. Suitable actions are initiated against the MTI in case major deficiencies are noted 
by the inspection team. The Directorate has taken strict action against MTI not 
meeting the DG Shipping Guidelines and having major deficiencies. In last five 
years the Directorate has closed down around 11 such MTIs.

5. Mumbai Port Trust  
Comments: (A) Background of Policy Guidelines for Land Management (PGLM) 2015: 
 
(1)          Mumbai Port Trust has about 275 Ha. of land falling under township areas and 
consisting of 524 Nos. of expired leases, 1977 Nos. of Monthly Tenancies & Fifteen Mon thly 
Leases and 250 Nos. of running leases. In the past when Mumbai Port Trust revised its rentals 
with effect from 1982 based on the valuation done by the Valuers in 1980, it led to a spate of 
litigations and the revision was struck down by the Hon‟ble Bo mbay High Court.   At the 
suggestions of the Hon‟ble Bombay High Court, the rates had to be substantially moderated 
under the “Compromise proposals” formulated by the Port, which was further adjudicated 
and the rates further moderated by the Hon‟ble Supreme  Court. These litigations continued 
for almost 24 (twenty-four) years with multiple litigations. Ultimately, the issue of revision of 
rent and Board‟s compromise policy was settled by the judgment given by the Hon‟ble 
Supreme Court in the Civil Appeal No.5 559 of 2001 dated 13th January, 2004 and 9th 
January 2006. The prolonged litigation affected the revenue from let out land of MbPT.  
  
(2)          Policy Guidelines for Land Management (PGLM), 2015 for all Major Ports of India 
and Clarification No.1 of 20 18 and Clarification No.2 of 2019 thereon were issued by 
Ministry.  Vide these clarifications, the PGLM 2015 guidelines were extended to township 
areas of the Port land which were earlier excluded from the PGLM 2015.   Many of the 
expired leases, which coul d not be renewed in the absence of policy guidelines for township 
areas from the Ministry for leases/ renewal of leases.   By clarification No.1 of 2018 and 2 of 
2019 and para 13 of PGLM 2015, Ministry laid down procedure for renewal of expired leases 
and allotment of vacant lands by computation of Schedule of Rates (SoR) based on highest of 
5 factors on the basis of approved land values.   In case of Township of MbPT, the revised 
SoR was due from 1.10.2012 onwards, since earlier rentals were fixed in accorda nce with the 
Compromise policy modified by the Hon‟ble Supreme Court Judgment dated 13.1.2004 and 
were valid upto 30.9.2012.  
 
Bottlenecks in implementation of the PGLM 2015: 
  
(1)          Most of the leases in township areas have expired and there is lar ge number of sub-
tenants/Third parties in occupation of the existing structures constructed by the lessees. In 
most of the cases, lessees/licensees have transferred possession of lands/tenements to third 
party occupants without the approval of the Board. T hus MbPT has to engage into protracted 
52

 
litigations with these sitting occupants to get these lands/tenements vacated. In some cases, 
these litigations take up to 20 years to be finally adjudicated by the courts. 
 
(2)          (i) As per Para 11 of PGLM 201 5, fresh allotment or renewal of expired leases 
without renewal clause should be allotted through e -Tender cum auction by public notice on 
the Reserve Price as per Para 13 of PGLM 2015. 
     
         (ii) The reserve price based on the upfront premium as p er the SoR is worked out in 
accordance with para 13 of PGLM 2015 as per highest of the five factors for determination of 
land values.  The revision of SoR rate are only 36 times more than the existing rentals billed 
by MbPT as per the Hon‟ble Supreme Court  Judgement rates.   The revised SoR are not 
acceptable to any of the Lessees / Tenants / Occupants. 
 
        (iii) The existing lessee is to be given RoFR and opportunity to match the highest tender 
offer, provided they clear all past dues as per the applic able SoR from the date of expiry of 
the lease and also payment of required charges of regularisation of breaches, if any in the 
matter.  The exorbitant increase in the revised SoR and considering high reserve price and 
recovery of differential arrears for retrospective period from 1.10.2012 onwards are not 
acceptable to many lessees and is a major deterrent in renewal of expired leases. 
 
(3)          There are large scale objections to the MbPT‟s proposal for revision of SoR 
w.e.f.1.10.2012, which was submi tted to the TAMP. Many lessees/tenants/ occupants have 
contended that proposed new rents are very high in comparison with present rentals fixed 
under Hon‟ble Supreme Court (Wadia) Judgement 2004 which are almost 36 times higher on 
an average, which is not acceptable to many of the lessee/tenants. Such disputes with 
lessees/tenants could lead to protracted litigation by disputing parties and could stall the 
process of recovery of the revised rates. Even the government bodies, public sector 
undertakings, oil companies, etc., have expressed their inability to make the payment of past 
rentals which is from retrospective period, i.e. from 1.10.2012 onwards and also the high 
upfront premium payable for further period of 30 years for grant of fresh lease. 
  
(4)          PGLM 2015 do not provide any provision to the existing tenants / sub -tenants / 
lessees /actual occupants to transfer the land under expired leases in the name of actual 
occupant/sub-tenant who are in occupation of these premises for more than 30/50 y ears or 
even more.  Some of the occupants are even protected under Rent Control Act. Eviction of 
such large number of sub -tenants/Third parties and lessees by due process of law is a tedious 
and long time consuming process which takes several decades by wa y of multiple litigations 
and appeals.   
  
53

 
(5)          Existing land use and the layout plans and infrastructure in many parts of the 
township area are unutilised potential of land and are outdated with the present urban 
planning norms. There is no provision in PGLM 2015 Policy for rehabilitation and relocation 
of existing occupants/lessees/tenants at other locations by reconstitution of plots for 
redevelopment with change of use. Lack of provision in PGLM 2015 has restricted the 
untapped and under-utilized the development potential of the prime land of Mumbai City. 
  
(6)          The maximum period of lease that can be granted by Ports under PGLM 2015 is 
only 30 years and beyond 30 years, proposal needs to be recommended to Empowered 
Committee constituted by Ministry of Shipping, Government of India. Limiting period of 30 
years is also proving to be deterrent for getting good response from the market for land 
monetization of Port Trust lands falling in township areas and may be changed to 60 years. 
Two of the vacant plots were put for tender cum auction for industrial purpose but have not 
received any single bid due to high reserve price, limited lease period and due to restriction 
on subletting and transfer of the lease premises. 
  
(7)          By Clarification No.1 of 2018, Port Trust vacant plots / lands cannot be put for real 
estate development / residential development.  As most of the vacant plots of MbPT township 
land are falling under residential zones / commercial / industrial zones as per the 
Development Plan of Municipal Corporation of Greater Mumbai and not suitable for port 
related activities.  Such restrictions on proposed use are the bottlenecks in asset monetization 
of Port land.  
  
These are some of the bottlenecks / deterrent factors, w hich needs to be examined by the 
Ministry as these provisions are leading to large scale disputes and increase in litigation with 
lessee/tenants/occupants, affected revenue from let out land in Township area. The relevant 
provisions of PGLM 11, 12 & 13 may  be suitably examined to remove these bottlenecks so 
that Port Trust can generate revenue and fair rental returns by its landed assets in township 
areas.

Annexure – F 
A write up on Tonnage Tax Scheme 
1. Tonnage tax is a presumptive method of taxation which gives a shipping company an 
option to have its profits derived from the operating of ships to be taxed on the net tonnage of 
the ships as against the actual variable business profits / losses. A shippin g company which 
has opted for tonnage tax has to fulfill the following statutory compliances as per provisions 
of Chapter XII -G (Special provisions relating to income of shipping companies) of the 
Income Tax Act, 1961.  
 
2. Two main requirements of Tonnage  Tax Scheme under  Income Tax Rules are i) to 
acquire new ships by utilizing minimum 20% of book profit for acquiring new ships and ii) to 
fulfill Minimum On Board Training Requirement.  
 
3. Minimum Training Requirement (MTR) for tonnage Tax Company: 
Section 115V of the Income Tax Act, 1961 deals with Minimum Training 
Requirement (MTR) to be fulfilled by a Tonnage Tax Shipping Company which highlights as 
under:  
i. A tonnage tax company shall comply with the minimum training requirement in 
respect of trainee officers in accordance with the guidelines framed by the Director -
General of Shipping and notified in the Official Gazette by the Central Government. 
ii. As per present rulings 15% of Compliment as per Safe Manning Document of a 
qualifying ship shall be provid ed on Board Training on qualifying ships by a 
qualifying co. every year. 
iii. Qualifying ships are: 
a) Sea going ships or vessel with 15 net tonnage or more 
b) Ships registered under Merchant Shipping Act, 1958 or a ship registered 
outside India for which license has  been issued by the Director General of 
Shipping 
c) Following ships are not included in qualifying ships –  
Fishing vessels, factory ships, pleasure crafts, and harbor and river ferries, 
offshore installations

INTRODUCTION 
 
I, the Chairman, Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Transport, 
Tourism and Culture, having been authorized by the Committee to present on its behalf, do 
hereby present this Three Hundred Tenth Report on ‘Functioning of Central Libraries in the 
country’.  
2. The Committee heard the views of the Secretary, Ministry of Culture on the subject 
on 1st November, 2021. The Committee heard the views of Additional Sec retary, Ministry of 
Culture; Prof. Alok Tripathi, Additional Director General; Archaeological Survey of India; 
Shri T. J. Alone, Joint Director  General; Archaeological Survey of India; Adv. A.D.N. Rao, 
Senior Advocate on the panel of Supreme Court of India; and Adv. Jayant Tripathi, President 
Legal Advisor to ASI, on the subject on 9 th December, 2021. The Committee heard the views 
of the Secretary, Ministry of Culture on the subject on 6th January, 2022.  
3.  The Committee wishes to express its thanks to the officers of Ministry of Culture and 
Domain Experts for placing before the Committee , the material and information desired in 
connection with the subject and for clarifying the points raised by the Members.
