65. The Committee notes that the Ministry of Tourism had assigned National 
Council of Applied Economic Research (NCAER) to prep are a report on the impact of 
the COVID -19 pandemic on the tourism sector. The Ministry has shared with the 
Committee the findings of the study conducted by NCAER. The Committee notes that 
one of the key findings of the study is that due to supply -side shock, tourism economy 
saw a fall of 42.8% in April -June 2020, 15.5% in July -Sep 2020 and 1.1% in October -
December 2020. The Committee also notes that NCAER in its Study Report has made 
certain recommendations for the revival of the tourism sector. The Commit tee desires 
to be kept apprised of the action taken by the Ministry on the findings of the NCAER. 
 
66. The Committee observes that the tourism and hospitality industry is one of the 
worst hit sectors by COVID -19 pandemic and is in huge financial distress. The highly 

 
33 
 
infectious novel coronavirus continues to thwart the sector as new COVID -19 variants 
keep on  emerging. Apart from providing mass employment, income and foreign 
exchange for the country, this sector has an economically beneficial cascading impact on 
other sectors such as airlines, infrastructure, transportation, accommodation, 
facilitations systems, etc. As per data furnished by the Ministry, during the year 2019 -
20, this sector provided 79.86 million jobs directly and indirectly and generated 5.16% 
of India's GDP. As per the data furnished by the Ministry in the Table 9 above, t he 
potential job loss in tourism has been estimated to b e 20.8% in the year 2020 falling 
from 4.01 crore in 2019 to  3.17 crore in 2020 and the total revenue loss suffered by the 
hospitality sector has been estimated to be Rs. 89,813 crore in 2020. Therefore, this 
sector ne eds an urgent boost for revival. The Committee notes that a proposal of the 
Ministry of Tourism regarding grant of infrastructure status to investment in hotel 
industry of Capex over Rs. 25 crore (excluding land) is under consideration of the 
Department of Economic Affairs since long. The Committee observes that construction 
of hotels is highly capital intensive and it takes long for hotel projects to reach 
operational profitability. COVID has aggravated this and the current crisis is 
threatening the existe nce of hotel business for organizations in the Hospitality Sector 
because availability of lending by banks and financial institutions who have turned risk 
averse, especially towards hospitality sector, have reduced for contact -intensive sectors. 
The Commit tee, therefore, recommends that hotel projects with capex above Rs. 25 
crore (excluding land) be accorded infrastructure status and included in the 
Infrastructure list of the RBI so that long term funds are accessible at lower interest 
rates and the gap between return expectations and debt cost is bridged. The Committee 
is of the view that according of infrastructure status to hotel projects with capex above 
Rs. 25 crore will not only help build quality accommodation supply, but will also have 
an enormous e conomic multiplier effect across the length and breadth of the country. 
The Committee, therefore, recommends that the policy stance of the Government in this 
matter be spelt out within three months from the presentation of this Report.  
67. The Committee takes  note of the submissions made for relief measures for the 
survival of the Travel, Tourism and Hospitality Industry. The Committee is aware that 
the Reserve Bank of India had constituted an Expert Committee with Shri K.V. 
Kamath as the Chairman to make reco mmendations on the required financial 
parameters in respect of borrowers eligible under the COVID Resolution Framework 

 
34 
 
and the recommendations of the Expert Committee on the key financial parameters, i.e., 
Total Outsid e Liabilities/ Adjusted Total  Net Wort h; Total Debt/ EBITA; Current 
Ratio; Debt Service Coverage Ratio; and Average Debit Service Coverage Ratio had 
been accepted by the Reserve Bank of India. The Committee has been informed that the 
timeline to achieve the four ratios has been moved from Marc h, 2022 to September, 
2022. However, the deadline for the most important financial metric, i.e., Total Outside 
Liabilities/ Adjusted Total Net Worth has remained unchanged, i.e., March 2022. The 
Committee observes that the Indian economy has encountered a "once in a century" 
crisis due to COVID -19 pandemic and the Travel, Tourism and Hospitality Industry is 
one of the hardest hit, revival from which is unlikely to happen for the next 3 -4 years 
because India is already facing a third wave of infections driven by the Omicron variant 
and tourists' footfall has come down significantly due to the vicious cycle of restrictions 
in the wake of COVID-19. The possibility of many more such waves and new variants of 
Coronavirus emerging in India cannot be ruled out. On account of the above factors, 
the Travel and Hospitality Industry has witnessed a huge dip in business. Since the 
Tourism and Hospitality Sector is a major engine of economic growth in terms of 
growth of GDP, forex earnings and employment generation, it is  imperative that the 
revival of this sector should be at the forefront of the efforts of the Government. There 
is, therefore, an imperative need for Government to pull this sector out of the COVID -
19 recessionary conditions. The Committee, therefore, lends  its Parliamentary support 
to the demand of the Travel, Tourism and Hospitality industry and recommends that in 
view of the adverse impact of the third wave of COVID -19 pandemic and the resultant 
recessionary conditions and the difficulties faced in reviva l of businesses and meeting 
the operational requirements, the deadline for achievement of all five financial 
parameters, i.e., (i) Total Outside Liabilities/ Adjusted Total Net worth, (ii) Total Debt/ 
EBITA, (iii) Current Ratio, (iv) Debt Service Coverage Ratio (DSCR) and (v) Average 
Debt Service Coverage Ratio under the Resolution Framework relating to operational 
performance of borrowing entities be deferred to September, 2023 and the repayment 
schedule be extended from December 2022 to December, 2023. 
 
68. Taking into account the fact that one of the bottlenecks in tapping the full 
potential of the hospitality sector is the high incidence and multiplicity of taxes in the 
country which has led to tourist packages being outpriced in comparison to those 

 
35 
 
available in competing destinations, the Committee in its 288 th Report had 
recommended that policy measures for according Industry status to hotels be initiated. 
The Committee notes that though some states like Maharashtra, Gujarat, Kerala, 
Madhya Pradesh, etc., h ave accorded Industry status to hospitality sector, there is no 
uniformity in the tax structure across States. The Committee, therefore, recommends 
that the Ministry of Tourism should work out a strategy for inclusion of Hospitality 
Sector in the State and Central industrial policy so that this sector is conferred Industry 
Status by all the States. The Committee is of the firm view that conferring of Industry 
status will give a big boost to this Sector and help its faster recovery as it will allow the 
Sector to avail lower electricity and water tariff, lower property tax, rationalization of 
license fees and simplified approval process for hotel projects and operations. The 
Committee desires to be kept apprised of the specific measures taken by the 
Government in this regard and the outcome thereof. 
 
69. The Committee in its 288th Report had recommended that to provide relief to the 
tourism and hospitality sector so as to enhance export competitiveness of Indian 
tourism, the payments received by all the tourism and  hospitality entities in convertible 
foreign exchange be considered as "deemed export" and exempted from GST and the 
concept of zero rating be applied to tourism foreign exchange earnings. In this 
connection, the Ministry in its action Taken Notes had stat ed that "…this is a policy 
decision to be taken by GST Council, a reference from Ministry of Tourism is being 
made to GST Council in this regard…" The Committee reiterates its recommendation 
that tourism services provided to foreign tourists in India on receipt of foreign exchange 
should be treated as "deemed export" and such transactions should be zero -rated for 
GST without stopping the flow of input credits. 
 
70. The Committee notes that Finance Act, 2020 which was announced just before 
the start of COVID -19 crisis, inter alia, came up with new insertion of Tax Collected at 
Source (TCS) provisions under Section 206C  (1G)(a) of Income Tax Act, 1961  
pertaining to TCS @ 5% on foreign remittance through Liberalized Remittance  
Scheme (LRS) and under Section 206 C (1G)(b) pertaining to TCS@5% on selling of 
overseas tour packages by tour operators. The Indian Tour Operators face challenges to 
match the prices offered for outbound tours in comparison to foreign tour service 

 
36 
 
providers due to additional burden of taxes which include GST and newly inserted TCS 
provisions under Section 206C of the Income Tax Act, 1961 because overseas agents and 
Online Travel Agents (OTAs) do not charge the same since their base is out of India. 
The Committee is of the view that the above TCS provisions will not only increase the 
cost of packages sold by Indian tour operators, they will also shift all sales of outbound 
tourism to overseas suppliers, thereby denying the Government of income tax and GST 
revenue. These newly inserted TCS provi sions, therefore, are detrimental to tourism 
business in India. The Committee, therefore, recommends that in order to allow 
domestic tour operators a level playing field in comparison with foreign tour operators 
in the market of outbound tourism, the above mentioned TCS provisions be rolled back. 
The Committee is of the view that once TCS on outbound tourism is withdrawn, it will 
enable the Indian Travel Agents and Tour Operators to stage a recovery post the 
pandemic. 
 
71. The Committee in its 288 th Report had observed that under the Service Exports 
from India Scheme (SEIS) the Government  offered domestic exports duty credit scripts 
in the range of 5% to 7% of the net foreign exchange earned depending upon the nature 
of services and recommended that at a time when the tourism sector is faced with the 
crisis of the century, the notified services be incentivized at an enhanced rate of 10% for 
both tour operators and hotels in order to provide them with cash flow support. The 
Committee notes that the much awaited extension and the details on the Services 
Exports from India Scheme for FY 2019 -20 have been notified by the Directorate 
General of Foreign Trade  vide notification No. 29/2015 -20 dated September 23, 2021. 
The Committee is, however, disappointed to note that SEIS benefits for the tourism 
sector has been granted  at 5 per cent on net fore ign exchange earnings as opposed to 
earlier 7 per cent. SEIS rates for hotels have been reduced to 3 per cent from earlier 
specified rate of 5 per cent. Entitlement under SEIS for services exports has also been 
capped at Rs. 5 crore per exporter. The Commi ttee observes that the reduction in 
percentage of SEIS benefits comes at a time when the tourism and hospitality industry 
is struggling to recover their losses or even to stay afloat in many cases. The Committee 
would like to point out that the travel and hospitality businesses are expected to be very 
subdued due to the decline in business scenario post COVID -19 pandemic and there is 
an imperative need to infuse some liquidity into this cash -strapped sector. The 

 
37 
 
Committee, therefore, recommends that the Min istry of Tourism should take the SEIS 
rate reduction issue with the Ministry of Commerce and impress upon them that the 
dependency of the hospitality industry is high on import of goods to maintain global 
standards which warrants SEIS benefits to be lucrat ive to reduce the import cost and, 
therefore, the scrips generated by the travel and hospitality sector should be allowed at 
the rate  of 10% vis -à-vis the existing rates and the SEIS benefits should also be 
extended for further period of two-three years for enabling cost savings. 
 
72. The Committee also observes that SEIS is the only incentive for service exporters 
and, therefore, imposing a limit on the total entitlement under the SEIS at Rs 5 crore 
per exporter will impact top revenue producers adversely. Lar ger organisations fetch 
volume based on higher reliability and are necessary to increase the footfall in India. 
Capping the SEIS benefit at Rs. 5 crore will force companies to split up entities to 
continue to avail full benefits which will not be helpful. The Committee, therefore, 
recommends that the Ministry of Tourism should take up with the Ministry of 
Commerce this issue so that the capping of Rs 5 crore for SEIS benefit is removed.

VIII. CRUISE TOURISM 
93. The Committee has been informed that the Ministry of Tourism provides  Central 
Financial Assistance (CFA) to the State Governments/ UT Administrations/ Central 
Government Agencies for development of Tourism including Cruise Tourism and Cruising 
along rivers. The Ministry of Tourism has also sanctioned various projects for th e 
development of Cruise Terminals and related infrastructure in Andhra Pradesh, Goa, 
Maharashtra, Kerala and Tamil Nadu at the major ports for Rs. 151.79 Crore under the 
Scheme for „Assistance to Central Agencies for Tourism Infrastructure Development‟. Th e 

 
45 
 
coastline of the country and its inland waterways have enormous potential to develop cruise 
tourism, both international and domestic. To harness this, a Task Force has been constituted 
with Secretary (Tourism) as the Chairman and Secretary (Shipping) as the Co-chairman. The 
Task Force consists of representatives from the ports, Ministries of Health, Home Affairs, 
External Affairs, Customs, CISF, Coastal States, etc. and meets  regularly. On the 
recommendation of the Task Force, Ministry of Shipping and Mi nistry of Tourism have 
jointly appointed a consultant for preparing Action Plan for the development of Cruise 
Tourism in India. The Consultant has prepared a report which provides a roadmap and action 
plan that is needed to move India from its current posi tion to become a preferred cruise 
destination in the world.  On the recommendation of Taskf orce, the following measures were 
taken for the development of cruise tourism:  
 Standard Operating Procedures (SOPs) have been formulated to be followed by the 
various agencies for handling cruise ships.  
 The SOPs have been revised during November, 2017 and since operationalized at 
all major ports.  
 The facility for e -tourist visa has been extended to passengers arriving at these 
ports of Mumbai, Mormugao, Mangalore, Kochi and Chennai and immigration 
counters have been set up at five major ports visited by cruise ships, thus 
facilitating the cruise passenger arrivals at the seaports.  
 
94. To address manpower, coordination and logistic issues for handling cruise vessels at 
ports, “Port Level Facilitation Committees” have been formed under the respective Chairman 
of the major ports to facilitate seamless handling of cruise ships and passengers. 
 
95. Foreign flag vessels carrying passengers have been allowed to call at Indian ports for 
a period of 10 years with effect from 6th February, 2009 without obtaining a licence from 
Director General of Shipping. This faci lity has been extended further for a period of 5years 
i.e. up to 5th February, 2024.  
 
96. The last two meetings of the Task Force on Cruise Tourism were held on 06.01.2021 
& 17.12.2021. The meetings were attended by various Central, State Governments and 
Industry Stakeholders. During the meeting, held on 06.01.2021 detailed deliberations were 
made on the following issues:- 

 
46 
 
I. Review of SOPs for Cruise tourism. 
II. Development of Infrastructure at various ports/cruise terminals. 
III. Tax related issues for promotion of cruise tourism. 
IV. Incentives for cruise and water transport on lines of “UDAN” Scheme. 
V. Making India “The Cruise Development Hub” of the world. 
VI. The status of SOPs was reviewed on 17.12.2021 as under: 
a) e-Landing Card (e -LC) to be standardized to a size of credi t card . 
Representative from Bureau of Immigration (BOI) informed that they had 
agreed to the suggestion provided that certain other features are incorporated 
and that can be done. 
b) Collective Clearance and the Biometric Exemption 
c) Temporary Immigration Facil ity (Immigration Process when ship berths at 
Non-cruise berths) 
d) Deputing Immigration officer for completing Immigration process enroute 
from the previous foreign ports 
e) It was also decided to Organise India Cruise Conference in Mumbai on 25 -
26th February, 2 022 for promotion of Cruise Tourism. The Cruise Shipping 
Policy of the Ministry of Shipping was approved by the Government of India 
on 26th June, 2008. The objectives of the policy are to make India as an 
attractive cruise tourism destination with the state-of-the-art infrastructural and 
other facilities at various ports in the country. 
 
97. Ministry of Ports, Shipping & Waterways (MoPS&W) is the nodal Ministry for 
formulation of policies for rationalizing the tariff rates for cruise vessels in the 
country.  MoPS&W has rationalized tariff for cruise vessels arriving in India vide their letter 
dated 14.08.2020 for a period of one year.  In view of the second wave of COVID, MoPS&W 
vide their letter dated 31.05.2021, has extended the validity of the said rationalized tariff for a 
further period of one year beyond 13.08.2021 i.e. up to 13.08.2022. 
 
98. The Committee observes that despite being endowed with 7500 km coastline and 
a vast network of lakes and rivers, and a steady increase in the number of ships and 
cruise passengers calling on Indian ports over the past few years, cruise tourism in 
India is still at a nascent stage. Though various initiatives have been taken by the 

 
47 
 
Ministries of Tourism and Ports, Shipping and Waterways to develop India as 
destination as well as source market for cruise tourism and increase the number of 
cruise shipping calls  and passenger arrivals, India's enormous cruise potential still 
remains untapped. While appreciating the initiatives taken by the Ministries of Tourism 
and Posts, Shipping and Waterways to develop India as an attractive cruise tourism 
destination, the Committee recommends that the following measures may also be taken: 
 
i. Training institutions for various services in cruise tourism be developed. 
ii. The taxation structure in this segment may be revamped to bring down 
cost for passengers, making cruise shipping af fordable for middle class 
population that constitute the major portion of Indian demographics. 
This will go a long way in boosting participation of the middle class in this 
segment of tourism. 
iii. Synergy between the various stakeholders of this industry like cruise 
companies; tour operators, and immigration and customs departments 
may be utilised to optimise the gains for all.  
iv. An effective promotional campaign be developed to put Indian Cruise 
industry on the Global map. 
 
IX. DOMESTIC PROMOTION AND PUBLICITY (DPPH) SCHEMEINCLUDING 
MARKET DEVELOPMENT ASSISTANCE 
 
99. The Committee has been informed that the Ministry of Tourism promotes tourism in 
the country in a holistic manner. It releases domestic and international print, electronic and 
online media campaig ns under the „Incredible India' brand-line, to promote various tourism 
destinations and products of the country. It also organizes and extends support to tourism 
related events, produces brochures, leaflets, maps, films, CDs, etc. on various themes and 
destinations, provides financial assistance to tourism service providers for undertak ing 
promotional activities etc. 
 
100. Domestic tourism plays an important role in the overall development o f the tourism 
sector in India. Ministry of Tourism undertakes various pr omotional activities for the 
promotion of Domestic Tourism and with the objective of increasing Domestic Tourist Visits. 

 
48 
 
These activities are primarily aimed at increasing awareness about tourism destinations and 
products, promoting tourism within the coun try with focus on priority areas like the North 
East and Jammu & Kashmir and spreading Social Awareness messages and promoting events 
which have the potential for attracting tourists. 
 
101. Due to the ongoing Covid -19 pandemic, promotion was largely undertaken through 
the different Social Media handles of the Ministry. The Ministry of Tourism, at present, has 
two sets of Social Media handles namely, @incredibleindia and @tourismgoi with accounts 
on 8 different social media platforms viz Facebook, Twitter, Instag ram, YouTube, LinkedIn 
for Incredible India and Facebook, Twitter and Instagram for the Ministry of Tourism 
respectively, to ensure its effective digital presence. 
 
102. An allocation of Rs. 144 crore was made in BE 2021-22 which was reduceddrastically 
to Rs. 60 crore at the RE stage u nder scheme for Domestic Promotion & Publicity including 
Market Development Assistance out of which  an amount of Rs. 21.06 crore has been utilized 
(Till January 2022). An allocation of Rs. 75 crore has been made in BE 2022-23. 
 
103. The Committee has been informed that t he second wave of the pandemic  and the 
subsequent lockdowns,  had substantially affected the promotional efforts being undertaken 
by the Ministry of Tourism. Planned promotions/ campaigns/ on ground events had to be 
deferred / cancelled in the view of the fluid situation. In view of the same, the allocation 
under DPPH Head 2021-22, had to be substantially reduced from Rs 144.70 crore to Rs 60.00 
crore at RE stage.   
 
104. The proposed amount of Rs 75.00 crore for BE 2022 -23 w ould be utilized for 
undertaking various outreach programs by offices of the Ministry across the country, 
undertaking promotional campaigns on digital, print and electronic media, as per 
requirement, promotional materials, collaterals and films, organizing  tourism promotional 
events and outreach programs   by the domestic India Tourism offices, organizing specific 
campaigns for the promotion of North East, Ladakh and Jammu & Kashmir, support to 
States/UTs for fairs, festivals, etc. 
 
105. The Director General (tou rism) during his deposition before the Committee informed 

 
49 
 
that domestic tourism visits during 2020 were 610.22 milliion as compared to 2321.98 
million during 2019. 
 
106. The Committee observes that in most countries with a large population, domestic 
tourism is the foundation of a vibrant tourism industry. India also has a strong domestic 
tourism base which is evident from the fact that Domestic tourism visits were 2321.98 
million during 2019. However, owing to the prolonged COVID -19 pandemic, the 
erstwhile boomi ng tourism and hospitality sector has taken a severe beating due to 
which the number of domestic tourists slumped to 610 .22 million during 2020 
registering a negative growth of 73.3%. The trajectory of international tourism remains 
uncertain because new COVID-19 variants are emerging in some parts of the world due 
to which new restrictions are being introduced. With the rapid pace of the nation -wide 
COVID vaccination, the revival of the Indian economy has gained momentum and 
Indian tourist destinations have  risen to prominence as a result of strong pent -up 
demand and the relaxation of domestic restrictions. The Committee, therefore, 
recommends that the publicity campaigns of the Ministry should be focused on 
following safety protocols and helping restore confidence among tourists and promoting 
domestic tourism.  
 
107. The Committee also recommends that niche tourism avenues such as medical 
tourism, Buddhist tourism, sports tourism, ayurveda tourism, yoga tourism, spiritual 
tourism, adventure tourism, culinary tour ism, cruise tourism, etc. should be promoted 
aggressively through the media campaigns. 
 
108. The Committee observes that high net worth Indian nationals opt for foreign 
tourism instead of domestic tourism. One of the reasons behind this is the exhaustion of 
the timeworn tourist destinations and absence of new avenues. The Committee, 
therefore, recommends that unexplored and unexploited tourist destinations should be 
identified, developed and marketed to revive the curiosity of high -end domestic tourists 
and the publicity campaign should aim at persuading high end domestic tourists to 
substitute domestic tourism for foreign tourism. 
 
109. The Committee recommends that on the lines of Wor ld Tourism Rankings and 

 
50 
 
"Swachh Survekshan ", a competitive Tourism Ranking System s hould be introduced 
amongst Indian cities which would provide the impetus for them to create, maintain 
and promote more and more tourist spots within their cities. This ranking system may 
be updated every year and the cities with podium finishes in varied categories may be 
incentivised. 
 
110. A very rapidly emerging trend in global tourism scenario, especially amongst the 
youth is that of Night Tourism. Though India has opened some of its monuments for 
public to visit in night, it is still in a very nascent stage. Sufficient information is also not 
available regarding the participating sites, their timings and other such details. The 
Committee, therefore, desires that the Ministry should focus on night tourism and make 
more sites available for visit during night,  allow extended hours, provide exhaustive 
information on websites and social media pages and aggressively market the concept. 
This will open a new dimension of looking at our existing tourism heritage and invite 
repeat visitors.

115. The Committee notes  with concerns  that in order to  generate sufficient

opportunities for employment generation in the tourism sector both in urban as well as rural

tourist or those involved in the important task of teaching, administerin g or planning. The

hospitality sector.

120. The Committee notes that tourism is a labour -intensive industry and a multi -
sector activity characterized by multiple services provided by a range of suppliers and, 
therefore, this sector has huge potential for generation of jobs and absorption of a 
substantially higher workforce. The Committee notes from the Market Pulse data 
supplied by the Min istry that the hospitality and allied sectors face huge deficit in 
trained manpower. As against annual requirement of 902890 for 2022, the total supply 
including attrition is only 84128 and the demand -supply gap is to the extent of 818762. 
Tourism sector is likely to witness a boom post pandem ic because there is lot of pent -up 
demand for travel. This boom may bring an exponential demand for the workforce at 
managerial, supervisor and skilled levels in hospitality and tourism sector. This leads 
the Committee  to the irresistible conclusion that the existing institutional capacities 
would be unable to fulfil the estimated additional requirement of manpower in the 
hospitality and allied sectors. The Committee is of the view that since training is a key 
intervention and issues of human resource development and capacity building are 
extremely important, the realization of the country's huge, barely tapped tourism 
potential cannot be realized without addressing the challenges of capacity constraints. 
The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Ministry should adopt a proactive 
interventionist approach to give a major boost to the various initiatives relating to 
human resource development for the hospitality and tourism sector through 
convergence with the private sector.  
 
121. The Committee is of the view that there is an imperative need for the hotel 
management institutes to be updated and integrated with the hotel industry. The 
Committee, therefore, recommends that the complete curriculum of the hotel 
management institutes be revised. The curriculum also needs to be updated regularly to 
reflect the constantly changing dynamics of the industry in the post COVID era. 
 
122. The Committee in its 288 th Report had observed that till the year 2015 -16, the 
Hunar Se Rozgar Tak Progra mme was geared only towards the creation of employable 
skills. However, with the adoption of Common Norms on Skill Development notified by 

 
57 
 
the Ministry of Skill development and Entrepreneurship, it has been made mandatory 
on the part of the Training Provid er Institutes to arrange placement/self -employment 
for at least 70% of the certified trainees within three months of completion of the 
course." The Committee would like to be updated whether the implementing agencies 
have adjusted to this provision. The Co mmittee also desires to be apprised of the 
Training Service Provider Institutes who have lagged behind the targets set in this 
regard. The Committee also recommends that the Ministry should closely put in place 
an intensive monitoring mechanism for fulfilm ent of the norms stipulated by the 
Ministry of Skill Development and Entrepreneurship. 
 
123. The Committee notes that a number of programmes like Hunar Se Rozgar Tak, 
Skill Testing and Certification, Entrepreneurship Programmes, Tourism Adventure 
Courses, etc., have been launched under the Scheme of Capacity Building for Service 
Providers to provi de education, training and certification to the tourism service 
providers. Though the Ministry have supplied the information regarding the number of 
persons trained and certified under the programmes of Capacity Building for Service 
Providers, it has not f urnished the annual targets fixed and the actual achievement 
made in respect thereof under the scheme of Capacity Building for Service Providers in 
2021-22. The Committee, therefore, desires to be apprised of the achievements made 
vis-à-vis the targets fixed, programme-wise, under the CBSP in 2021-22. 
 
XI. ASSISTANCE TO CENTRAL AGENCIES FOR TOURISM INFRASTRUCTURE 
DEVELOPMENT:  
 
124. Development of tourism infrastructure at tourism destinations could create a critical 
mass for achieving its targeted objectives an d other socio -economic benefits to the society. 
The holistic development of tourism infrastructure at all important tourist destinations 
through Central Financial Assistance(CFA) to the States/UTs may not be possible since, 
many of the potential destinations are under the jurisdictions/ control of Central Agencies like 
ASI, Railways, Port Trusts in India, ITDC etc. and the overall development of places of 
tourist interest under their control may not be possible through their own resources and may 
require convergence of resources, expertise and experience for maintenance and management 
after development. In order to remove these shortcomings and to bring in the active

II) ANALYSIS OF BUDGETARY ALLOCATIONS FOR 2022-23 
The Committee notes that although there has been marginal increase in the 
budgetary outlay for the Ministry from Rs. 2026.77 crore for FY 2021 -22 to Rs. 2400.00 
crore for FY 2022-23, it is still lesser than the BE 2020-21 allocation of Rs. 2499.83 crore. 
Though the BE 2022-23 allocation is 18-41% higher than the BE 2021 -22 outlay, there is 
a substantial shortfall of Rs. 537.92 crore vis -à-vis the projected demand of Rs. 2937.92 
crore by the Ministry for FY 2022 -23 and that too at a time when this sector is reeling 
under losses in the wake of COVID -19 pandemic. The Committee notes that this 
budgetary outlay for 2022 -23 has been reduced to Rs 416 crore as compared to the BE 
2021-22 of Rs. 668.72 crore under the head - Promotion and Publicity. The Committee 
finds this reduction alarming because the tourism and hospitality sector has been hit the 
hardest by COVID-19 pandemic and with massive job and revenue losses, it is essential 
that the Government promotes India on all possible platforms, both national and 
international, as a safe and must -visit destination and for this, instilling confidence 
among tourists through use of technology with the help of skilled manpower, investment 
in skilling, reskilling and upskilling is an imperative need. The Committee, therefor e, 
apprehends that the marginal increase of Rs. 333.77 crore in the budgetary allocation for 
2022-23 is inadequate as it will be consumed by inflation. The Committee is 
simultaneously appreciative of the fiscal constraints faced by the Ministry of Finance 
due to deceleration in the growth rate in the Indian economy on account of global and 
domestic slowdown in the aftermath of COVID -19 pandemic. The Committee observes 
that with the accelerated pace of vaccine roll -out and easing of restrictions, the Indian 
economy has started to rebound and the additional resources would become available as 
a result of revenue buoyancy in FY 2022 -23. Given the fact that the activities of the 
Ministry harness the direct and multiplier effect on economic development and 
employment generation in the country and integrated development of infrastructure and 
facilities through effective partnerships and convergence with stakeholders can propel 
India to a higher growth trajectory, the Committee recommends that depending on 
better financial performance and greater absorption capacity of the Ministry, quantum 
of funding for the Ministry of Tourism be enhanced at the RE 2022 -23 stage. 
Simultaneously, the Committee recommends that the Ministry should initiate and 

 
65 
 
implement better fiscal discipline and ensure that the scarce financial resources do not 
remain parked idelling. 
(Para 19) 
From a perusal of Table No. 2, the Committee is constrained to note that there is 
a substantial underutilization of the budgeted funds during the FY 2021 -22. Against the 
RE 2021-22 allocation of Rs. 969.80 crore, only 47.70% amounting to Rs. 462.55 crore 
could be spent till the 31st January, 2022. It means that the remaining expenditure would 
have to be squeezed in the last two months of FY 2021 -22. Since as p er norms stipulated 
by the Ministry of Finance, there is a ceiling of 25% on expenditure in the last quarter, 
occurrence of huge savings is a certainty. It may be pertinent to mention here that a zero 
based budgeting exercise which requires that budget req uest be evaluated thoroughly, 
starting from zero base, is in practice and the financial outlays are earmarked based on 
factors like past trend of expenditure, stages of formulation/implementation of various 
projects, the pre-projects approvals etc. Therefore, savings of Rs. 1056.97 crore vis -à-vis 
the BE 2021-22 allocation not only betrays fiscal indiscipline by way of underutilization 
of the earmarked funds which will have an adverse bearing on infrastructure 
development oriented activities of the Ministry , but is also indicative of shortcomings in 
budgetary planning and monitoring of the budgeted funds. The Committee observes that 
a resource constrained country like India cannot afford to keep a vast chunk of its 
resources locked up and surrendered towards  the end of the financial year. The 
Committee, therefore, recommends that realistic projection of fund requirements should 
be given utmost priority at the highest level of the Ministry so that the Budget Estimates 
are formulated with application of proper financial yardsticks and large variations 
between the Budget Estimates, Revised Estimates and Actual Expenditure needs to be 
avoided. The Ministry must also pay attention to streamlining its monitoring mechanism 
and ensure optimal and more efficient deploy ment and utilization of its financial 
resources for smooth execution of its programmes within the approved cost and 
designated timeline. 
(Para 20) 
The Committee also takes a serious note of keeping the unspent provision of Rs. 
1056.97 crore till the close of financial year 2021 -22 despite reduction in the budgetary 
outlay at the RE 2021-22 stage, in disregard of the provisions of General Financial Rules 
requiring the unspent provisions in a grant to be surrendered to the Ministry of Finance 

 
66 
 
as soon as these  are foreseen, without waiting for the last day of the financial year. The 
Committee, therefore, recommends that the Ministry should exercise greater fiscal 
prudence, and ensure that unspent budgetary provisions are surrendered timely in 
future. 
(Para 21)

III) CONTRIBUTION OF TOURISM TO GDP 
 
The Committee notes that as per the World Travel and Tourism Council 
(WTTC), prior to the COVID-19 pandemic, Travel and Tourism accounted for 10.4% of 
global GDP. In many parts of the world, tourism is a major engine of growth. The 
Committee in its 275th R eport presented to the Parliament on the 3rd March 2020 had 
noted that the contribution of tourism to national GDP was over 10% for most countries 
where tourism happens to be the main driver of national economy. However, in India 
which has unique endowment s of biodiversity, forests, rivers, its rich culture and 
heritage and many World Heritage sites, the tourism sector has not proved to be the 
proverbial engine of growth for our economy. This is evident from the fact that India's 
total share in global inter national arrivals remains a modest 1.57% against the target of 
3 per cent set by the NITI Aayog to be achieved by 2022. Similarly, the contribution 

 
67 
 
(direct and indirect) of tourism in the GDP and the total jobs in the country are 
estimated to be 5.16 per c ent and 15.34 per cent respectively during 2019 -20. The 
Committee is of the firm view that if India has to move towards becoming USD 5 trillion 
economy and a global economic powerhouse, as envisioned by our Hon'ble PM Shri 
Narendra Modi, then the contribut ion of tourism to India's GDP has to be raised from 
the current 5.16% to 10% in the next five years. The Committee, while welcoming the 
various measures taken by the Ministry to double the contribution of tourism to India's 
GDP, feels that the vast untappe d potential of India as a tourism destination cannot be 
realized unless tourism is included in the Concurrent List of the Constitution of India. 
Taking note of the fact that Travel and Tourism does not figure in the Centre, State or 
Concurrent Lists and si nce in a federal polity like ours, the responsibility for policy 
making and implementation of tourism projects are fragmented across different levels - 
Central and State Governments and coordination between them is often lacking due to 
absence of clearly d efined mandate, the Committee in its 288th Report had 
recommended inclusion of tourism in the Concurrent List. Since tourism is yet to be 
included in the Concurrent List, the Committee reiterates its recommendation for 
inclusion of tourism in the Concurren t List of the Constitution of India. The Committee 
is convinced that this will go a long way in channelising the development of tourism and 
positioning and maintaining tourism development as a national priority.  
(Para 30) 
The Committee observes that Emira te of Dubai does not have the abundant 
wealth of natural oil reserves and nor does it have a pre -existing plethora of natural, 
historical and internationally significant tourist sites. Despite that, it has emerged as a 
multi-billion dollar economy and amon gst the world's most visited tourist destinations, 
all based on the Government's tourism centric approach towards national policy 
making. The Committee wishes that India should also endeavour to imbibe creating 
potential for tourism in the very core of its  policy making. Although tourism is an 
important activity in India, its share in global market is extremely small and the 
potential of tourism sector in India is yet to be unleashed. The actual implementation of 
tourist projects takes place at State/UT level but in most of the States/UTs, the outlay for 
Department of Tourism is meagre. The Committee, therefore, recommends that in order 
to give policy push to the tourism industry, a National Tourism Council chaired by the 
Prime Minister and composed of Chief  Ministers or Tourism Ministers of all States 

 
68 
 
should be established. This National Council should be an empowered legislative body on 
the lines of GST Council. This will enable fast -track Centre-State level tourism decision 
making, leveraging and utilising  full synergies of India's tourism potential across all our 
States. 
(Para 31) 
The Committee observes that despite the fact that India offers a diverse portfolio 
for travel and tourism, the share of India's International Tourist Arrivals (ITAs) in the 
ITAs of the world was merely 1.57 per cent in 2020. There is increased competition 
among various countries to attract foreign visitors. There is, therefore, an imperative 
need for India to prepare suitable market strategy to attract foreign visitors. The 
Committee, therefore, recommends that the Ministry in collaboration with a professional 
body should carry out market research of foreign tourist source markets to identify the 
expectations, requirements, psychographics, demographics and many other aspects of a 
foreign tourist willing to travel to India, thereby enabling to create a strategic plan to 
revive inbound tourism. The research should be conducted with an objective to provide 
an authentic feedback, roadmap and recommendations to the Ministry of Tourism wi th 
respect to inbound tourism in India and provide a blueprint on the various policy 
objectives and infrastructure development needed to strengthen inbound tourism in the 
country. 
(Para 32) 
 
IV) IMPACT OF COVID -19 PANDEMIC ON TOURISM, TRAVEL AND 
HOSPITALITY SECTOR 
 
The Committee notes that the Ministry of Tourism had assigned National Council 
of Applied Economic Research (NCAER) to prepare a report on the impact of the 
COVID-19 pandemic on the tourism sector. The Ministry has shared with the 
Committee the findings of the study conducted by NCAER. The Committee notes that 
one of the key findings of the study is that due to supply -side shock, tourism economy 
saw a fall of 42.8% in April -June 2020, 15.5% in July -Sep 2020 and 1.1% in October -
December 2020. The Committee also notes that NCAER in its Study Report has made 
certain recommendations for the revival of the tourism sector. The Committee desires to 

 
69 
 
be kept apprised of the action taken by the Ministry on the findings of the NCAER. 
(Para 65) 
The Committee observes that the tourism and hospitality industry is one of the 
worst hit sectors by COVID -19 pandemic and is in huge financial distress. The highly 
infectious novel coronavirus continues to thwart the sector as new COVID -19 variants 
keep on emer ging. Apart from providing mass employment, income and foreign 
exchange for the country, this sector has an economically beneficial cascading impact 
on other sectors such as airlines, infrastructure, transportation, accommodation, 
facilitations systems, et c. As per data furnished by the Ministry, during the year 2019 -
20, this sector provided 79.86 million jobs directly and indirectly and generated 5.16% 
of India's GDP. As per the data furnished by the Ministry in the Table 9 above, the 
potential job loss in  tourism has been estimated to be 20.8% in the year 2020 falling 
from 4.01 crore in 2019 to 3.17 crore in 2020 and the total revenue loss suffered by the 
hospitality sector has been estimated to be Rs. 89,813 crore in 2020. Therefore, this 
sector needs an urgent boost for revival. The Committee notes that a proposal of the 
Ministry of Tourism regarding grant of infrastructure status to investment in hotel 
industry of Capex over Rs. 25 crore (excluding land) is under consideration of the 
Department of Economic Affairs since long. The Committee observes that construction 
of hotels is highly capital intensive and it takes long for hotel projects to reach 
operational profitability. COVID has aggravated this and the current crisis is 
threatening the existence of hotel business for organizations in the Hospitality Sector 
because availability of lending by banks and financial institutions who have turned risk 
averse, especially towards hospitality sector, have reduced for contact -intensive sectors. 
The Committee, th erefore, recommends that hotel projects with capex above Rs. 25 
crore (excluding land) be accorded infrastructure status and included in the 
Infrastructure list of the RBI so that long term funds are accessible at lower interest 
rates and the gap between return expectations and debt cost is bridged. The Committee 
is of the view that according of infrastructure status to hotel projects with capex above 
Rs. 25 crore will not only help build quality accommodation supply, but will also have 
an enormous economic  multiplier effect across the length and breadth of the country. 
The Committee, therefore, recommends that the policy stance of the Government in this 
matter be spelt out within three months from the presentation of this Report.  

 
70 
 
 (Para 66)

survival of the Travel, Tourism and Hospitality Industry. The Committee is aware that 
the Reserve Bank of India had constituted an Expert Committee with Shri K.V. Kamath

is already facing a third wave of infections driven by the Omicron variant and tourists'

imperative need for Government to pull this sector out of the COVID -19 recessionary

Outside Liabilities/ Adjusted Total Net worth, (ii) Total Debt/ EBITA, (iii) Current

Ratio under the Resolution Framework relating to operational performance of

borrowing entities be deferred to September, 2023 and the repayment schedule be 
extended from December 2022 to December, 2023. 
(Para 67) 
Taking into account the fact that one of the bottlenecks in tapping the full 
potential of the hospitality sector is the high incidence and multiplicity of taxes in the 
country which has led to tourist packages being outpriced in comparison to those 
available in competing destinations, the Committee in its 288th Report had 
recommended that policy measures for according Industry status to hotels be initiated. 
The Committee notes that though some states like Maharashtra, Gujarat, Ker ala, 
Madhya Pradesh, etc., have accorded Industry status to hospitality sector, there is no 
uniformity in the tax structure across States. The Committee, therefore, recommends 
that the Ministry of Tourism should work out a strategy for inclusion of Hospita lity 
Sector in the State and Central industrial policy so that this sector is conferred Industry 
Status by all the States. The Committee is of the firm view that conferring of Industry 
status will give a big boost to this Sector and help its faster recover y as it will allow the 
Sector to avail lower electricity and water tariff, lower property tax, rationalization of 
license fees and simplified approval process for hotel projects and operations. The 
Committee desires to be kept apprised of the specific measures taken by the Government 
in this regard and the outcome thereof. 
(Para 68) 
The Committee in its 288th Report had recommended that to provide relief to the 
tourism and hospitality sector so as to enhance export competitiveness of Indian tourism, 
the payments received by all the tourism and hospitality entities in convertible foreign 
exchange be considered as "deemed export" and exempted from GST and the concept of 
zero rating be applied to tourism foreign exchange earnings. In this connection, the 
Ministry in its action Taken Notes had stated that "…this is a policy decision to be taken 
by GST Council, a reference from Ministry of Tourism is being made to GST Council in 
this regard…" The Committee reiterates its recommendation that tourism services 
provided to foreign tourists in India on receipt of foreign exchange should be treated as 
"deemed export" and such transactions should be zero -rated for GST without stopping 
the flow of input credits. 
(Para 69) 

 
72 
 
The Committee notes that Finance Act, 2020 which wa s announced just before 
the start of COVID -19 crisis, inter alia, came up with new insertion of Tax Collected at 
Source (TCS) provisions under Section 206C (1G)(a) of Income Tax Act, 1961 pertaining 
to TCS @ 5% on foreign remittance through Liberalized Remittance  Scheme (LRS) and 
under Section 206C(1G)(b) pertaining to TCS@5% on selling of overseas tour packages 
by tour operators. The Indian Tour Operators face challenges to match the prices 
offered for outbound tours in comparison to foreign tour service providers due to 
additional burden of taxes which include GST and newly inserted TCS provisions under 
Section 206C of the Income Tax Act, 1961 because overseas agents and Online Travel 
Agents (OTAs) do not charge the same since their base is out of India. The Committee is 
of the view that the above TCS provisions will not only increase the cost of packages sold 
by Indian tour operators, they will also shift all sales of outbound tourism to overseas 
suppliers, thereby denying the Government of income tax and  GST revenue. These 
newly inserted TCS provisions, therefore, are detrimental to tourism business in India. 
The Committee, therefore, recommends that in order to allow domestic tour operators a 
level playing field in comparison with foreign tour operators in the market of outbound 
tourism, the above mentioned TCS provisions be rolled back. The Committee is of the 
view that once TCS on outbound tourism is withdrawn, it will enable the Indian Travel 
Agents and Tour Operators to stage a recovery post the pandemic. 
(Para 70) 
The Committee in its 288th Report had observed that under the Service Exports 
from India Scheme (SEIS) the Government offered domestic exports duty credit scripts 
in the range of 5% to 7% of the net foreign exchange earned depending upon the  nature 
of services and recommended that at a time when the tourism sector is faced with the 
crisis of the century, the notified services be incentivized at an enhanced rate of 10% for 
both tour operators and hotels in order to provide them with cash flow support. The 
Committee notes that the much awaited extension and the details on the Services 
Exports from India Scheme for FY 2019 -20 have been notified by the Directorate 
General of Foreign Trade vide notification No. 29/2015 -20 dated September 23, 2021. 
The Committee is, however, disappointed to note that SEIS benefits for the tourism 
sector has been granted at 5 per cent on net foreign exchange earnings as opposed to 
earlier 7 per cent. SEIS rates for hotels have been reduced to 3 per cent from earlier 
specified rate of 5 per cent. Entitlement under SEIS for services exports has also been 

 
73 
 
capped at Rs. 5 crore per exporter. The Committee observes that the reduction in 
percentage of SEIS benefits comes at a time when the tourism and hospitality industry is  
struggling to recover their losses or even to stay afloat in many cases. The Committee 
would like to point out that the travel and hospitality businesses are expected to be very 
subdued due to the decline in business scenario post COVID -19 pandemic and th ere is 
an imperative need to infuse some liquidity into this cash -strapped sector. The 
Committee, therefore, recommends that the Ministry of Tourism should take the SEIS 
rate reduction issue with the Ministry of Commerce and impress upon them that the 
dependency of the hospitality industry is high on import of goods to maintain global 
standards which warrants SEIS benefits to be lucrative to reduce the import cost and, 
therefore, the scrips generated by the travel and hospitality sector should be allowed at  
the rate of 10% vis-à-vis the existing rates and the SEIS benefits should also be extended 
for further period of two-three years for enabling cost savings. 
(Para 71) 
The Committee also observes that SEIS is the only incentive for service exporters 
and, therefore, imposing a limit on the total entitlement under the SEIS at Rs 5 crore per 
exporter will impact top revenue producers adversely. Larger organisations fetch 
volume based on higher reliability and are necessary to increase the footfall in India. 
Capping the SEIS benefit at Rs. 5 crore will force companies to split up entities to 
continue to avail full benefits which will not be helpful. The Committee, therefore, 
recommends that the Ministry of Tourism should take up with the Ministry of 
Commerce this issue so that the capping of Rs 5 crore for SEIS benefit is removed. 
(Para 72) 
 
V. INTEGRATED DEVELOPMENT OF TOURIST CIRCUITS AROUND SPECIFIC 
THEMES (SWADESH DARSHAN) 
 
The Committee notes that some projects under the Swadesh Darshan Scheme 
which aims to develop world-class infrastructure in the circuit destinations and enhance 
the contribution of tourism to the local economies, have witnessed massive financial and 
physical underperformance. Out of the 76 projects sanctioned for a revised cost of Rs. 
5503.83, 34 projects have been physically completed and 9 projects sanctioned for Rs. 

 
74 
 
671.32 crore have registered physical progress and financial performance ranging from 
10 per cent to 49 per cent and 4 per cent to 55 per cent respectively. The projects 
witnessing physical and financial underperformance pertain to the Himalayan Circuit in 
Jammu and Kashmir; Eco Circuit in Jharkhand, rural circuits in Kerala. Spiritual 
Circuits in Maharashtra, Eco Circuit in Punjab and North -East Circuit in Tripura. The 
Committee observes that the creation of tourism infrastructure is the very foundation on 
which Indian tourism is to be built and a prerequisite towards improving the country's 
tourism productive capacity and attaining economic growth. The Committee, therefore, 
recommends that the Ministry should analyse the reasons behind the underperformance 
of the above infrastructure projects and take remedial measures accordingly. The 
Committee desires to be apprised of the measures taken to speed up execution of the 
above projects. 
(Para 78) 
The Committee observes that Spiritual Tourism holds a special place in India and 
also appeals to international tourists as it presents an immersive spiritual experience. 
The presence of several sacred destinations of various faiths in the c ountry makes these 
destinations among the most visited sites globally. Since infrastructure sector is a key 
driver for spiritual tourism, the Committee recommends to streamline the development 
of the entire religious tourism circuit in each region/area as it will increase the carrying 
capacity of these destinations which is required to meet the large influx of tourists at 
these destinations. 
(Para 79) 
The Committee recommends that the various circuits under the Swadesh 
Darshan Scheme should be developed using the Hub and Spoke Model which can draw 
tourists from the popular religious destinations towards other unexplored destinations 
that are positioned near the major destinations. 
(Para 80) 
The Committee also desires to be apprised whether any of the proj ects being 
implemented under the Swadesh Darshan Scheme have witnessed cost escalation and 
time overruns. If so, the details thereof, may please be informed to the Committee at the 
earliest.  

 
75 
 
(Para 81) 
The Diamond Triangle of Odisha comprising of three Buddhist sites, namely 
Ratnagiri, Udayagiri and Lalitgiri, is a lesser known tourist destination and is largely 
unexplored. The Committee recommends that the Diamond Triangle be included under 
the Swadesh Darshan Scheme for development of tourist facilitie s around these 
important Budhist sites. 
(Para 82) 
 
VI.  THE NATINOAL MISSION ON PILGRIMAGE REJUVENATION AND 
SPIRITUAL AUGMENTATION DRIVE (PRASHAD) 
 
The Committee notes that as on 31.01.2022, 37 projects have been approved 
under the PRASHAD at an approved c ost of Rs. 1210 crore and the total release at the 
end of FY 2021 -22 is expected to be to the tune of Rs. 807.00 crore. The Committee 
observes that India is a land of pilgrimages and this scheme focusses on developing and 
identifying pilgrimage sites acros s India for enriching the religious tourism experience 
and is, therefore very important from the point of view of overcoming seasonality and 
promoting India as a 365 days destination. The Committee, therefore, desires to be 
furnished with a status note on the physical and financial progress of each of the projects 
under the PRASHAD Scheme since its launch. 
(Para 86) 
The Committee also notes that 3 -4 new projects are proposed to be sanctioned 
under the PRASHAD Scheme and exhorts the Ministry to quickly move towards 
completing all pre -project activities and obtaining statutory clearances so that all the 
bottlenecks are removed and the financial outlay earmarked for the purpose could be 
made full use of. The Committee desires to be kept apprised of the progress  made 
towards finalization and operationalization of the above new projects under the 
PRASHAD Scheme. 
(Para 87) 
 
VII. DEVELOPMENT OF ICONIC TOURIST DESTINATIONS 

 
76 
 
 
The Committee notes that the proposal of the Ministry of Tourism for 
development of 19 iconic tourist sites as world class tourist destinations has been 
approved by the Expenditure Finance Committee on the 15th October 2020 with an 
outlay of Rs. 5109 crore for the period FY 2020-21 to FY 2025-26 and been submitted for 
seeking approval of the Cabine t. The Committee is dismayed at the snail's pace of 
progress made in the matter which is evident from the fact that almost five months have 
elapsed since the proposal was approved by the EFC but the approval of the Cabinet is 
still pending. The Committee, therefore, urges the Ministry to expedite addressing all 
pending issues and start expeditious implementation of this project of vital importance 
so that the allocated sums of Rs. 130 crore for 2022 -23 could be utilized efficiently and 
the avowed objectives of this project achieved. 
(Para 91) 
Besides the Tourism Ministry which is the nodal Ministry, several other Ministry 
such as Ministries of Culture, Road Transport and Highways, Ports, Shipping and 
Waterways, etc., are involved in the Iconic Sites Projects . The Committee, therefore, 
reiterates its recommendation made in its 288th Report that convergence among the 
Ministries concerned should be ensured and role of these Ministries in implementing the 
projects should be clearly delineated so that they are able to pinpoint the roadblocks and 
concrete action can be taken while implementing the projects. 
(Para 92) 
 
VIII. CRUISE TOURISM 
 
The Committee observes that despite being endowed with 7500 km coastline and 
a vast network of lakes and rivers, and a steady in crease in the number of ships and 
cruise passengers calling on Indian ports over the past few years, cruise tourism in India 
is still at a nascent stage. Though various initiatives have been taken by the Ministries of 
Tourism and Ports, Shipping and Waterw ays to develop India as destination as well as 
source market for cruise tourism and increase the number of cruise shipping calls and 
passenger arrivals, India's enormous cruise potential still remains untapped. While 
appreciating the initiatives taken by t he Ministries of Tourism and Posts, Shipping and 

 
77 
 
Waterways to develop India as an attractive cruise tourism destination, the Committee 
recommends that the following measures may also be taken: 
i. Training institutions for various services in cruise tourism be developed. 
ii. The taxation structure in this segment may be revamped to bring down cost for 
passengers, making cruise shipping affordable for middle class population that 
constitute the major portion of Indian demographics. This will go a long way in 
boosting participation of the middle class in this segment of tourism. 
iii. Synergy between the various stakeholders of this industry like cruise companies; 
tour operators, and immigration and customs departments may be utilised to 
optimise the gains for all.  
iv. An effective promotional campaign be developed to put Indian Cruise industry on 
the Global map. 
(Para 98) 
IX. DOMESTIC PROMOTION AND PUBLICITY (DPPH) SCHEMEINCLUDING 
MARKET DEVELOPMENT ASSISTANCE 
The Committee observes that in most countries with a large popu lation, 
domestic tourism is the foundation of a vibrant tourism industry. India also has a 
strong domestic tourism base which is evident from the fact that Domestic tourism visits 
were 2321.98 million during 2019. However, owing to the prolonged COVID -19 
pandemic, the erstwhile booming tourism and hospitality sector has taken a severe 
beating due to which the number of domestic tourists slumped to 610.22 million during 
2020 registering a negative growth of 73.3%. The trajectory of international tourism 
remains uncertain because new COVID -19 variants are emerging in some parts of the 
world due to which new restrictions are being introduced. With the rapid pace of the 
nation-wide COVID vaccination, the revival of the Indian economy has gained 
momentum and Indi an tourist destinations have risen to prominence as a result of 
strong pent -up demand and the relaxation of domestic restrictions. The Committee, 
therefore, recommends that the publicity campaigns of the Ministry should be focused 
on following safety proto cols and helping restore confidence among tourists and 
promoting domestic tourism.  
(Para 106) 

 
78 
 
The Committee also recommends that niche tourism avenues such as medical 
tourism, Buddhist tourism, sports tourism, ayurveda tourism, yoga tourism, spiritual 
tourism, adventure tourism, culinary tourism, cruise tourism, etc. should be promoted 
aggressively through the media campaigns. 
(Para 107) 
The Committee observes that high net worth Indian nationals opt for foreign 
tourism instead of domestic tourism. One of the reasons behind this is the exhaustion of 
the timeworn tourist destinations and absence of new avenues. The Committee, 
therefore, recommends that unexplored and unexploited tourist destinations should be 
identified, developed and marketed to revive t he curiosity of high-end domestic tourists 
and the publicity campaign should aim at persuading high end domestic tourists to 
substitute domestic tourism for foreign tourism. 
(Para 108) 
The Committee recommends that on the lines of World Tourism Rankings an d 
"Swachh Survekshan", a competitive Tourism Ranking System should be introduced 
amongst Indian cities which would provide the impetus for them to create, maintain 
and promote more and more tourist spots within their cities. This ranking system may 
be updated every year and the cities with podium finishes in varied categories may be 
incentivised. 
(Para 109) 
A very rapidly emerging trend in global tourism scenario, especially amongst the 
youth is that of Night Tourism. Though India has opened some of its mon uments for 
public to visit in night, it is still in a very nascent stage. Sufficient information is also not 
available regarding the participating sites, their timings and other such details. The 
Committee, therefore, desires that the Ministry should focus on night tourism and make 
more sites available for visit during night, allow extended hours, provide exhaustive 
information on websites and social media pages and aggressively market the concept. 
This will open a new dimension of looking at our existing t ourism heritage and invite 
repeat visitors. 
(Para 110) 

 
79 
 
 
X HUMAN RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT 
 
The Committee notes with concerns that in order to generate sufficient 
manpower in order to meet the needs of the tourism and hospitality industry, the 
Ministry extends assistance to State Governments and Union Territories for 
establishment of Institutes of Hotel Managements and Food Craft Institutes. As of now 
47 Institutes of Hotel Management and 14 Food Craft Institutes have been set up with 
the support of the Ministry and one Central IHM at Jagdishpur, Uttar Pradesh is under 
construction. Given the fact that India faces intense shortage of trained manpower at 
various levels of the travel and hospitality sector, the Committee is of the view that the 
existing institution al capacities would not be able to meet the requirement of trained 
manpower in the tourism and hospitality sector. As this sector has great potential for 
creating enormous number of jobs, the Committee recommends that the gap at the skill 
level should be b ridged and new IHMs and FCIs in the States/UTs that have not been 
covered as yet, should be established to enlarge the quality and quantity output of 
human resources required by the hospitality sector. 
(Para 115) 
The Committee also desires to be apprised o f the physical and financial progress 
in respect of the 3 Food Craft Institutes which have been sanctioned to be set up in the 
State of Madhya Pradesh. 
(Para 116) 
The Committee notes that tourism is a labour -intensive industry and a multi -
sector activity c haracterized by multiple services provided by a range of suppliers and, 
therefore, this sector has huge potential for generation of jobs and absorption of a 
substantially higher workforce. The Committee notes from the Market Pulse data 
supplied by the Mini stry that the hospitality and allied sectors face huge deficit in 
trained manpower. As against annual requirement of 902890 for 2022, the total supply 
including attrition is only 84128 and the demand -supply gap is to the extent of 818762. 
Tourism sector is likely to witness a boom post pandemic because there is lot of pent -up 
demand for travel. This boom may bring an exponential demand for the workforce at 
managerial, supervisor and skilled levels in hospitality and tourism sector. This leads the 
Committee to the irresistible conclusion that the existing institutional capacities would 

 
80 
 
be unable to fulfil the estimated additional requirement of manpower in the hospitality 
and allied sectors. The Committee is of the view that since training is a key interventi on 
and issues of human resource development and capacity building are extremely 
important, the realization of the country's huge, barely tapped tourism potential cannot 
be realized without addressing the challenges of capacity constraints. The Committee, 
therefore, recommends that the Ministry should adopt a proactive interventionist 
approach to give a major boost to the various initiatives relating to human resource 
development for the hospitality and tourism sector through convergence with the private 
sector.  
(Para 120) 
The Committee is of the view that there is an imperative need for the hotel 
management institutes to be updated and integrated with the hotel industry. The 
Committee, therefore, recommends that the complete curriculum of the hotel 
management institutes be revised. The curriculum also needs to be updated regularly to 
reflect the constantly changing dynamics of the industry in the post COVID era. 
(Para 121) 
The Committee in its 288th Report had observed that till the year 2015 -16, the 
Hunar Se Rozgar Tak Programme was geared only towards the creation of employable 
skills. However, with the adoption of Common Norms on Skill Development notified by 
the Ministry of Skill development and Entrepreneurship, it has been made mandatory 
on the part of the Training Provider Institutes to arrange placement/self-employment for 
at least 70% of the certified trainees within three months of completion of the course." 
The Committee would like to be updated whether the implementing agencies have 
adjusted to thi s provision. The Committee also desires to be apprised of the Training 
Service Provider Institutes who have lagged behind the targets set in this regard. The 
Committee also recommends that the Ministry should closely put in place an intensive 
monitoring me chanism for fulfilment of the norms stipulated by the Ministry of Skill 
Development and Entrepreneurship. 
(Para 122) 
The Committee notes that a number of programmes like Hunar Se Rozgar Tak, 
Skill Testing and Certification, Entrepreneurship Programmes, Tou rism Adventure 
Courses, etc., have been launched under the Scheme of Capacity Building for Service 

 
81 
 
Providers to provide education, training and certification to the tourism service 
providers. Though the Ministry have supplied the information regarding the number of 
persons trained and certified under the programmes of Capacity Building for Service 
Providers, it has not furnished the annual targets fixed and the actual achievement made 
in respect thereof under the scheme of Capacity Building for Service Prov iders in 2021-
22. The Committee, therefore, desires to be apprised of the achievements made vis -à-vis 
the targets fixed, programme-wise, under the CBSP in 2021-22. 
(Para 123) 
 
XI. ASSISTANCE TO CENTRAL AGENCIES FOR TOURISM INFRASTRUCTURE 
DEVELOPMENT 
The Committee observes that the creation of tourism infrastructure by way of 
roads, cruise terminals, railway connectivity, and medical facilities has its multiplier 
effect in terms of overall economic growth and employment generation and acts as a 
catalyst to economic development of the country. Under the Scheme, "Assistance to 
Central Agencies for Tourism Infrastructure Development", a total of Rs. 62.85 crores 
has been released to various Central Agencies for creation of tourism related 
infrastructure. T o make an assessment of the success of this Scheme, the Committee 
desires to be furnished with the total number of projects sanctioned and taken up for 
implementation, along with the released amount vis -à-vis the sanctioned budget during 
the last 5 years, year-wise.  
(Para 125) 
The Committee observes that easy access to tourism destinations and facilities for 
easy movement within the destinations are prerequisites for the development of tourism. 
However, road connectivity has been one of the impediments for the growth of tourism 
in India. It is in this context that the list of 50 Tourist Destinations submitted by the 
Ministry of Tourism to the Ministry of Road Transport and Highways assume 
significance. The Committee notes that out of the 50 destinations selected for road 
connectivity, 23 destinations fall under the purview of Ministry of Road Transport and 
Highways/NHAI where the work is going on. However, no forward movement seems to 
have been made as regards road connectivity to the remaining 27 tourist sites which are 
under the  purview of the State Governments. Though the Ministry of Tourism have 

 
82 
 
taken up the matter with the concerned State Governments, it has not had the desired 
result. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Ministry of Tourism should once 
again take up this matter at the highest level with the concerned State Governments and 
impress upon them that better connectivity to the tourist sites will unlock more tourism 
opportunities for the State and the economic benefits will flow into their economy in the 
shape of increased State revenues and employment as road connectivity is one of the 
fundamental components for successfully developing tourism market. The Committee 
desires to be apprised of the efforts made in this regard and the outcome thereof. 
(Para 127) 
The Committee notes that Ministry of Tourism has shared with the Ministry of 
Road Transport and Highways a new list of 114 destinations for improving connectivity 
to these destinations. Good road, railway or air connectivity to tourist destinations is of 
paramount importance to attract domestic as well as foreign tourists because when these 
destinations are well connected, entrepreneurs in hospitality sector, tour and travel 
operators become confident of making investments and promoting these destinations. 
The Committee, therefore, recommends that a dedicated mechanism be put in place for 
planning, coordination and completion of the road connectivity projects to the 114 
tourist destinations. 
(Para 128) 
The Committee observes that last mile connectivity to se veral tourist 
destinations is a deterrent to promotion of tourism. Since last mile connectivity is a key 
driver for promotion of tourism, the Committee recommends that while preparing 
Master Plan for connectivity to tourist destinations, last mile connecti vity should 
mandatorily be included in the concept and the Detailed Project Report. 
(Para 129) 
There is lack of good wayside amenities including toilets at several tourist 
destinations which causes inconvenience to tourists and discourages them from visiti ng 
such places. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Ministry should focus more 
on the improvement of wayside amenities at tourist destinations to facilitate travelers. 
(Para 130) 
The Committee notes that with a view to providing enhanced amenitie s and 

 
83 
 
facilities for tourists at railway stations, 22 projects have been sanctioned by the 
Ministry of Tourism at a cost of Rs. 108.54 crores. Though more than ten years have 
elapsed since their sanction in FY 2011 -12, their full operationalization is stil l a far cry. 
The Committee is unhappy at the continuing delay in full operationalization of these 
projects and constrained to observe that the desired priority has not been accorded to 
the upgradation of facilities and amenities at the 22 railway stations selected for the 
purpose. The Committee, therefore, recommends with all the power at its command that 
concrete steps be taken to translate into reality the vision of developing top -class 
facilities at the 22 railway stations within a designated timeline. T he Committee desires 
to be kept apprised of the progress made in this regard. 
(Para 133) 
 
XII SAFE AND HONOURABLE TOURISM 
The Committee notes that 14 States have deployed tourist police in one form or 
the other. Keeping in mind the importance of safety and  security of tourists, the 
Committee in its 275th and 288th Reports presented to the Parliament on the 3rd March 
2020 and 9th March 2021 respectively, hadrecommended that the Ministry of Tourism 
should take up the matter with the remaining States. The Comm ittee is, therefore, 
dismayed to note that no further headway has been made by the remaining States 
towards creation and deployment of tourism police at major tourist destinations. Safety 
and security of the tourists are a determining factor for choosing a  destination and also 
vital for providing quality services in tourism and, therefore, the destinations must have 
an image of utmost tourist safety and security. The Committee, therefore, reiterates its 
earlier recommendation that Tourist police should be s et up in all important tourist 
destinations of each State/UT and should provide travelers security through a spirit of 
courtesy and friendliness. 
(Para 139) 
The Committee is aware that the tourist police system prevails in other countries 
also. The Committee would like the Ministry of Tourism to document such best practices 
from these countries and help adopt such practices in our country. The Committee 
desires to be kept apprised in this regard.  
(Para 140) 

 
84 
 
 
MISCELLANEOUS 
Adventure tourism in India has a huge potential for growth as India offers the 
keen adventurers a fascinating range of thrills and activities to choose from. The 
Ministry of Tourism has issued guidelines for approval of Adventure Tourism Operators 
which is  a voluntary scheme. The Committee notes that Adventure Tourism is largely 
unorganized and unregulated. The Committee, therefore, feels that there is an urgent 
need to regularize the Adventure Tour Operators Market and promote registration of 
companies indulging in these activities on a centralized platform to increase credibility 
and enforce safety regulations.  
(Para 141)
