At the outset, the Chairman welcomed the Members to  the meeting of the Committee 
and the representatives of the Ministry of Ports, S hipping and Waterways (M/o PS&W), 
apprising them of the agenda of the meeting i.e. to  deliberate on ‘Progress made in 
implementation of Sagarmala Project.’ 
2.         Initiating the discussion, the Chairman stated that ‘Sagarmala Project’ concept was 
initially approved by the Union Cabinet in 2015 as a part of the National Perspective Plan (NPP), 
which was released by the Hon’ble Prime Minister, f or the development of India’s 7,500 km 
coastline, 14,500 km potentially navigable waterway s and maritime sector. ‘Sagarmala Project’ 
intends to enhance the capacity of major and non-ma jor ports, modernize them, strengthen port 
connectivity and evacuation infrastructure, simplif y procedures adopted in ports, promote usage 
of electronic channels for information exchange lea ding to hassle-free and seamless cargo 
movement. He asked the Secretary to apprise the Com mittee of the efforts made by the Ministry 
towards achieving port-led direct and indirect deve lopment, provision of cost-effective and 
efficient infrastructure in ports, holistic develop ment in harnessing the potential of India's 
coastline and river network and improving export co mpetitiveness. He queried about the 
challenges faced by the ports across the country in  terms of last-mile connectivity, multi-modal 
transportation, connectivity with airways, highways  and railways as envisaged in the ambitious 
Prime Minister's Gati-Shakti National Master Plan a nd measures taken thereof for their 
successful implementation. 
  
3.               It was pointed out by the Chairman  that the infrastructure plan of a country must 
seamlessly & efficiently move goods & people across  various modes of transport. However, this 
requires a coordinated approach, as roads would fee d into railway lines, which in turn would 
feed into ports, efficiently moving goods from the hinterlands to the ports. This would further 
48

 
lead to and enable the development of multiple urba n, industrial centres across India. These 
urban centres in turn, would enable balanced region al development, as multiple industrial 
clusters could sprout up across India. Both Central  as well as various state government revenues 
would be scaled up many times, enabling higher spen ding on social sectors and would have the 
spill-over effect of easing pressure on existing ur ban agglomerations, leading to a higher quality 
of life across the board. 
4.               Furthermore, while many economic z ones, industrial parks, logistics hubs and ports 
have been planned, they often fail to deliver to th eir optimal levels, owing to inefficient multi-
modal connectivity, and also due to their small siz e. The fragmented nature of decision making, 
with each department working in silos meant that a disjointed industrial network was created. 
While several issues have been sorted out, in many areas, some co-ordination issues still remain 
to be resolved and remain unconnected as well. Such  issues are responsible for the lack of scale 
in Indian manufacturing sector which coupled with r elatively inefficient logistics network has 
hampered India's global competitiveness disallowing  us to harness our complete growth 
potential. 
5.               He desired to be apprised of prepa redness of the Ministry in terms of provision of 
sustainable infrastructure to ancillary manufacturi ng clusters in port vicinity, seamless last-mile 
connectivity of ports through multi-modal transport ation, shifting movement of industrial goods 
to coastal and inland waterways, employing funding solutions for NPP and ‘Sagarmala Projects’ 
on Central, State and port level and the obstacles faced by the Ministry. 
6.         The Secretary, M/o PS&W, before making h is presentation, apprised the Committee that 
the Ministry has been working towards modernization  of ports lagging behind in terms of 
connectivity through PPP, technological development  of cargo-handling, multi-modal 
transportation to connect all ports under the PM's ‘Gati-Shakti’ programme, building energy-
49

 
efficient technology to curb waterways pollution, r egulation and operation of ports under the 
Major Port Authorities Act, 2021, planning and impr oving investment in initiatives identified 
under the Vision-2030 policy. The Committee was fur ther apprised of the Ministry’s efforts to 
achieve desired goals in  port-improvement, cargo c ost reduction, smooth and licensed cargo 
handling, maritime safety, developing coastal jetti es and fishing harbours for welfare of the 
fishermen, RORO Pax ferries for seamless transfer o f vehicles, cargo and passengers. He also 
informed the Committee of the enactment of the Majo r Port Authorities Act, 2021, the Marine 
Aids to Navigation Act, 2021 and the New Inland Vessels Act, 2021to boost the port sector. 
7.         Through his presentation the Secretary, M/oPS&W focused on the progress made in the 
‘Sagarmala Projects,’ expanding areas such as Inlan d Waterways cargo volume-growth over the 
last 5 years, coastal traffic growth of 10.2% in Indian Maritime Sector, reduction of logistic costs 
for EXIM and domestic trade, multi-modal transporta tion, monitoring of industries/ 
manufacturing centers vis-a-vis  ports, bridging skill-gap through job creation in the Indian 
maritime sector, port-led industrialization, coasta l community development, jetty/ RORO Pax 
construction in coastal and inland waterways, promo ting coastal and cruise tourism  etc. The 
Committee was apprised of the Institutional Mechani sms employed by the Ministry in 
implementation of the ‘Sagarmala Projects’ viz. Sagarmala Coordination and Steering 
Committee (SCSC) to enable coordination among vario us organizations of the government, 
National Sagarmala Apex Committee (NSAC) to guide a nd review the progress of the project, 
and State Sagarmala Committee (SSC) to oversee Stat e-level coordination over the project. The 
Committee was further apprised of the milestones ac hieved by the Ministry in completion of 181 
projects under the NPP and that the ‘Sagarmala Proj ects’ have borne fruits in the domains of last 
mile rail and road connectivity enhancement, coasta l berths fishing harbor, jetty/ Roll-on-Roll-
off (RORO) ferry construction at Major ports, holis tic development of islands/ coastal districts, 
50

 
etc. The Secretary apprised the Committee that the Ministry is pushing to ensure feasible 
implementation of projects through PPP mode and fun ding of high social impact projects with 
zero Internal Rate of Return (IRR) through Sagarmala Programme. 
8.         The Committee was also informed of the e stablishment of Technological centers/ 
institutes for Maritime and Shipbuilding research a nd training, skill development 
training,  functioning under the ‘Sagarmala Project s’ Scheme, viz. Center of Excellence in 
Maritime and Shipbuilding (CEMS), National Technolo gy Center for Ports, Waterways and 
Coasts (NTCPWC), and Center for Inland and Coastal Maritime Technology (CICMT) with the 
intent to make India a leading player in shipbuildi ng, innovative ship-designing, cryogenic cargo 
handling and renewable energy harvesting from inland waters. 
9.         The Chairman, while mentioning about the  recent Study Visit of the Committee to 
Andaman and Nicobar Islands, expressed his disappoi ntment at the lack of coordination among 
various Ministries/ Departments/ Agencies and the n eed for a master-plan thereof to tackle 
transportation issues arising in interlinking ports  with railways, airways and roadways. He also 
stated that marketing is crucial to identify and de velop tourism at Andaman and Nicobar Islands. 
He also suggested that Ministry should assign matte rs relating to safety/ security at ports, as per 
ISO Standards, to affordable private agencies. He p ointed out that as tourism is also an aspect of 
Sagarmala Project, in addition to goods transfer he  suggested that the Ministry should ensure 
connectivity facilities to attract tourists, such a s building tourist terminals and hotels. He also 
mentioned about a specific Maritime University, und er the Ministry, where funds have been 
unscrupulously withdrawn, from the development fund s/ Grants of Autonomous bodies/ 
Universities and desired that recoveries should be initiated and strict action should be taken 
against them. He expressed the dire need to have tr ained staff to manage shortage in Civil

Aviation, Tourism and Shipping sectors and expediti ous system to obtaining environmental 
clearance from Ministry of Environment for future port projects. 
10.         Members raised several queries such as ferry development of ferries, public amenities 
around areas connecting all three sectors viz. tourism, aviation and ports, development of 
lighthouses and coastlines. The Chairman then direc ted that written replies to the queries raised 
by Members may be sent to the Secretariat within a week, by the respective Ministries and other

REPORT 
 
  India is an all year around tourist country, offering anything and everything to tourists 
from an incredible geographical diversity of lofty mountains , golden  beaches, deserts and serene  
backwaters to secluded islands , an ancient and mesmerizing cultura l history reflected in its 
myriad historical monuments including the seventh wonder of the world, the Taj Mahal, palaces 
and forts, places of interests for all religions, ancient cities, diverse art forms and lively local 
bazaars, the most diverse cuisine in the world which changes every 100 km, all of which combine 
to make India a vibrant, eclectic fusion of the traditional and the modern, the historical and the 
contemporary. Every scene evokes countless imaginations and every sight, a million more sights.  
From the northern most Jammu & Kashmir proclaimed to be ―heaven on earth‖ to the rapturously 
acclaimed ―God‘s own country‖ Kerala in the south, from the lofty peaks of the Himalayas to the 
rolling hills of the Eastern and Western Ghats, from the lush Gang etic plains to the sandy dunes 
of Rajasthan, the landscape of India is as ever-changing and diverse as its culture. 
 
“If I were to look over the whole world to find out the country most richly endowed with all the 
wealth, power, and beauty that nature can bestow – in some parts a paradise on earth – I 
should point to India.” 
~ German Philosopher Max Mueller 
 
2. There is no fall from Eden, no divide of matter and spirit in ancient Indian cosmology. 
Instead, nature flows from the Creator  as a fountain of divinit y into space and time.   India has an 
outstanding and unmatched diversity of religions, languages, and cultures. It has beautiful green 
crops, it has many rivers flowing through  its fertile soil, it has variety in flora and fauna, and it 
has the great  Himalayas as its majestic crown. The Sun plays hid e and seek in its  hill stations, 
providing relief from scorching heat.  Its western region has a potpourri of Ghats, caves while the 
southern region boasts of exquisitely carved temple architecture and beauteous beaches. India has 
something for ever yone, history buffs , spiritual seekers, adventure tourists, wildlife enthusiasts, 
tourist shoppers, luxury travelers and backpackers.   
3. Indian tourism industry contributes to around 4.7 percent of the country's GDP and 
provides employment to around 3 1.8 million of inhabitants.  By attracting a huge number of both 
foreign and domestic tourists for professional as well as holiday purpose s, the tourism industry in 
India has displayed remarkable growth. India has popularized the entire South Asia as one of the 
most spectacular tourist hotspots. International tourists bring significant income, foreign currency, 
and jobs. The more investment is there  to improve the infrastructure in the tourists  hotspots, the 

2 
more at tractive the destination will be, for both domestic and foreign  tourists. Given that the 
investment in tourism and hotel industry/ recreation facilities can mobilize the resources of the 
entire society, India‘s share in Foreign/ Inter national Tourist Arrivals at a mere 1.59% [India 
Tourism Statistics 2021] is certainly low given the huge tourist potential India has in its resources. 
It is thus evident that the vast tourism potential of India remains untapped. Foreign tourism is of 
considerable value to the I ndian Tourism and Hospitality Se ctor as is evinced by the fact that 
foreign exchange earnings from tourism in India amounted to Rs. 50,136 Crores (US$ 6.958 
Billion) in the year 2020. [Source: India Tourism Statistics, 2021].  
4. Infrastructure—both physical and soft – serves as the arteries of the industry and 
amplifies the  travel and tourism competitiveness . A country‘s tourism automatically becomes 
attractive if there are all possible alternative and reasonably priced transport and lodging facilities 
which streamlines the overall travel experience for tourists. Given that the investment in the 
tourism and hotel industry/ recreation facilities is a substantial amount requiring the mobilization 
of the resources of the entire society,  in this backdrop, the Committee decided to take up the 
subject ‗Development of Tourism Infrastructure in the country‘ for examination and report 
thereon. 
5. In this co nnection, the Department -related Parliamentary Standing Committee on 
Transport, Tourism and Culture heard the views of the Ministry of Tourism on the subject at  
Parliament House Annexe, New Delhi on 1 st November, 2021. Major points discussed during the 
deliberations of the Committee are:-  
(i) Tourism Infrastructure Development Schemes; 
(ii) Swadesh Darshan Scheme (SDS); 
(iii) PRASHAD Scheme; 
(iv) Assistance to Central Agencies Scheme; 
(v) Adopt a Heritage Scheme (in collaboration with Ministry of Culture and ASI); 
(vi) Development of Iconic Tourist Sites; 
(vii) Land availability and statutory clearance; 
(viii) Central Road Fund (CRF); 
(ix) Generating revenue and overall tourist satisfaction; and 
(x) Promotion and Publicity 
 
TOURISM INFRASTRUCTURE DEVELOPMENT SCHEMES 
6. Tourism infrastructure is the basis of tourism development and utilization of existing 
destination resources. Tourism infrastructure includes  ancillary and complementary facilities, 

3 
equipment, systems, processes, and resources necessary for functioning of every tourist 
destination, to meet the needs of the tourist and to increase their satisfaction during their stay at 
the destination. A Tourist destination is made accessible to the tourists through rail , road, air and 
port connectivity. Tourism industry st imulates investments in new infrastructure, most of which 
improves the living conditions of local residents as well as generate tourist satisfaction. 
7. The infrastructure for tourism includes basic infrastructure like airports, railways, roads, 
waterways, electricity, water supply, drainage, sewerage , solid waste disposal systems, and 
amenities like accommodation, restaurants, recreational facilities, and shopping facilities . The 
Ministry of Tourism is the nodal agency to formulate national policies and pro grammes for the 
development and promotion of tourism. Augmentation of quality tourism infrastructure 
throughout the country is a key area of functioning of the Ministry of Tourism. More than 50% of 
the Ministry's expenditure on Plan Schemes is incurred for development of quality tourism 
infrastructure at various tourist destinations and circuits in the States/UTs. To facilitate p lanning 
for sustainable develo pment of Tourism Infrastructure  and provide basic amenities in a balanced 
manner, the Ministry of Tourism with due emphasis has launched schemes like Swadesh Darshan 
Scheme (SDS), Pilgrimage Rejuvenation and Spiritual, Heritage Augmentation Drive 
(PRASHAD), Adopt a Heritage Site (in collaboration with Ministry of Culture and ASI), 
Development of Iconic Tourist Sites with a goal to attract tourists from every nook and corner of 
the world towards various Indian destinations through thema tic circuits, pilgrimage sites and 
excellent amenities at the hotspots.  
 
SWADESH DARSHAN SCHEME (SDS) 
8. Envisioned to synergize with other Government of India initiatives like ‗Swachh Bharat 
Abhiyan,‘ Skill India,‘ ‗Make in India‘ etc., the Ministry launched the Swadesh Darshan Scheme 
(SDS) in January, 2015 with objectives to: 
 Position tourism as a major engine of economic growth and job creation;  
 Develop circuits having tourist potential in a planned and prioritized manner;  
 Promote cultural and heritage value of the country to generate livelih oods in the identified 
regions; 
 Enhance the tourist attractiveness in a sustainable manner by developing world class 
infrastructure in the circuit/destinations;  
 Follow community based development and pro-poor tourism approach;  

4 
 Create awareness among the local communities about the impor tance of tourism for them in 
terms of increased income sources, improved living standards and o verall development of 
the area; 
 Create employment through active involvement of local communities; 
 Harness tourism potential for its effects in employment gener ation and economic 
development; 
 Make full use of the potential and advantages in terms of available infrastructure, national 
culture and characteristic strong points of each and every region throughout the country by 
development of theme-based circuits; and 
 Develop tourist facilitation services to enhance visitor experience/satisfaction. 
 
9. The site-wise detailed tourism infrastructure inventory is an important part of the DPR 
so as to get the idea of the existing tourism infrastructure, its adequacy and envis aged tourist flow 
in the future and the necessary action required to mitigate the infrastructure gap. Selection and 
evaluation criteria is divided into three levels based on the need  assessment and stakeholder 
interaction for SDS: 
I. Ministry of Tourism 
II. Central Agencies 
III. State Governments/ UT Administrations. 
10. Concept presentation would be made to MoT highlighting the potential, need, impact of  
the project by the agency proposing the p roject and its alignment to the Detailed Perspective Plan 
(DPP) prepared by the ministry. After in-principle approval, site evaluation would be carried out 
and Conceptual Detailed Project Report (DPR) would be prepared. 
11. Fifteen thematic circuits have been identified  namely: North -East India Circuit, 
Buddhist Circuit, Himalayan Circuit, Coastal Circuit, Krishna Circuit, Desert Circuit, Tribal 
Circuit, Eco Circuit, Wildlife Circuit, Rural Circuit, Spiritual Circuit, Ramayana Circuit, Heritage 
Circuit, Tirthankar Circui t and Sufi Circuit  for development of 76 sanctioned projects for 
development across 31 States and UTs with a budgetary allocation of Rs. 5526.71 crores for the 
year 2021 -22. The projects are being implemented in 917 Tier -II and Tier -III destinations. 16 
projects have been completed while 30 projects have been completed upto 80% and above. The 
various projects sanctioned under the Scheme are given at Annexure –I. The major interventions 
under the Swadesh Darshan Scheme are:- 
 
 
 

5 
Nature of facilities No of facilities 
Log Hut Facilities 16 
Tourist Facilitation Centres 20 
Craft Haats/ Souvenir Shops 12 
Open Air Theatre / Sound & Light 20 
Cafeteria  and Way Side Amenities 20 
Convention Centres/ Exhibition Centres 8 
Museum/ Interpretation Centre 9 
Adventure Activities 15 
Wellness Centre 7 
Helipad 4 
Golf Course 1 
Beach/ Ghat Development 6 
 
12. The Ministry further informed the Committee that the Swadesh Darshan Scheme is 
currently under review and therefore no pro posals are under consideration.  State Governments 
have been advised that proposals may be submitted once the review is finished  and new 
guidelines are issued. 
13. The Committee observes that infrastructure for tourism includes basic 
infrastructure components like roads, railways, airports, water, electricity, hotels etc.  The 
Committee recommends that interconnectivity of roads, ports, airports, railways and 
waterways should be part of the infrastructure planning process while preparing the 
Detailed Appraisal Report of any Tourism project.  Service roads and linkage of nearby 
places should also be included. Transport infrastructure plays a vital role in connecting 
origin and destination locations while ensuring safe, comfortable and efficient 
transportation to tourists. While evaluating trave l experiences, transport is one of the main 
factors which has a great bearing on trip satisfaction. The Committee therefore 
recommends that multi -modal transport should be envisaged while preparing DPR for 
facilitating tourism in the country.  This will no t only facilitate free flowing traffic but also 
serve to make tourist destinations more attractive and accessible. 
14. The Committee observes that in its earlier report, it had noted that only one of the 
fifteen thematic circuits under the Swadesh Darshan Sche me had been completed till that 
time and had recorded its disappointment about the slow progress in the projects under the 
Scheme. Now, since all the projects under the Scheme are being reviewed, the Committee 
urges the Ministry to complete the review in a  time bound manner so that the Scheme may 

6 
be completed without undue delay. Since the projects under the Scheme are spread 
throughout the country and involve local bodies, the Committee recommends the Ministry 
to hear the views of all stakeholders involved  or ensure that the agencies implementing the 
Scheme do so, and take due cognizance of local sentiment so that once streamlined the 
projects under the Scheme would be able to be implemented without any hindrance. The 
Committee also recommends that the yardstick to review the project should only be whether 
it would be truly effective in increasing the tourist potential of the area. 
15. The Committee also suggests that the Ministry should build a systematic approach 
towards restoration/ conservation of historic structures under the SDS Scheme as buildings 
of very rich historic background add character, distinctiveness, and a sense of identity to the 
places they belong to . The Committee desires t hat the Ministry promote heritage through 
branding and use it as a potential factor in tourism development. 
16. The Committee is of the opinion that  in order to successfully implement tourism 
infrastructural Schemes,  the state governments should carry out due diligence in 
consultation with the nodal agencies during conceptualizing the projects and ensure the 
completion of tendering process of projects in a time bound manner to enable the Ministry 
to release funds for such projects. The Committee recommends the Ministry to create a 
mechanism for proactive project monitoring and reviewing the same to avoid delays in 
implementation as per agreed schedules and in compliance with the approved DPRs. 
 
PRASHAD SCHEME 
17. This Nati onal Mission on Pilgrimage Rejuvenation and Spiritual, Heritage  
Augmentation Drive (PRASHAD ) was launched in the year 2015  to develop tourism 
sustainability and harness pilgrimage tourism so that it directly affects and multiplies the 
employment generation and economic developmen t.  The vision of this Scheme is to rejuvenate 
the pilgrimage and spiritual experience of the tourists as well as preserve the soul of the 
pilgrimage/heritage city. 
18. PRASHAD covers Ghats, Tourist Reception/ Facilitation Centers, Public Amenities, 
Open-air Amphitheatres, Museums, Medicine Centers, external infrastructure such as water 
supply, sewage, drainage, electricity, roads and use of renewable source of energy in the sites, 
namely, Ama ravati, Srisailam, Simhachalam and Annavaram (Andhra Pradesh), Parashuram 
Kund (Lohit Distt., Arunachal Pradesh), Kamakhya and Srikrishnaguru Sevashram, Nasatra 
(Assam), Patna and Gaya (Bihar), Balmeshwari Devi Temple (Rajnandgaon, Chhattisgarh), St. 
Bom J esus Church  (Goa), Dwarka, Somnath and Ambaji in Banaskantha (Gujarat), Panchkula 

7 
for development of Gurudwara Nada Saheb and Maa Mansha Devi Temple (Haryana), Maa 
Chintpurni (Una, Himachal Pradesh), Hazratbal, Katra and Sundarbani in Rajauri district (Ja mmu 
& Kashmir), Deogarh and Parasnath (Jharkhand), Chamundeshwari Devi (Mysuru District, 
Karnataka), Guruvayoor, St. Thomas International Shrine, Cheraman Juma Mosque (Kerala), 
Chawkihang Vihara (Leh), Omkareshwar and Amarkantak (Madhya Pradesh), Trimbakes hwar 
(Maharashtra), Charanthala Durga Temple - Babedpara, Nartiang Shakti Temple, Nongsawlia 
Church- Sohra, Madan Air Nar Sacred Pool Near Jowai (Meghalaya), Aizawl, Ailwang, 
Khawrulian and Lunglei -Serkawn (Mizoram), Cathedral of Kohima, Noksen Church, Miss ion 
Compound, Aizuto, Molungkimong, Zunheboto Mission Compound and Vankhosung -Wokha 
(Nagaland), Puri (Odisha), Amritsar and Ropar for development of Chamkaur Sahib (Punjab), 
Ajmer (Rajasthan), Yuksom (Sikkim), Kanchipuram, Vellankani and Rameshwaram (Tamil  
Nadu), Jogulamba Devi Temple and Bhadrachalam (Telangana) Tripura Sundari - Agartala 
(Tripura), Varanasi, Mathura and Ayodhya (Uttar Pradesh), Bad rinath, Kedarnath and Gangotri -
Yamunotri (Uttarakhand) and Belur (West Bengal). 
19. 61 sites in 29 States have been identified for development of tourism infrastructure and 
37 projects have been sanctioned in 24 States and UTs for an amount of Rs. 1214.19 crores under 
this scheme as given in Annexure – II. 17 projects have been completed and 13 projects are in the 
pipeline in 11 states. The major interventions under this Scheme are: - 
Admissible Components 
Tourist Reception / Facilitation Centers 
Public Conveniences, wayside amenities 
Site Illuminations, development / Landscape 
Restoration/ conservation of historic structure/ monuments 
Museums, interpretation centers and socio-cultural spaces 
Open-Air Theatres/ Amphitheaters 
Ghat Developments, Shoreline development/ Rejuvenation of natural water bodies 
First Aid Centers/ Indian Medicines Systems 
Craft Haats/ Bazaars/ Souvenir Shops/ Cafeteria/ Food stalls 
Use of renewable sources of energy/ clean technology/ e-vehicles 
External infrastructure such as water supply, sewerage, drainage, electricity and roads 
 
20. The Ministry informed that some of the challenges faced in execution of the tourism 
infrastructure projects were a delay in land availability and statutory clearances, delayed tendering 
and slow project implementation by State Governments.   The Ministry opined that the challenges 
could be overcome if Stat e Governments carried out due diligence to check land availability and 

8 
statutory clearances and consulted nodal agencies while conceptualizing the projects , ensure 
completion of tendering processes in a time bound manner and have a mechanism for proactive 
project monitoring and reviewing the same to avoid delays in implementation as per agreed 
schedule and in compliance with the approved DPR.  
21. The Committee observes that religious tourism is unlike leisure tourism in as much 
that in building a religious tourism product, it is essential to build in community 
participation at the given location. The participation of local nodal agencies along with State 
Governments in the PRASHAD Scheme is therefore of utmost importance and  the Ministry 
should endeavour to make all efforts to ensure their involvement and not leave it to the 
responsibility of the State Governments alone.  
22. The Committee is of the view religious tourists come from all economic strata and 
there is enormous need for hotels especially in the Budget and Economy categories. The 
Committee is also of the opinion that local families willing to provide homemade food and 
homestay facilities in the ir abodes to the tourists should be identified and given training by 
the Ministry in handling the process  to promote local Indian cuisine among foreign tourists 
and at international level. The Committee is sanguine that such a novel step will unlock job

ASSISTANCE TO CENTRAL AGENCIES SCHEME 
27. The Scheme of ‗Assistance to Central Agencies ‘ (also called Central Financial 
Assistance (CFA)) was proposed to provide financial assistance to the Central Agencies owning 
the assets in Tourism industry  as well as encourage the State Tourism Departments to take major 
IT initiatives as marketing and publicizing their tourist products  so that they develop and upgrade 
basic tourism infrastructure with the aim to: 
a) Improve efficiency at Govt. of India tourist Offices and the Ministry Headquarters 
b) Improve Tourist information to tourists 
a) Improve Tourist facilitation 
28. This Scheme has 55 projects in pipeline with budgetary allocation of Rs. 629.06 Crores 
and has 19 completed projects  till date. The details o f projects sanctioned under this Scheme are 
given in Annexure – III. 
29. The responsibilities of Central Agencies will be to: 
(i) Ensure land availability for development; 
(ii) Implement Rehabilitation package in shifting dwellings or commercial units or provide 
assistance for construction of Tourist Reception Centres to house the displaced shops; 
(iii) Ensure any restoration work is done by experts/specialized agencies only. 
(iv) Submit an Undertaking for providing the necessary assistance to make the land available 
& other allied facilities related to execution of the project. Other authorities/ stakeholder 
shall also submit a letter of authorisation to the Central agency to implement the show on 
their behalf. 
(v) Follow Challenge Method Guidelines to envisage an innovative project and submit the 
project report for consideration. This is to encourage induction of new technology, 
promotion of unique solutions, provide for financially sustainable solutions, and to bring 
in finance and expertise in project execution. This method is to provide transparency and 
induction of Capital for infrastructure where innovative  proposals are received. This is to 
ensure certainty of success under this Methodology. 
(vi) It would be mandatory for the Central Agency who is recipient of the funds released from 
this scheme to put up a signage of the Ministry of Tourism  with the logo ‗Incredible 
India‘ stating that the project has been funded by the Ministry of Tourism. 

10 
30. The Financial sanction by the Ministry of Tourism under this Scheme would be released 
in three installments to the implementing/ central agencies: 
i. First installment – 50% of the Central Financial Assistance amount at the time of sanction 
ii. Second installment- 30% of the sanctioned amount on submission of Utilization Certificate 
of the first installment 
iii. Third installment- 20% of the sanctioned amount on submission of final Utilization 
Certificate by the imple menting agency after the entire work is completed along with an 
affidavit for Management of Assets created and an undertaking for maintenance of the

through Central Financial Assistance to the States/ UTs may require convergence of 
resources, expertise and experience for maintenance and management after development

India, ITDC etc. and the overall development of places of tourist interest under their control 
may not be possible through their own resources. In order to remove these bottlenecks, the 
Committee suggests the Ministry to devise mechanisms to build infrastructure with the 
assistance of state governments and other agencies to bring a world standard spot with all 
the amenities. 
32. The Committee is pleased to note that the Ministry is facilitating development of 
lighthouses as tourist hotspots to provide panoramic view of scenic  coastline and marking 
historic importance of their times through developing museums , open-air amphitheatres,

33. ‗Adopt a Heritage: Apni Dharohar, Apni Pehchaan‘ is a collaborative effort between the 
Ministry of Tourism, Ministry of Culture, Archaeological Survey of India (ASI), and State/UTs 
Governments launched i n 2017, aiming to provide basic amenities including cleanliness, public 
convenience, drinking water, ease of access, signages, TFC, Souvenir Shops, Cafeteria etc.  to 
make sites tourist-friendly and increase its potential by enhancing tourist experience.  
34. The Scheme envisages that selected public sector companies, private sector companies, 
and individuals will develop tourist amenities at heritage sites  and would become ‗Monument 
Mitra‘ by adopting the sites essentially under their Corporate Social Responsi bility (CSR) 
activity. They would also look after the operations and maintenance of the adopted site initially 
for the 5 years subject to review at any time.  29 MoUs have been signed for 29  sites under this 
Scheme as shown in Annexure IV. The main objectives of this Scheme are : 

11 
 Developing basic tourism infrastructure. 
 Inclusive tourist experience for heritage site/monument or tourist site. 
 Promoting cultural and heritage value of the country to generate livelihoods. 
 Enhancing the tourist attractiveness in a sustainable manner through world-class 
infrastructure at the site. 
 Creating employment through the active involvement of local communities. 
 Harnessing tourism potential for its effects in employment generation and economic 
development. 
 Developing sustainable tourism infrastructure and ensuring proper operations and 
maintenance.

opting for a green category monument will have to choose at least one orange or blue category

LAND AVAILABILITY AND STATUTORY CLEARANCE  
45. Tourism development is highly dependent on the availability, quality, quantity and 
characteristics of land, and a plethora of issues like  land acquisition, encroachment,  use of land 
for recreation, conservation, overcrowding and disturbance of local people etc. tend to be 
magnified in developing countries like India where economic transformation and urbanization are 
rapidly going on. 
46. The Committee feels that efficient combination of sea and land accessibility is 
necessary - if not vital – to port activity and to the expansion of wider supply chain systems. 
Taking into account the  land and maritime networks  of the country , the Committee 
recommends that the Ministry should focus on d eveloping port cities for lower logistics 
costs, better infrastructure, and jobs  in the Indian maritime sector . The Committee also 
recommends that the Ministry take h elp of the local administration and  district authorities 
for removal of encroachments at coastline and port peripheries. 
 
CENTRAL ROAD FUND (CRF) 
47. The Central Road Fund (CRF) is used to mainta in State roads interconnecting S tates, 
railway under/over bridges, rural roads, National Highways and Waterways.  The Committee was 
informed that the process to develop highways and roads out of CRF money was ongoing process 
and some of the connectivity projects had already been undertaken by NHAI.

other branches of a country’s economy, without which the travel and tourism industry will 
not reach a desired place of development. The Committee expresses concern over the delay 
in formulation of master plan for roads -railway-port-air connec tivity across the country 
and desires the Ministry to set up a timeline to speed up the process.

tourist spots with road -rail-water-air, which will boost the competitiveness of  India in the 
world tourism market if proper funding and development is expedited in connectivity 
projects. 
50. The Committee is also concerned about lack of funding assistance to states in 
capacity building, which is a major hurdle in elevating India in the r anking of countries 
with maximum tourist satisfaction.

production, services and pricing sectors, opens new gates of employment, resource sharing,

55. Based on scrutiny of the submissions made by way of Background Note and Oral 
Evidences tendered, the Committee makes the following recommendations: 
56. The Committee observes that m odern tourism industry is a key driver of socio -
economic growth through creation of jobs, infrastructure development, and the export 
revenues earned because it has potential to stimulate other sectors through its backward 
and forward linkages and cross -sectoral synergies with airlines, transport, basic 
infrastructure like hotels, guides, road connectivity , agriculture, handicrafts etc.  The 
Committee notes that despite the fact that India offers a diverse portfolio for travel, tourism 
and hospitality, the s hare of its International tourist Arrivals (ITAs) is merely 1.59% in 
2021. With the obvious that there is an increased competition among various countries to 
attract more foreign visitors, it is an imperative need for India to prepare a better 
marketing strategy by hiring marketing experts to attract foreign visitors.  The Committee, 
therefore, recommends that the Ministry should formulate an integrated marketing and 
promotional strategy in collaboration with a professional body to carry out market research 
to identify expectations, requirements, psychographics, demographics and many other 
aspects of a foreign tourist willing to travel to India, thereby enabling to create a strategic 
plan to revive the pandemic-hit tourism sector. The Committee feels that one of the effective 
steps in this direction would be re -casting the website of the Ministry in an attractive and 
user-friendly manner. 
57. Since seaports are the wealth generators of a country and the beauty of landscape 
just increases during Monsoon season, the  Committee is of the view that promoting Seaport 
tourism, Cruise tourism and Monsoon tourism will give a boost to the Indian tourism 
industry.   The Committee also is of the opinion that there is tremendous scope for 
popularizing seaplane services especially among the more affluent travelers who may prefer 
to avoid crowded airport terminals and among adventure tourists.  Seaplane services will 
benefit travelers by providing air connectivity to numerous remote, religious places and 
unexplored places adjacent to water bodies.  

16 
58. The Committee finds that hearing about a place that has never been explored 
before generates a sense of awe and curiosity am ong foreign and domestic travelers alike, 
pulling them towards that place. Curiosity plays a c rucial role in shaping attitude, 
motivation and influencing tourist loyalty. In order to magnify the role of curiosity and 
boost tourism market, the Committee rec ommends that various unexplored/ lesser -known 
tourist spots may be added/ highlighted on the homepage of the Ministry’s website portal to 
attract more tourists to such places. 
59. Tourism Police: The Committee notes that Safety and security of the tourists bot h 
domestic and foreign are paramount importance for projecting the country as a safe haven 
for tourism. There are occasional reports of incidents of misbehaviour, cheating, 
malpractices etc. at various tourist places. This gives a bad publicity for that pa rticular 
tourist destination and the country as a whole. Therefore, it is essential that the Government 
should take all the available measures to provide a safe environment for the tourists. The 
Committee therefore recommends that in every tourist place, t here should be a provision 
for tourism police, as a separate wing of the police force to provide safety and security to the 
tourists. The Committee is fully aware that law and order is a part of the State subject. 
Therefore, the Ministry of Home Affairs should issue an advisory to all the State 
Governments to create tourism police in their State to provide safety and security to the 
tourists in tourist destinations. The Ministry of Tourism should also take up the matter with 
all the State Governments for creation of separate tourism police in their respective States. 
The Committee may be apprised of the action taken by the  Ministry of Home Affairs and 
the Ministry of Tourism and the feedback received from the State Governments  in this 
regard.

infrastructure components like roads, railways, airports, water, electricity, hotels etc.  The 
Committee recommends that interconnectivity of roads, ports, airports, railways and 
waterways should be part of the infrastructure planning process while preparing the 
Detailed Appraisal Report of any Tourism project. Service roads and linkage of  nearby 
places should also be included. Transport infrastructure plays a vital role in connecting 
origin and destination locations while ensuring safe, comfortable and efficient 
transportation to tourists. While evaluating travel experiences, transport is one of the main 
factors which has a great bearing on trip satisfaction. The Committee therefore 
recommends that multi -modal transport should be envisaged while preparing DPR for

to avoid crowded airport terminals and among adventure tourists.  Seaplane services will 

23 
benefit travelers by providing air connectivity to numerous remote, religiou s places and 
unexplored places adjacent to water bodies.  
(Para 57) 
The Committee finds that hearing about a place that has never been explored 
before generates a sense of awe and curiosity among foreign and domestic travelers alike, 
pulling them towards that place. Curiosity plays a crucial role in shaping attitude, 
motivation and influencing tourist loyalty. In order to magnify the role of curiosity and 
boost tourism market, the Committee recommends that various unexplored/ lesser -known 
tourist spots may be added/ highlighted on the homepage of the Ministry’s website portal to 
attract more tourists to such places. 
(Para 58) 
Tourism Police: The Committee notes that Safety and security of the tourists both 
domestic and foreign are paramount importance for p rojecting the country as a safe haven 
for tourism. There are occasional reports of incidents of misbehaviour, cheating, 
malpractices etc. at various tourist places. This gives a bad publicity for that particular 
tourist destination and the country as a who le. Therefore, it is essential that the 
Government should take all the available measures to provide a safe environment for the 
tourists. The Committee therefore recommends that in every tourist place, there should be 
a provision for tourism police, as a s eparate wing of the police force to provide safety and 
security to the tourists. The Committee is fully aware that law and order is a part of the 
State subject. Therefore, the Ministry of Home Affairs should issue an advisory to all the 
State Governments to create tourism police in their State to provide safety and security to 
the tourists in tourist destinations. The Ministry of Tourism should also take up the matter 
with all the State Governments for creation of separate tourism police in their respective  
States. The Committee may be apprised of the action taken by the Ministry of Home 
Affairs and the Ministry of Tourism and the feedback received from the State 
Governments in this regard. 
(Para 59)

1 
REPORT 
1. Barring the slowdown caused in the Civil Aviation sector by the Coronavirus pandemic, 
the aviation sector in India has witnessed tremendous growth in the last decade. Although flying 
is considered to be one of the safest modes of transportation, concerted efforts have to be put in 
to maintain and further improve the highest possible levels of safety in the aviation sector. The 
rapid pace of increase in air traffic across the world brings new challenges that must be resolved 
in order to ensure that the increased traffic can be handled safely and smoothly by minimizing 
chances for both human and mechanical failure to the extent possible. 
2. Given the crucial importance of ensuring topmost safety standards in the aviation sector 
in the country, the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Transport, Tourism 
and Culture decided to take up the subject ‘Issues related to Safety in Civil Aviation Sector’ for 
detailed examination and Report thereon. 
3. In this connection, the Committee heard the views of the Secretary, Ministry of Civil 
Aviation; Director General (DG), Directorate General of Civil Aviation (DGCA); DG, Aircraft 
Accident Information Bureau (AAIB); DG, Bureau of Civil Aviation Security (BCAS); Member, 
Airport Authority of India (AAI); and other senior officials of the Ministry and its various 
organizations, on the subject in its meeting held on 21st December, 2021. 
4. In its written note on the subject, the Ministry informed the Committee that the provision 
of safe & secure air transport services is one of the primary responsibilities of the Ministr y of 
Civil Aviation. The following are the implementing agencies for achieving this objective:- 
 
(i) Directorate General of Civil Aviation 
 
The Directorate General of Civil Aviation is the principal regulatory body in the field of 
civil aviation. It is not only responsible for regulation of air transport services to/ from 
/within India, formulation and enforcement of civil air regulations, air safety and 
airworthiness standards, but also co-ordinates all regulatory functions with International 
Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO). 
 
(ii) Aircraft Accident Investigation Bureau 
 

2 
Aircraft Accident Investigation Bureau (AAIB) was established in 2012 as an 
independent organization from DGCA for investigation of Accidents and Serious 
Incidents. 
 
(iii) Bureau of Civil Aviation Security 
The Bureau of Civil Aviation Security (BCAS) is an attached office of the Ministry o f 
Civil Aviation. The aim of BCAS is to safeguard civil aviation operations against acts of 
unlawful interference. The Bureau is responsible for laying down the standards for 
security in respect of civil flights operating to / from India and ensuring their compliance 
through regular inspections and security audits.  
 
Directorate General of Civil Aviation
 
5. Directorate General of Civil Aviation (DGCA) is the regulatory body in India governing 
safety aspects of civil aviation, which includes certification of airlines and aerodromes, 
airworthiness of aircraft, licensing of personnel, implementation of Safety Management System, 
investigation of incidents and surveillance of aircraft operations in India. Functions of DGCA 
have been derived from the Aircraft Act, 1934 and the Aircraft Rules, 1937. 
6. The Committee enquired from the Ministry regarding the existing mechanism in DGCA 
to prevent aircraft accidents and the bottlenecks and lacunaes in this regard. In its written reply, 
the Ministry informed the Committee that DGCA has taken the following steps to prevent 
aircraft accidents and enhance the level of safety: 
i. Regulatory Audit of Operators: 
Regulatory Audit teams of DGCA periodically carry out regulatory audit of 
operators and maintenance organizations. The deficiencies pointed out in the 
regulatory audit reports are immediately brought to the notice of the operators for 
taking necessary remedial measures. DGCA, in its effort to make the operators 
more responsible for quality control and safety, has stressed that operators should 
also conduct their internal audit apart from DGCA regulatory audit. 
ii. Periodic Spot Checks: 

3 
Periodic spot checks on the operations and maintenance activities of the operators 
have been intensified by DGCA officers to ensure observance of the laid down 
procedures. 
iii. Implementation of Recommendations Emanating from Investigation of Aircraft 
Accidents and Hazardous Incidents: 
Safety recommendations emanating from investigation of various aircraft 
accidents, Serious Accidents and incidents are followed up for implementation 
with the concerned agencies so as to prevent recurrence of similar 
accidents/incidents.  
iv. Issue of Air Safety Circular/Civil Aviation Requirements: 
Accidents/Incidents are regularly analyzed and based on these analyses, Air 
Safety Circulars are issued to bring important observations/findings to the notice 
of the operators to avoid the recurrence of the accidents. Safety precautions are 
also circulated through the Air Safety Circulars. Whenever a requirement is felt, 
regulatory changes are done by issuing Civil Aviation Requirements.  
v. Special Operating Precautions in Poor Weather Conditions: 
Operators and Airport authorities have been advised to take specific actions 
during periods of monsoon and fog. Airline pilots are subjected to special checks 
to ensure their proficiency in monsoon conditions. 
vi. Prevention of Bird Strike Incidents: 
Continuous efforts are being made in association with airport authorities and local 
civic authorities to take effective measures to reduce bird strike menace.  
vii. Action against defaulters: 
Whenever it is found that there is a gross violation of the laid down norms or 
compromise of safety, strict action is taken against the defaulters. 
7. The Committee notes the mechanism existing at present in order to prevent air craft 
accidents and thus ensure safety in civil aviation. The Committee recommends that the 
DGCA must regularly coordinate with AAI, various airport operators and airline 
operators and ensure the implementation of its specifications and guidelines regardin g 
aviation safety. State- of-art technology may be installed and utilized for prevention of 
aircraft accidents/ malfunctioning. The Committee further recommends that the Ministry 

4 
may ensure that the budgetary allocation made to DGCA is sufficient to meet its 
requirements and it does not face any budgetary shortfall. Due focus may also be lai d on 
ensuring that the human resource requirements of DGCA are met at all times so that it can 
effectively carry out the important mandate of ensuring safety in the civil aviation sector in 
the country. 
8. The Committee desires to be apprised of the past aircraft/helicopter accidents in the 
country or involving Indian airlines. The Committee may also be informed about the 
guidelines issued by DGCA in view of aircraft/helicopter accidents in India and the 
monitoring mechanism in place for implementation of the same by the concerned 
organizations across the country. 
 
Safety of Air Transport Operations
 
9. The Ministry, in its written note, informed the Committee that in line with the standards 
laid down by ICAO, following processes are put in place for ensuring safety of air transport 
operations: 
(a)  Issuance of Air Operator’s Certificate: 
ICAO Annex 6 lays down the standards for the operation of aircraft. Accordingly, 
before carrying out air transport operations in India, a prospective operator is required to 
comply with this Annex. Schedule XI of the Aircraft Rules, 1937 lays down the 
requirements for grant of an Air Operator’s Certificate (AOC) for scheduled operations. 
The detailed requirements for the issuance of a permit are contained in the Civil Aviation 
Requirements and involve a number of steps leading to issuance of an Air Operator’s 
Certificate (AOC) by DGCA under Rule 134 of the Aircraft Rules, 1937. The steps 
involved in the process of the issuance of the AOC includes issuance of an initial No 
Objection Certificate (NOC) for starting an airline, setting up of the facilities and 
infrastructure by the proposed operator, grant of permission for import/acquisition of 
aircraft and the issuance of Air Operator's Certificate. Before the AOC is issued, DGCA 
ensures compliance with safety requirements (operational and airworthiness).  

5 
(b)  Airworthiness of an aircraft:  
(i)  ICAO Annex 8 lays down the standards for the airworthiness of aircraft. 
The Aircraft Rules, 1937 state that no civil aircraft shall be flown unless it is 
certified as airworthy and is maintained in an airworthy condition. DGCA issues 
Certificate of Airworthiness (C of A), under the provisions of rules, to an 
individual aircraft signifying that the aircraft conforms to its applicable type 
design and is in a condition for safe operation. The C of A is issued only after an 
inspection to ensure that the aircraft is of approved Type Design and has been 
maintained in accordance with periodic inspection schedules stipulated by the 
manufacturer of the aircraft.           
During the course of validity of Certificate of Airworthiness (C of A) of 
an aircraft, officers of DGCA monitor routine maintenance, major checks and 
significant defects through spot checks and surveillance.   
(ii)  The maintenance of aircraft is required to be carried out by an organisation 
specifically approved by DGCA for the purpose. For approval, an organisation 
requires proper infrastructure, appropriate tools including special tools, updated 
manufacturer’s documents and aircraft maintenance engineers holding appropriate 
licences for the maintenance work. Aircraft Maintenance Organisations are 
approved for specific ‘Scope of Work’ and approval is valid for five years. The 
approvals are renewed after an inspection to ensure that the capability of the 
organisation has not deteriorated. The organisation is required to show that they 
have carried out an internal audit and have rectified the deficiencies found during 
their internal audit. 
(c) Licensing of Personnel: 
ICAO Annex 1 stipulates International Standards and Recommended Practices for 
licensing various categories of Pilots, other Flight crew members, Aircraft Maintenance 
Engineers, Air Traffic Controllers etc. These standards have four features namely i) 
Minimum Age for a licence, ii) Knowledge, iii) Experience, and iv) Skill Test. In case of 

6 
licensing of Flight Crew members and Air Traffic Controllers, Medical Standards have 
also been stipulated. Indian regulations meet ICAO standards. In addition, Indian 
regulations stipulate minimum education qualifications in respect of pilots and aircraft 
maintenance engineers. DGCA conducts written examinations to test the knowledge of 
the applicant. Syllabus for these examinations is as prescribed by ICAO. Online/ OMR 
based computerised system is used for the examination. 
(d) Safety management system: 
ICAO Annex 19 requires that all approved maintenance organisations as well as 
commercial air operators are required to establish a safety management system for the 
identification of hazards and associated risks and take adequate mitigation actions. The 
ICAO SARPs are contained in Rule 29D of the Aircraft Rules 1937 and relevant Civil 
Aviation Requirements. Accordingly, during the course of day- to-day activities, these 
approved organisations identify hazards and take corrective/ mitigating measures. 
(e) Licencing of Aerodrome: 
 
ICAO Annex 14 lays down the Standards and Recommended Practices (SARPs) 
for developments of aerodromes. DGCA has issued requirements for licensing of 
aerodrome through Civil Aviation Requirement section 4 series F Part-I. Inspection of 
aerodromes to verify infrastructure, services, procedures and documentation are carried 
out periodically as per annual surveillance program. 
10. The Committee recommends that the Ministry may review the efficiency of the 
mechanism presently in place for implementation of the processes recommended by ICAO 
for safety of air transport operations, from time to time so that these processes are 
implemented by the concerned organizations in letter and spirit. DGCA may hold 
periodical meetings with the stakeholders involved in the implementation of such processes 
and iron out any difficulties/bottlenecks being faced in following the processes laid down 
under the various ICAO Annexes. Concrete timelines may be prescribed by DGCA for 
effectuating any changes made by ICAO in its Annexes so as to ensure that best possible 
safety practices are employed in the Indian civil aviation sector. 

7 
11. The Committee feels that the licensing of personnel including pilots, other Fli ght 
crew members, Aircraft Maintenance Engineers, Air Traffic Controllers etc. is a cru cial 
process with a direct effect on the safety of the air transport operations in the country and  
thus utmost care must be taken to ensure that the licensing process for all such personn el is 
carried out strictly as per the established norms. The licences thus issued should  be 
renewed periodically after carrying out necessary inspection and tests necessary for su ch 
approval. The Committee further recommends that training programmes may be arranged 
for different aviation sector personnel from time to time in order to keep them  updated 
regarding the best safety practices in the aviation sector. 
 
Safety of Workers/Employees including those operating the Aircraft
 
12. The Ministry apprised the Committee that the following measures based on the 
regulations are in place to ensure safety of workers/ employees including those operating the 
aircraft: 
(a) Safety of aircraft operations:  
The maintenance of aircraft is carried out by an approved organisation. For the 
maintenance of aircraft, the manufacturer of the aircraft provides detailed procedures 
including timelines for carrying out the maintenance which form part of the approved 
maintenance programme of the operator. On detection of a fault, the fault is corrected 
based on manufacturer’s recommendation and the aircraft thereby maintains continuous 
airworthiness for continuing operations. 
On completion of the maintenance, the aircraft is released by an appropriately licensed 
maintenance engineer to certify that all checks due on the aircraft have been carried out 
in accordance with the manufacturer’s maintenance manual and any faults/ malfunction s 
have been duly rectified. 
(b) Operation of aircraft by a pilot: 

8 
An aircraft is flown by a pilot who is licensed on the type of aircraft. The safety of a pilot 
operating the aircraft is ensured by a number of means. These include: 
(i) Maintenance of currency on the aircraft during the period of validity of the 
pilot licence as per the laid down regulatory requirements. 
(ii) Providing continuous training during the lifetime of the pilot. Various 
regulations on crew training and operations provide for detailed training 
curriculum to be followed, which ensure safety of both the individual concerned 
and the organization. Training is conducted in the following manner: 
1. Initial Training     
2. Recurrent Training        
3. Specialised Training 
4. Training on aviation security, the same is conducted by BCAS 
5. Training on handling & recognition of dangerous goods 
The goal of training is to ensure that all employees are safe in the area of 
operations dealt by them. 
(iii) Ensuring the pilot is physically and mentally alert before undertaking any 
flight by providing adequate opportunity for rest by way of Flight Duty Time 
Limitation: 
The same is ensured through regulations both for cockpit crew and for the cabin 
crew. The regulations address minimum rest post a flight, maximum allowable 
flight duty & duty periods on a weekly, monthly & annual basis. Through the 
implementation of regulation within the organization, safety of aircraft and its 
occupants is ensured by having well rested crew members on duty.        
(iv) Ensuring the pilot is not in an inebriated state before undertaking any flight 
by mandatorily conducting a breath analyser check:  
The regulations lay down the procedure to be followed for the breath-analyser 
examination of the crew members for consumption of alcohol and actions to be 

9 
taken by the operators. It also dwells on the procedure to be followed by the 
authorities concerned in the event of an accident. 
Through the regulations, it is ensured that no crew member operates the  flight in 
an intoxic ated state. With strict implementation of this regulation, individual’s 
and the organisation’s safety is ensured. 
(v) Monitoring the performance of the pilot through a system established by the 
operator in accordance with the requirements stipulated by the DGCA: 
Any adverse indications, which may affect safety of the aircraft operation are 
proactively detected and corrective action is taken. 
(c) The cabin crew onboard the aircraft undergoes training on safety and emergency 
procedures for ensuring the safety of aircraft operation. 
13. While the Committee feels that the mechanism presently in place to ensure safety of 
workers/ employees including those operating the aircraft, is satisfactory, steps may be 
taken to review the same from time to time to avoid any complacency. The curriculum of 
the training programme for the aviation sector workers/ employees may also be refreshed 
from time to time and best global safety practices may be incorporated in the same.

increased in order to ensure that the guidelines and instructions issued by DGCA are

Accident Investigation
 
18. The Ministry, in its written note, stated that International Standards of ICAO stipulates 
that the purpose of investigation should be prevention of similar accident in future. Indian 
regulations regarding aircraft accident investigation are laid down in the Aircraft (Investigation 
of Accidents and Incidents) Rules, 2017 and are in accordance with the ICAO standards. An 
independent aircraft accident investigation organisation ‘Aircraft Accident Investigation Bureau’ 
(AAIB) has been set-up for the investigation of serious incidents and accidents under the 
Ministry of Civil Aviation. AAIB investigates all accidents and serious incidents involving 
aircraft with ‘All Up Weight’ more than 2250 Kgs and gives safety recommendations. AAIB 
also makes “Safety Recommendations” on the basis of safety studies conducted from time to 
time. For the investigation of major accidents of public importance, the Central Government has 
the power to set up Court of Inquiry for investigation. To fulfil its obligation under ICAO Annex 
19, DGCA investigates incidents and serious incidents to the aircraft with ‘All Up Weight’ up to 
2250 kg. 

11 
19. The Committee notes that Aircraft Accident Investigation Bureau (AAIB) has been 
allocated a meager allocation of Rs. 1 crore, against its projected requirement of Rs. 4.40  
crore in B.E. 2022-23. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Ministry may 
request the Ministry of Finance to provide AAIB with higher allocation at the R.E. 2022-23 
stage so as to enable it to perform its functions in the desired manner and contribute 
towards improving the safety aspect of the civil aviation sector in India. 
20. The Committee further recommends that the Ministry may ensure that the 
methodologies adopted and technology used by AAIB for investigation of aircraft acciden ts

similar accidents do not recur in the country.

provided to collect Bio hazardous garbage. Bio hazardous waste is being disposed

Air Traffic Controllers (ATCOs)
 
30. The Ministry informed the Committee that although Airport Tower Controllers or 
terminal controllers watch the overall movement of aircraft travelling through the 
airport’s airspace, their main responsibility is to organize the flow of aircraft into and out 

16 
of the airport. The controller in the radar room, just beneath the control tower, has a copy 
of the plane’s flight plan and has the plane on radar. After each plane departs, airport 
tower controllers notify enroute controllers who will take charge next. If two planes are 
scheduled to enter the team’s airspace at nearly the same time, location, and altitude, this 
controller may arrange with the preceding control unit for one plane to change its flight 
path. As a plane approaches a team’s airspace, the radar controller accepts responsibility 
for the plane from the previous controlling unit. The controller also delegates 
responsibility for the plane to the next controlling unit when the plane leaves the team’s 
airspace. 
31. The Committee feels that Airport Traffic Controllers play an indispensable role in 
the safe operations of aircrafts. The Committee notes that there is a backlog of 
vacancies in the post of ATCOs. The Committee is of the opinion that the demand 
for ATCOs will rise exponentially with the growth of the aviation sector in the 
country and feels that the Ministry should have anticipated the requirement of more 
number of ATCOs well in advance and inducted ATCOs continuously over the 
years. The Committee, therefore, recommends that procedural issues regarding 
manpower requirements of ATCOs should be addressed in a proactive way to 
ensure operationalization of new airports that are being constructed in near future 
do not suffer due to lack of ATCOs. 
 
Night Landing
 
32. The Ministry apprised the Committee that Runway lighting system is one of the critical 
part of airport lighting system for night landing. The types of lights used include the 
following:  
a) Approach lights are the first that pilot will reach during landing and are of white colour, 
unidirectional, blinking or steady type of lights. 
b) The threshold lights of green colour of unidirectional type, installed at the beginning of 
the runway. 
c) Runway end lights which identify the end of a runway. Runway end lights are 
unidirectional red colour aviation lights. 

17 
d) Runway edge lights which are located on the left and right sides of a runway (edges) and 
illuminate the part of the runway for safe landings. 
e) Precision Approach Path Indicator (PAPI): These lights are normally located on the left 
side of the runway. Each PAPI light usually consists of four lighting fixtures (4 x Li ght 
Assemblies). 
f) Obstruction aviation lights are red colour omni-directional lights that illuminate airport 
buildings, observations, closed areas, temporarily unavailable area on the airfield. 
33. The Ministry further informed that airports with non-precision runways usually install a 
simple runway lighting system that includes runway edge lights, PAPI lights, runway 
threshold end lights, aerodrome beacon, Apron floodlighting and taxiway lights. 
34. In view of the significant safety that Instrument Landing System offers in landing of 
aircrafts at night time or in bad weather conditions, the Committee recommends 
that the Ministry may make arrangements for installation of Instrument Landing 
Systems at all functional airports across the country at the earliest and a strict 
timeline may be devised for the same. The Ministry of Civil Aviation may work 
closely with the Ministry of Defence to ensure that approvals, if any, that might be 
needed for installation of ILS at civil enclaves, are processed in a time-bound, 
streamlined manner so as to avoid undue delays. 
 
 
Air India Express Crash at Kozhikode Airport
 
35. The Ministry informed the Committee that Air India Express operated a flight AXB 
1343/1344 on Kozhikode-Dubai-Kozhikode sector on 07 August, 2020 using a Boeing 
737-800 type of aircraft with registration VT-AXH. The flight was operated under 
‘Vande Bharat Mission’ by an ATPL holder PIC and a CPL holder Co -Pilot, to repatriate 
passengers from Dubai who were stranded due to the closure of airspace and international 
flight operations. The aircraft during final approach, landing and landing roll overshot the 
runway at Calicut. The aircraft could not stop on the runway and went down the slope 
beyond the runway end safety area (RESA). There were 184 passengers, 2 Pilots and 4 
Cabin Crew onboard. The 02 pilots and 19 passengers (17 adults and 02 Infants) 

18 
succumbed to injuries. 165 passengers and 4 cabin crew members sustained injuries. The 
Aircraft Accident Investigation Bureau (AAIB) had ordered an investigation on 
13th August, 2020  to inquire into the circumstances of the Air India Express crash at 
Kozhikode Airport for determining the probable cause and contributory factors leading 
to the accident. The Final Investigation Report was submitted on 17 Aug 2021 and was 
accepted by DG, AAIB on 20 th August, 2021. As per findings in the report, the direct 
cause of the accident is as under:- 
“The probable cause of the accident was the non-adherence to SOP by the PF, wherein, 
he continued an unstabilized approach and landed beyond the touchdown zone, half way 
down the runway, in spite of ‘Go Around’ call by PM which warranted a mandatory ‘Go 
Around’ and the failure of the PM to take over controls and execute a ‘Go Around’.” 
36. The Ministry further informed that a committee has been constituted by the Ministry of 
Civil Aviation co-opting aviation experts to oversee the implementation of the recommendations 
made in the report of the investigation conducted by AAIB in the accident at Kozhikode Airport 
and the execution of the steps required for implementation of the recommendations. One of the 
mandates of the committee is to study the feasibility of operation of wide-body aircraft at 
Kozhikode airport and to give its recommendations thereof. The committee is yet to submit its 
final report. 
37. The Committee would like to emphasize upon the need to ensure that runway 
accidents such as the ones that happened in Mangalore (May, 2020) and Calicut (August, 
2020) do not recur. The Committee recommends that the latest advanced technological 
instruments should be installed at all the airports in the country so that there is smooth and 
safe landing during thick fog conditions, when there is near zero visibility. It has come to 
the notice of the Committee that the Report on the aircraft accidents sometimes take too 
long to be finalized. The Committee feels that a strict timeline should be pre scribed for 
submission of final report after an accident has occurred since laxity in the same can  cause 
accidents happening because of similar reasons, which could otherwise be avoid ed if the 
actual reason is known at the earliest and steps are taken timely to ensure that similar 
instances do not recur.

Unmanned Aircraft Systems 
38. The Ministry informed the Committee that  Unmanned Aircraft Systems (UAS), 
commonly known as drones, offer tremendous benefits to almost all sectors of the 
economy like – agriculture, mining, infrastructure, surveillance, emergency response, 
transportation, geo-spatial mapping, defence, and law enforcement etc.  Drones can be 
significant creators of employment and economic growth due to their reach, versatility, 
and ease of use, especially in India’s remote and inaccessible areas. In view of its 
traditional strengths in innovation, information technology, frugal engineering and huge 
domestic demand, India has the potential to be a global drone hub. In order to encourage 
usage of drones while maintaining a safe and secure ecosystem for the same, the 
following steps have been taken:- 
(i)    Drone certification
 
The provisions for drone certification are as under: 
a)    The Director General or an entity authorised by the Director General, on the 
recommendation of Quality Council of India (QCI), may issue a type certificate for 
any particular type of unmanned aircraft system, on an application filed by a 
manufacturer or importer on the digital sky platform, if such type of unmanned 
aircraft system meets the specified certification standards. 
b)    Any standards and processes notified by the QCI for the certification of drones as 
well as all hardware and technical requirements prescribed shall be designed to 
further the ease of doing business and shall be commensurate to the purposes for 
which such drone can be utilised. 
c)    QCI or the authorised testing entity shall examine the proposal and submit the test 
report and its recommendations to the Director General within 60 days of the date of 
application. 

20 
d)    Based on the test report of QCI or the authorised testing entity, the Director General, 
shall issue a type certificate for the specific type of unmanned aircraft system, to the 
applicant, within 15 days of receiving the test report. 
e)    A six-month lead time for installing mandatory safety features on drones may be 
provided which shall include 'No Permission – No Takeoff' (NPNT) hardware and 
firmware; real-time tracking beacon; and geo-fencing capability. 
(ii)  Drone Registration
 
The provisions for drone registration are as under: 
a)    No person shall operate a drone without a Unique Identification Number (UIN). The 
Digital Sky Platform shall verify the details and issue UIN to the applicant. 
b)    In order to register a drone, an individual (or Director in case of a corporate entity) 
will only need to submit the Indian passport number, Aadhaar, DIN (for corporate 
entity), mobile number, the unique serial number provided by the manufacturer; 
unique serial numbers of its flight control module and remote pilot station and three 
photographs of the drone on the Digital Sky Platform.  No prior security clearance of 
the individual or entity shall be required. 
(iii) Airspace map
 
The Government has published an airspace map on the Digital Sky Platform for drone 
operations segregating the entire airspace of India into red zones, yellow zones and green  
zones.  
a)    Red zone means the airspace of defined dimensions, above the land areas or 
territorial waters of India, or any installation or notified port limits specified by the 
Central Government beyond the territorial waters of India, within which unmanned 
aircraft system operations shall be permitted only by the Central Government. 

21 
b)    Yellow zone means the airspace of defined dimensions above the land areas or 
territorial waters of India within which unmanned aircraft system operations are 
restricted and shall require permission from the concerned air traffic control authority. 
The airspace above 400 feet or 120 meter in the designated green zone and the 
airspace above 200 feet or 60 meter in the area located between the lateral distance of 
8 kilometer and 12 kilometer from the perimeter of an operational airport, shall be 
designated as yellow zone. 
c)    Green zone means the airspace of defined dimensions above the land areas or 
territorial waters of India, upto a vertical distance of 400 feet or 120 meter that has 
not been designated as a red zone or yellow zone in the airspace map for unmanned 
aircraft system operations and the airspace upto a vertical distance of 200 feet or 60 
meter above the area located between a lateral distance of 8 kilometer and 12 
kilometer from the perimeter of an operational airport. 
(iv)  Penalties
 
 a) Penalty shall not exceed Rs. 1 lakh  
b) Criminal prosecution for serious offences  
c) Violating zone restrictions and carrying arms, ammunition etc. shall be cognizable 
d) IPC and other applicable laws shall apply concurrently. 
39. The Ministry further submitted that airspace map for drone operations shall be designed 
to be programmatically accessible and interactive so that remote pilots will be able to plot 
their proposed flight plan and easily identify the zone(s) within which it falls so as to 
assess whether or not they need to make an application for prior approval. 
40. The Committee appreciates the introduction of liberalized Drone Rules by the 
Ministry and feels that the same will bring much-needed clarity and regulation for 
the drone industry which is rapidly gaining traction in India and across the world. 
The Committee recommends that the Ministry may come up with policy provisions 
for the promotion of local manufacture of drones in the country, working in

Audits by international agencies
 
45. With regard to audits by international agencies, the Ministry furnished the following 
information: 
(i) International Civil Aviation Organisation
 (ICAO): 
 
a) International Civil Aviation Organisation (ICAO) is a specialized agency of 
UNO. It works to achieve its vision of safe, secure and sustainable development 
of civil aviation through the cooperation of its Member States. ICAO has been 
created to promote the safe and orderly development of international civil aviation 
throughout the world. It sets standards and regulations necessary for: 
● aviation safety,  
● security,  
● efficiency and regularity 
● aviation environmental protection 

24 
b) ICAO conducts regular, mandatory, systematic and harmonized safety audits of 
all the contracting States under its Universal Safety Oversight Audit Program- 
Continuous Monitoring Approach (USOAP-CMA) to ensure that the States are 
fulfilling their obligation of safety oversight under the Chicago Convention. 
 
c) Effective Implementation (EI) based on the last ICAO Audit conducted in 
November 2018 is 71.86%. The present EI score is 72.93%. 
 
d) ICAO will conduct an audit of India in 2022 in the areas of legislation, 
organization, personnel licensing, aircraft operations and airworthiness. 
 
(ii) Federal Aviation Administration
 (FAA): 
 
a) Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) of USA conducts audit under its Internal 
Aviation Safety Assessm ent (IASA) program. It determines whether another country’s 
oversight of its air carriers that operate, or seek to operate, into the U.S., or codeshare 
with a U.S. air carrier, complies with safety standards established by ICAO. 
 
b) Under ‘International Aviation Safety Assessment’ (IASA), FAA audited India in October 
2021 and raised 36 findings. 
 
c) DGCA is taking action to address the findings. 
d) Final Consultations are scheduled for January 2022, post which IASA rating will be 
determined by FAA. 
e) Currently, India’s IASA rating is Category 1. 
46. The Ministry informed the Committee that India, is a signatory to the Chicago 
Convention, 1944, and, as a Contracting State is required to adhere to International 
Standards and Recommended Practices (SARPs) of International Civil Aviation 
Organisation (ICAO). SARPs contained in the ICAO Annexes and other related ICAO 
documents have been adopted to lay down rules, regulations and requirements in the form 
of the Aircraft Act, 1934 and the Aircraft Rules, 1937, The Aircraft (Demolition of 
obstructions caused by Buildings and Trees etc.) Rules, 1994, the Aircraft (Carriage of 
Dangerous Goods) Rules, 2003, Civil Aviation Requirements, Aeronautical Information 
Circulars (AIC), etc. India has adopted most of the International standards of ICAO.
